item.description:
## 一个让人意外的观察：这不是"制造业回流"，而是"**消费者补贴国防**"的历史性反转
过去 80 年美国的技术扩散逻辑是：政府出钱做第一代（阿波罗、互联网、核能），然后"长尾"溢出到消费市场。但这期对话里埋着一个几乎没被明说的、方向相反的新模式——**国防买单，但消费者最终定义质量上限**。Aaron 那句"美国最大的礼物是美国消费者的挑剔"，和 Conor 讲的"国防承担前 100 件的高单价 CapEx"，拼在一起等于说：
> 政府不再是技术的*定义者*，而是技术的*融资者*；真正把东西逼到便宜又好用的，是消费电子级的客户纪律。
这其实是把一个军工复合体，重新组装成一个**由消费者精细度反向驱动的、以国防订单做种子轮的通用工业栈**。DJI 的轨迹（消费无人机 → 国防 → 人形机器人执行器）不是巧合，而是这个新物理定律的第一个经验数据点。
## 跨领域连接：这波"美国动能"的底层结构，和 **Y Combinator 早期的 Silicon Valley 像到诡异**
Aaron 自己在最后半不经意地说出了关键隐喻："人们嘲笑 YC 公司互相卖东西，但生态就是这么

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller: Turning Stranded Energy Into Intelligence
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Bitcoin 不是"旧业务"，而是一台把电子变成现金的套利机器——AI 真正到来之前的融资工具

大多数人把 Crusoe 卖掉比特币业务读作"转型 AI"。但 Chase 自己把这段历史讲得很清楚：比特币从来不是业务，而是现金流泵。

真正的论点一直是——"用计算把搁浅能源变成市场"。油井旁被点燃的伴生气、冰岛过剩的地热、北欧低价水电——这些都是没人愿意要的电子。比特币挖矿恰好是人类发明过的最流动、最 24/7、最不挑剔的"电子变现引擎"：它不要求你有光纤，不要求你有客户，只要你有瓦特。

于是真正发生的事情是：Crusoe 用一台金融抽水机，把世界各地无人问津的电子抽成资本，再在 ChatGPT 这个历史时刻来临时，把积累的能源头寸转化成 AI 工厂。

这几乎是一个"打井是为了造油轮"的操作顺序倒置。类比：亚马逊早年卖书不是终局，而是训练仓储肌肉；SpaceX 搞 Starlink 是为了资助去火星。比特币对 Crusoe 的角色属于同一个物种——用一个成熟市场为一个尚未诞生的市场做财务预热。

二、他爬珠峰的方式，就是他建数据中心的方式——意外的"随机风险 vs 自觉风险"二分法

这是整段访谈里最被低估的洞见，Chase 自己都没有说破：

2014 年珠峰雪崩之后，他和搭档没有按商业队的标准路线走——因为标准路线要在最危险的昆布冰瀑穿越 8 次。他们重新设计了方案：到附近的山上做适应性训练，把冰瀑的穿越次数从 8 次压缩到 4 次。

他的原话是："我愿意承担的是我能通过训练管理的风险，我不愿意承担的是冰柱随机掉下来砸到我的风险（stochastic risk）。"

现在把这句话原封不动地搬到 Crusoe 的能源策略上：

  • 建在电网背后（behind-the-meter）——减少对电网互联这一随机变量的暴露（少过几次冰瀑）
  • 用天然气、SMR 核能、地热、小型模块化发电——自己可训练、可管理的风险
  • 不对单一技术路线下重注——类似他在珠峰上同时携带多套适应方案

绝大多数能源公司和数据中心公司对"风险"的定价是单维的（成本/收益）；Chase 的定价是风险的来源结构——这个心智模型几乎可以肯定来自雪崩那年。那场雪崩杀死了 15 名夏尔巴人，也许同时塑造了一家公司的架构。

三、他是在做"极端环境资本主义"——跨界到生物学的隐藏结构

你注意到了吗？Crusoe 建数据中心的地点有一个共同点：都是其他生物不去的地方。

  • 北达科他州巴肯油田（燃烧放空的废气）
  • 冰岛（火与冰的无人区）
  • 挪威（过剩水电）
  • 爱达荷国家实验室（SMR 实验堆旁边）

这在生物学上有一个精确的对应词——嗜极生物（extremophile）。它们不与主流物种竞争阳光和温带，而是寄生在深海热泉、火山口、永冻层。它们的生存策略不是"更强"，而是"去没人想去的地方，吃没人想吃的能量"。

Chase 的公司在做的事情，本质上是嗜极资本主义：在能源价格为负、甚至为负负（排放责任）的地方，长出一个计算物种。

这个框架同时也解释了他为什么对竞争几乎零焦虑——嗜极生物从不卷。热泉管虫不与珊瑚竞争，它们的生态位根本不重叠。当他说"我们更多的是在互相帮助而不是互相竞争"时，这不是公关辞令，这是生态位几何学的事实陈述。

四、一个让人不舒服的隐藏命题："人线性成长，公司指数成长"

他引用的 First Round 的一句话，是整期播客里最接近热力学第二定律的论断：

People scale linearly, companies scale exponentially.

这意味着什么？意味着即使你的每一位早期员工每天都在进步，他们在数学上注定会落后于一家真正在爆发的公司。 这不是品格问题，不是努力问题——是成长曲线函数形式的不匹配。

这解释了一个所有 CEO 都私下承认但很少公开说的残酷事实：你和创业初期最忠诚的战友，大概率要在某个时点分开——不是因为谁背叛了谁，而是因为公司生长在指数函数上，而人只能活在线性时间里。

这跟进化生物学里的一个概念几乎同构："红皇后假说"——你必须拼命奔跑，才能停留在原地。但 Chase 的版本更冷酷：即便你拼命奔跑，公司跑得比你更快。

五、最意外的观察：他的整个职业生涯是在系统性地反转自己的舒适区

量化基金做的是什么？保密、技术、不公开说话、不告诉任何人你的 alpha。 CEO 做的是什么？公开、政治、不断重复、把自己掏空给媒体和社区听证会。

Chase 从一个最反社交、最隐秘的职业，走到了最公众、最沟通密集的职业。他承认公开演讲"从来不是自然的事"，承认他需要教练来撬开自己。

这是一个比"从量化到创业"更深的身份反转——他把自己整个认知操作系统做了相反方向的刷机。而他的教练 Shane 扮演的角色，和他 2018 年在珠峰 8,600 米处的搭档扮演的角色，是同一个：在你准备放弃的那个海拔，有一个人让你继续走。

Crusoe 公司的核心价值观里有一条叫"think like a mountaineer"——现在你知道了，这不是比喻。这家公司的组织文化，字面意义上是从昆布冰瀑搬下山来的。

📝 转录文本

开场：垂直整合的复杂业务

We have a complex business because it's vertically integrated and it spans like a huge scope of different work streams. Everything from energy generation and bringing electrons online, building power plants, working with independent power producers and utilities to building data centers, operating at scale very large scale AI factories to very small scale AI factories and then building and operating a managed AI cloud platform with managed AI services.

What's made me very scalable as a leader is that we have these critical areas of domain expertise where I can move around and I can go very deep with any individual but I trust them a lot to be making the right decisions as we're sort of scaling things and everybody has a broad perspective of you know what we're doing at the macro scale and how each individual leader contributes to that vertically integrated AI infrastructure platform that we're building here at Crusoe.

嘉宾介绍

Okay, everybody. Today we have on Chase Lockach Miller. Russo is building so many of the data centers that power the age of intelligence. He's a very professional CEO and he talks all about the road from zero beginnings to a $31 billion valuation that he just closed. He gets into the nuts and bolts of scaling a very operationally intensive business. I think you're going to like it.

Chase, welcome to the long strange trip. — Brian, thanks for having me.

一条非线性的职业轨迹

We call this the long strange trip because my journey as a CEO was a very long strange trip. Kind of tracking your career. You've had a long maybe not strange but interesting trip like you were on track to become a professor. You became a hedge fund trader. You became a mountaineer climbing Mount Everest among other things. You're kind of an energy entrepreneur at least through my lens when you first got going and now you're the world's best data center builder. Is there a through line in all of this?

Chase: Um, as a person, I've always been uh attracted to trying to solve hard problems. That's I think that's been the throughline of my career. Take on big challenges, solve hard problems that are exciting and inspiring to me.

CEO 的"温水煮青蛙"优势

One hard problem is becoming a CEO and scaling as a CEO is in and of itself is a hard problem. What has surprised you about, you know, all of a sudden you're a CEO and you got to build this company? What is what what do people have wrong about the CEO journey?

It can sometimes be misleading to just take a snapshot of someone like deep into it and and just assume it's some linear path on on on how you actually get there. I was actually having this discussion with another CEO. you know, when you're a founder CEO, you sort of have this benefit of uh sort of, you know, the the boiling frog syndrome where, you know, right now things are really crazy at Cruso. There's just so much happening. Everything's happening very quickly. The scale at which it's happening is crazy.

Uh, you know, when people get dropped into Crusoe and they start working at Crusoe, it's like it's intense and there's there's just a lot going on across the company. And you know there's a question of like how do you actually hold that all in one person's head and you know when you're the founder CEO you have so much context of like the history of how you got here and it wasn't always this crazy right like when we first started it was just me and my co-founder it was just the two of us for for for you know quite a while and then we you know had our first hire and we had our first you know incremental hires and you know when we were 10 people it felt crazy but it's nothing compared to what it is today.

And the journey of a CEO is journey of a founder CEO is like you have to continually be upping your game. You have to be continually investing in yourself to be able to scale if if you want to have a scaled business. And you know this is partially reflected like you know at Cruso we have a core company value that's like live on the infinite growth loop — like nobody is nobody's a finished product right no nothing we've done here is a finished product uh everything is a work in progress every person is a work in progress and every single day we try to improve on who we were yesterday and if you look at those compounding returns of those continuous focus on improvements and how how you actually get better when you zoom back out over you know the course of a month, a year, five years. Uh the results can be astounding.

"我的业务复杂得让我头晕"

Okay. My I had an actually I had quite an interesting day today. I run something called the kids table and the adults table for SEOA. And it's basically getting a bunch of CEOs together, all founder CEOs to kind of talk about their problems and try to help each other with the journey. And we've got a bunch of them between 20 and 2,000 employees. All of them are ripping, like really ripping. And I got a quote from one of the CEOs today. My business is becoming dizzyingly complex beneath me. How the hell do I keep up? Did you do you have that feeling today or did you have that feel?

I had that I had that feeling. If someone were to take me off the streets and parachute me in and drop me in and say, "Hey, go run this company, Cruso." I would absolutely 100% have that have that dizzying, paralyzing anxiety feeling. Um, I actually feel great about where we're at within Cruso because I've been there for every step of the journey and I've been able to surround myself with incredibly dynamic and capable leaders that I'm able to offload and trust a lot of responsibility and resources to.

And you know we we sort of you know we have a complex business because it's vertically integrated and it spans like a huge scope of different work streams. Everything from you know energy generation and you know bringing electrons online building power plants working with independent power producers and utilities to building data centers operating at scale very large scale AI factories to very smallcale AI factories and then building and operating a managed AI cloud platform and with managed AI services.

It's it's a whole wide spectrum of uh different employees and you know we have factories where we're manufacturing critical electrical equipment for data centers and then we have uh AI researchers that are working on the best most effective ways to serve and host AI models and manage the KV cache and uh you know there's there's a whole bunch of different different folks in between.

So what's made me very scalable as a leader is that I have been able to find domain experts in each of these key verticals from energy, data centers, manufacturing and AI cloud computing. And if you look at the the the folks here at Crusoe, we have these critical areas of domain expertise where individually I can I can move around and I can go very deep with any individual. Uh but I trust them a lot to be making the right decisions as we're sort of scaling things and everybody has a at least a broad perspective um of you know what we're doing at the macro scale and how each individual component each individual leader uh contributes to that broader vertically integrated AI infrastructure platform that we're building here at Crusoe.

信任与 DRI（Directly Responsible Individual）

Trust is an interesting word. We talked about it on the call. Actually I just finished a call before this. I kind of said to everybody like how many people in your organization do you deeply trust enough to say you're the DRI on this thing that cuts across the whole org and have deep trust and it was like three to four people on average. Are you just a naturally trusting fellow? Did you have to learn to let go?

I don't think my team would describe me as like a just naturally very trusting person. I look I it's it's not that I'm like you know hands off go you know go for it you know you know go go do whatever you want that's that's not really my approach to management it's it's really uh I want to understand what we're doing in this vertical we're we have alignment on a direction we're headed I get it and I get how it influences the other pieces of the business and then I hold you know my team accountable to go execute on what we agreed upon you know from a plan perspective.

跨组织协作的张力

Okay. On that DRRi topic, it seems to me as CEOs grow, like they've got their orgs. Those orgs get bigger, they struggle with getting things done across the orgs. They at some point are like, "We need DRRI. We need to entrust those DRIs. And the bigger the orgs get, the harder it gets." And you're you've got like four different major orgs underneath you. How do you get someone that cuts across? How do you have many versions of you?

You know, we we struggle with this problem just like any organization, right? Anytime you're trying to do something that is crossorg, you know, pulling in resources from one team to work with another resource from another team. You know, it it just is complicated. You know, we we we we do have a program management function which helps, but you know, who's ultimately accountable for delivery of a lot of these things?

The way I find is like, you know, I run a I run a staff meeting once a week that like has, you know, a lot of the, you know, key executives and and my direct reports in the meeting and we cover things across the whole business and, you know, when there are pain points of how teams are working together, they they surface in those meetings and, you know, we try to address them. But, you know, it there is an inherent tension to doing things that that are are are crossunctional or across across organization. We we've sort of had to figure it out though, you know, just being a vertically integrated business, having collaboration between those layers that are where where you're transitioning across the stack, I think is a a critical function if you're going to be successful as a vertically integrated company.

沟通的"重复到自己都烦"法则

And then like what have you learned about that? Like you must have skinned your knees on it. Any ahas other than the staff meeting?

You know, I was I was always used to just working in smaller teams and smaller organizations. And if I said something once, people kind of listened and, you know, we worked in a small group and, you know, it all kind of worked itself out. I I found it that as soon as I'm sort of getting sick of hearing myself say something, then we're just scratching the surface of when when I'm just hitting the the point where I, you know, I'm saying it enough times.

And so just that that whole communication layer about getting people on the same page to march in the same direction. it it's sometimes like painful the amount of times you have to remind people um of what we're doing and why we're doing it and who's doing what and but you know that that's sort of what it takes to get alignment and I think that is one of the challenges of running a bigger organization and it's why there are opportunities always for startups is that they can be more nimble they can move quicker uh than than than bigger companies and we're trying to fight that inertia of a bigger company to be able to continue to move fast and uh capture the opportunity at this moment in time when it it it's sort of required to be a dynamic dynamic organization to succeed in you know today's today's business age.

速度、紧迫感与 Elon 式张力

Yeah. Your business is such that you have to go fast like you can't take your time. Most CEOs complain that as they get bigger they slow down. Have you figured out ways to keep the pace up or have you slowed down?

I mean, it feels faster and crazier than it's ever been. Like at at Cruso, there's a lot of big things happening uh on a daily basis. So, I I I I would say we are we are continuing to move with incredible urgency.

You know, I I think Elon's probably like the best in the world at this, but like you know, just trying to eliminate any sense of like entitlement or uh you know, eliminate any sense of like hey just you should be comfortable like we made it like we're here now we just have to coast. Elon has this superpower of, you know, simultaneously enabling people to believe that if they're successful, they're going to change the world and there will be this incredible financial outcome and this incredible outcome that's driving massive impact. uh while also holding people accountable through the high pressure of like we're going to go out of business tomorrow and if you don't act within, you know, the the greatest degree of urgency that you're physically capable of, we're going to we're going to die.

And you know that that like holding that tension is is is quite a quite a superpower. Um, I would say that I'm not quite as extreme as Elon uh in in in driving this tension of we're going to go out of business tomorrow versus hey, the opportunity we have to change the world is, you know, should inspire you to work hard. But I I I do think that, you know, threading the needle of that is is an incredibly important thing to be able to drive a large organization to move quickly and with a high degree of urgency.

从没当过"大公司"的 CEO

Okay, this is your first time running a company like this. Do you study other CEOs and try to borrow pieces of their playbook? And is Elon your guy? You're trying to borrow big pieces. Um, who do you look up to?

It's kind of funny. Um, Cruso is now the largest company I've ever worked for. Uh, and uh, you know, we we we recently surpassed uh, 2,000 employees. And you know I used to read a ton of books across fiction, non-fiction um you know kind of whatever I was interested in sort of a wide ranging things from you know science fiction and you know technical books to you know novels and you know whatever the latest and greatest you know economist book was but uh I shifted when I started cruso there was like a period where I just binged on like every you know every good business book recommendation anybody would give me I would like you know binge those things.

And I got to you I had the fortune of having a number of great mentors. I had a great coach um that that really helped me grow into becoming a leader of of people because I'd never really been a leader of a big organization before starting Crusoe either. I think like, you know, I often have very strong opinions, but I can always change them in light of new information and new facts. So, like that's like uh I think it's important to have that like intellectual flexibility to say like, "Hey, I had high conviction that we were doing things the right way. upon learning this new thing, we should probably be doing this differently and we could probably be doing this better."

And I think like that is like an inherent growth mindset that we have here as a company and you know I've tried to channel as a leader like to you know have uh you know the the ability to listen to you know these these these these criticisms and and and uh you know try to try to filter out like what is crazed hysteria that's you know unfounded in truth and what's like legitimate critical feedback that we should you know be using to become a better steward of of these communities.

厚脸皮与"主动找坏消息"

Do you think having thick skin is a very important attribute for a CEO?

100%. Uh yeah, I mean just your job is to like consu be the receiver of bad news very frequently and then be able to think with a clear mind and you know make decisions in light of that that that bad news.

And I think the other thing that you know is important for a leader is like and you know frankly something that I I'm always struggling with is like as the company grows and the company gets bigger I I'm like I'm like further from like a a distance from like individuals you know on the front lines of the company. So trying to like close the gap, making sure that I'm always approachable to like that people can speak truth to power, right? You want to be in a position where people can voice their concerns and be heard and, you know, in light of presenting truth, you know, in the context of everything else that's happening that you can actually adjust uh, you know, the the direction of your business.

怎么鼓励员工挑战你？

Do you have methods to encourage that to make sure people will stand up to you? Like do you cuz the 2,000th person you hire, they put you on a pedestal. The 20th person's beating you up day to day.

Yeah. I mean, honestly, it's it's it's like uh mining for it, just asking for it relentlessly. Uh I think when people see examples of you taking criticism and feedback, responding to it, changing your mind, I think it empowers people to be like, "Oh, actually my voice should, you know, I should voice my concern."

And you know, like I think people often have this perspective that you as the leader, you as the CEO, you want only want to hear the good news generally. Like the good news is great. Like I want to hear it, but like I care way less about the good news than I do about the bad news. So like trying to trying to like run into those like what what's going wrong? Like what are we bad at? Like you know how do we fix these things? What are the problems? How do I go resolve those? like you know I I think that is a critical characteristic of a CEO is like being that willingness to go seek out and like run into the burning buildings figure out the problems and you know go try to you know help help resolve them.

珠峰：公司文化的字面出处

Okay, this question is for me and I would imagine other people are interested. I've never met someone that climbed Mount Everest and I'm really impressed. What is it like? What is the training like? What does it feel like when you get to the top of that mountain?

Uh, you know, in a lot of ways, like a company culture is sort of a reflection of, you know, the CEO or the founders's culture. And, you know, that's really what's happening at Cruso. Like, we we actually have a core company value to think like a mountaineer. Um, which is like this sense of cultural resilience and preparation and planning and, you know, willingness to endure the expedition. a lot of that value and the practices that we've written about for that value describe a lot of what it's like to climb Mount Everest.

2014 年的雪崩

and so you know there's actually this whole internal presentation I have around you know the various Everest trips that I had because I actually tried to climb Mount Everest once in 2014 and there was a big avalanche that occurred and it it ended up killing 15 sherpas in the Kumbu icefall and um you know I made sort of this conscious decision like you know I came back and my wife was like oh thank god like that chapter is done and like you don't have to do this anymore. And I was like, "Look, this thing like haunts me and like it's all I think about and like I like have to go back." She's like, "You're insane." Um, but like if you're going to do that, please do it before we have kids.

死亡区 vs 昆布冰瀑

Um, so, uh, but when I thought about that, it was like very much like when you think about Mount Everest, you know, and and I climbed on the south side, which is, you know, the Nepal side, uh, through the Kumbu Valley. There's this, you know, you basically start at base camp and then or you trek up to base camp and then you go from base camp to camp 1 and then there's camp 2, camp 3, camp 4 and then you you have this push to the summit.

Well, the two most dangerous areas on the mountain are basically from camp 4 to the summit, which is which is frequently referred to as the death zone. This is where you're above 8,000 meters. So, you know, very intuitive why that's dangerous. You're at very very high altitude where humans really shouldn't be living.

Um but the other most dangerous area is this area between base camp and camp 1 which is called the Kumbu icefall. So this was the area where uh you know this disaster occurred when I was there in 2014. And uh the thing about the Kumbu icefall is that you know it's it's a glacier that's sort of falling right. So it's this beautiful like really cool ice jungle gym but there's a lot of things that are just like stochastic risk right? It's like these things that are totally outside of your control where it's like a S rock falls or an avalanche occurs and you know oops you die.

自觉风险 vs 随机风险

And that was the type of risk where I was like look I know there are ways I can consciously train and prepare for the high elevation and you know I can manage my risk up there like more effectively and I know consciously I'm taking that risk. The risk I felt less comfortable with was this stochastic risk.

And a traditional Everest expedition involves going from base camp to camp 1 and you're you actually have climatize on the mountains. You go base camp 1 back to base camp base camp 1 camp 2 back to base camp up to camp 3 back to base camp. And you actually end up doing eight trips through the Kumbu icefall. So like four round trips on a typical commercially guided expedition.

In order to derisk that, me and my climbing partner actually designed a different approach to climbing Everest, which was we ended up going and climbing a bunch of mountains nearby and spending a lot of time at the summits of those mountains so that we would acclimatize without taking this stochastic risk in the Kumbu icefall. And we actually only did one big acclimatization trip up Mount Everest and then back to base camp. So we ended up doing basically four passes through the Kumbu icefall instead of eight.

I was conscious of the risk that I wanted to take. Um you know the planning, preparation, you know all that. You know we had to think through a ton of stuff. A lot of training, a lot of long-distance trail running and uh you know a couple of different like al high altitude you know training training trips. But you know the the point I want to get across is like you know conscious risk-taking and intense planning and preparation that really went into uh a very successful Everest summit in 2018.

登顶时刻

You worked so hard at it and you wanted it so badly. What was the feeling inside of you when you got to the top?

It was like because I almost turned around at this uh this area called the balcony. It's about 8,600 meters. Um so the summit's 8848. Um and and so you know not too far from the summit in terms of elevation, but like it felt impossibly far and it was still dark out, right? So we had left camp 4 at like 11 p.m. It was still dark out when we got to the balcony. My, you know, you feel terrible like, you know, I hadn't eaten much in the last 48 hours. Like I was dehydrated. I felt awful. My legs were cramping. Like and it was dark, right?

And you know, my partner was really the person who inspired me to continue. I I like I felt fine apart from those things. So I wasn't like felt like I was putting myself at risk. And once once the sun came up and you start seeing the sunrise and you're you're sort of high up in this mountain, you're like you're just inspired by, you know, your surroundings. you're, you know, it was this elevation of your spirits and, uh, gave you the adrenaline to kind of like make the push through that final, uh, you know, 250 meters.

And uh you know when I got to the summit I think you know my feeling was was really one of just sheer awe just like you know just a a sense of awe for the universe and you know an awe for you know this that you know being on this summit and and sort of experiencing you know the the whole the whole world around me. um you know I think I think was just a really special one and it makes you feel small right.

and uh you know I think I think there's something uh very interesting about like you know having that sense of like I'm small and I'm inspired by the world around me and just like the magnificence of existence and uh you know that was kind of my my experience on the summit we we it was beautiful we had about we had a very sunny day so we spent about an hour uh up at the summit and you know just took a bunch of pictures uh you know just really enjoyed this this this uh heroic moment of achievement.

Congratulations and all your success. I'm rooting for you. You're a fantastic CEO. Thanks for coming on. — Brian, thanks for having me. This was really fun.

主持人收尾：五点收获

Okay. Hope you like that episode with Chase. He is a very legit CEO scaling that business really well. I give you a couple of my takeaways.

1. 热爱难题的物种

My first takeaway is kind of on him as a homo sapien. He's a person who really likes hard challenges and like when I recruit and I fund CEOs, that's definitely a quality that I look for.

2. 学习机器 + 教练

I liked how he talked about just how much the CEO job changed. He had never done anything like that before. Uh he's eight years into the journey and man, he's a learning machine. He read a lot about it. He hired a coach. It sounds like his coach was really useful and I coach a bunch of Sequoia CEOs and you know some of it is giving them advice but a lot of it is gaining context and listening to the problems and empathizing and really kind of being like a therapist. So he benefited a lot from that.

3. 公开表达是训练出来的

The other thing he worked hard on sounds like his public speaking he's very smooth like really articulate and smooth and sounds like that wasn't his default setting. He's had to really work at that. And I think that's important. Like if if you're up in front of your company, you're up in front of investors. I don't think it hurts to be articulate and smooth.

4. 竞合优于偏执

I like the way he talked about competition. He said something we used to say at HubSpot all the time. You're much more likely to die of suicide than murder. Um it was very much our case. It sounds to me he's really into coopetition. And I think a lot of founders frown on that. We had major coopetition over many many years with Salesforce.com. So I wouldn't shy away from that. The other thing I always did is I always got to know our competitors just because you never know. Um and so don't don't be afraid to reach out your to your competitors and have coffee.

5. 主动找坏消息 + 愿意改变主意

The last thing I took that I really liked is as the organization gets bigger and I felt this at HubSpot, everyone wants to give you good news. you're the CEO and they expect you want to hear good news and you really want the opposite. You want to hear the bad news and you want to train the organization to give you that bad news. So almost encouraging people when they push back at you and when they give you bad news inside of a you know a pretty good size setting. I think that's a really important quality in CEOs.

The other thing that I think is an important CEO quality that I think he does and you might too, but he has very strong opinions as you've heard, but if the facts change, he's willing to change his mind. And being stubborn is a really tough quality in a CEO and makes you quite hard to follow.

Anyway, those are some of my takeaways. I thought he was great. Um, it's an amazing business. He's an amazing CEO. I hope you liked it and I'll see you next time on Long Strange Trip.

## 一、Bitcoin 不是"旧业务"，而是一台把电子变成现金的套利机器——AI 真正到来之前的融资工具
大多数人把 Crusoe 卖掉比特币业务读作"转型 AI"。但 Chase 自己把这段历史讲得很清楚：**比特币从来不是业务，而是现金流泵。**
真正的论点一直是——"**用计算把搁浅能源变成市场**"。油井旁被点燃的伴生气、冰岛过剩的地热、北欧低价水电——这些都是没人愿意要的电子。比特币挖矿恰好是人类发明过的**最流动、最 24/7、最不挑剔的"电子变现引擎"**：它不要求你有光纤，不要求你有客户，只要你有瓦特。
于是真正发生的事情是：**Crusoe 用一台金融抽水机，把世界各地无人问津的电子抽成资本，再在 ChatGPT 这个历史时刻来临时，把积累的能源头寸转化成 AI 工厂。**
这几乎是一个**"打井是为了造油轮"**的操作顺序倒置。类比：亚马逊早年卖书不是终局，而是训练仓储肌肉；SpaceX 搞 Starlink 是为了资助去火星。比特币对 Crusoe 的角色属于同一个物种——**用一个成熟市场为一个尚未诞生的市场做财务预热**。

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Taking on ServiceNow: Coding Agents for the Rest of Us with Serval Co-Founder and CEO Jake Stauch
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：权限的"反向通胀"是 Serval 的真正护城河

多数人以为 AI agent 的未来是"每个员工变得更强大、能做更多事"。Jake 揭示的真相恰恰相反——企业内个人的权限将被大幅收缩，而不是扩张。这是一个被严重低估的二阶效应：

"访问权限将变得越来越严格……你会想把每个人的权限缩减到真正的最小特权。"

这意味着 Serval 的商业模式本质上是在押注一场"权限紧缩周期"：AI 让每个员工的"杠杆"变大 → 企业必须相应地缩短"杠杆的支点" → 日常例外请求爆发 → Serval 成为"例外经济"的唯一枢纽。

这里有个让我忍不住拍案的隐喻：Serval 不是在卖自动化，它是在卖"企业权限的中央银行"——它控制的不是劳动力，而是"临时特权"的发行、审计与回收。ServiceNow 卖的是工单流转，Serval 卖的是信任的即时结算系统。

二、跨领域连接：Serval 的架构哲学 ≈ 金融市场的"熔断机制"+ 生物学的"血脑屏障"

Jake 反复强调一个词：boundary（边界）。这与两个看似无关的领域惊人地同构：

  • 金融熔断：越聪明、越快的交易算法，越需要越严密的熔断器。模型能力越强 → 客户越想"进一步收紧"护栏。这是一个负反馈循环，而非正反馈。
  • 血脑屏障：大脑是全身最活跃的器官，但正因如此才拥有最严格的物质通过机制。企业的核心系统（ERP、HR、ITSM、CRM）就是企业的"大脑"，Serval 想做的是在智能爆炸中担任选择性通透膜。

一个让人意外的推论：Serval 的长期价值不与 LLM 能力正相关，而是与 LLM 能力的 "方差" 正相关。模型越不可预测，边界的定价越高。这意味着 Jake 实际上在做一笔"反脆弱"押注——他从 AI 的失败里赚钱，而不是从 AI 的成功里赚钱。

三、组织层面的隐藏模式：Serval 自身就是它卖的产品

一个几乎没有人注意到的结构性对称——Jake 描述团队运作时提到： - 没有产品经理，决策"下沉到工程师"； - 愿意反复"杀死 darlings"、推翻过去的架构； - 工程师每天沉浸在客户 Slack 里。

这正是他卖给客户的那套："用代码+护栏取代流程+审批"。他内部用的治理哲学和外部产品的哲学是同一套——用高频反馈+可回滚取代中央规划。

这里有个尖锐的预测：Serval 真正的竞争对手不是 ServiceNow，而是"企业中产阶级管理层"本身。它卖的产品的终极形态，是让"审批"从一个人的工作变成一条代码，让"流程设计"从一个岗位变成一次对话。所以你会看到，它越成功，客户内部的 PMO、流程治理团队、IT 中台的岗位结构就越被重塑——这才是真正的"SaaS Apocalypse"的隐藏剧本：不是软件消失，而是"中间管理"消失。

四、一个大胆的猜想：个人 agent 和企业 agent 的分裂，会复刻 Gmail/企业邮箱的历史，但以更剧烈的方式

Jake 说"你会有一个个人 agent 和一个工作 agent"。表面上这是常识。但如果你把它推到极限：你的个人 agent 将拥有关于"你"的真实偏好记忆，而你的工作 agent 只拥有关于"岗位"的权限集合。那么两者之间会出现一种新型冲突——员工 vs. 雇主的"认知资产"所有权之争。

未来 2-3 年真正的监管焦点，可能不是"AI 会不会取代人"，而是：员工离职时，谁拥有那个"懂你"的 agent？ 这将催生一个全新的法律与基础设施层，Serval 恰好站在这个裂缝的边缘。

📝 转录文本

开场：企业软件的终极登月计划

"This is the ultimate moonshot in enterprise software. These agents that go off and do work for you and magically discover all your problems and solve all your problems. And I think no one's really figured out how to do this well."

Jake: This is kind of the OpenAI Hugging Face incidents or other things where agents are given a task and then they do something that's unexpected. The agent becomes pretty competent. They could theoretically just start writing code that could take action on your systems. And that is an unbounded security risk that I don't think anyone's going to be able to take anytime soon.

On the one hand, you want these to be very autonomous without somebody babysitting them. On the other hand, autonomy is very scary in the enterprise. Serval is the boundary. Serval is the guardrails. We are the way that a large enterprise with a lot of rules and approvals and process and politics can adopt these tools safely and comfortably at scale.

嘉宾介绍

Host: Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today Allah and I are here with Jake Stauch, co-founder and CEO of Serval. Serval, with all the speed of the African wildcat, is trying to attack ServiceNow and more broadly bringing the power of code generation to IT and enterprise teams overall. Welcome Jake.

Jake: Great. Great to be here.

为什么创办 Serval：从 Verkada 到 ServiceNow 的替代者

Host: Yeah, maybe you could tell us a little bit more about your history and how you started Serval and what is the problem that you started with — or why did you start working on this to begin with?

Jake: So background — Serval is enterprise automation, enterprise service management. The idea is you can ask questions and get help at work and automate a lot of the parts of the job you don't enjoy, and we do that through codegen agents. So that's what the company does. We compete with companies like ServiceNow, the big legacy provider in the space.

I discovered this category actually working at a previous company called Verkada, where we sold enterprise physical security products to IT teams. Spent many, many years talking to IT teams figuring out what to build for them. One of the things I love to do with these teams is ask them what do you spend the most money on and what do you hate the most? And ServiceNow would top a lot of those lists.

So I was always interested in this category of — maybe there's a better solution here. But it wasn't clear for most of my time there how you'd ever beat ServiceNow. They're a great company. They've done so much so well, and why would you be able to compete with them?

用户为什么对 ServiceNow 不满？

Host: What was frustrating for users about it?

Jake: It's so hard to build in the platform. It's a very robust, customizable, powerful platform that can map to all these enterprise workflows — fundamentally it's a workflow automation platform. So it can do so much, but every idea you have for doing something cool, you have to go and implement. And a lot of times you're bringing in consultants to implement it. So it's always kind of running 6 to 12 months behind where you want it to be.

It's fine if you're building something that's going to last 5-10 years — like a big onboarding flow and nothing about your business is going to change. You can invest all that upfront effort and then it gets deployed and it works for a while. But for just trying to keep up with all the automation that you want to build, ServiceNow is not able to catch up — and then it's very expensive and it keeps getting more expensive over time.

So that frustration of "it's not keeping up with where I want to go as a business and it keeps getting more expensive" — that's what was driving a lot of the frustration.

"Coding Agents for the Rest of Us"：把编程能力扩展到非工程师

Host: One thing you mentioned that's really interesting about what you do: if you look at the world of AI adoption, a lot of the really early adoption is coding agents — engineers using it to build applications for their business or products. What you folks have been doing is really pioneering expansion of the category in terms of saying "we should let anybody internally — an IT person, etc. — build internal products or tools that can be used broadly across the enterprise." You're basically providing coding agents for all the internal stuff, for people who often aren't that adept at coding. So can you talk more about that? It's super fascinating.

Jake: Yeah, I love this idea of "coding agents for the rest of us." So much of the early enterprise adoption in AI has been engineering teams, and you think about why that is — there's a lot of reasons, obviously early adopters in a lot of different technologies. But also they're able to build and experiment with these tools because they have this process of code review. It's very safe for even a 19-year-old intern to build something very powerful and then go through this process before it goes into production.

We want to bring that same capability to the rest of the enterprise. So we build a platform that brings coding agents to IT departments, who then can bring it to HR and finance and people teams and legal teams. And they can do it because under the hood it's coding agents, but then you have all these abstractions and guardrails and controls. Things go through approval, they go through a staging and approval cycle and audit trail — all of that.

So it's: how do you build a system that makes it easy for everyone to be a builder? The core insight here was that IT actually wants to build stuff. For most of the world, they don't have an engineering department — they have an IT department. Most companies have an IT department, not a team of software engineers. So IT is what's building and configuring technology for the company, and we're building essentially the AI platform for them.

与消费级 "workforce agents" 的区别

Host: How does that run into things like all the different workforce agents that are being developed — like .do from OpenAI, or you know, some of these things where you almost have a virtual assistant that will go and do things for you?

Jake: I think those really work well for consumers and SMB and even a lot of the mid-market organizations. In a large enterprise there's so much — and I didn't even really appreciate this going in — there is so much process around approvals, around what you can and can't do. The permission sets of any individual are so limited that even if you were allowed to bring your agent to work (which in a lot of cases you're not), what it can do is so incredibly limited. It can barely even read your emails.

So when you think about all the stuff you need to do at work and all the systems you want to touch and all the interesting automations you could build, your personal permissions end up being so limited that these personal agents are also incredibly limited and not all that useful.

What we can do, because we work with these IT teams that can connect with service account credentials and admin-level permissions, is create a structure where people can access elevated permissions and do all these crazy things in the org — but with very, very strict deterministic approval cycles, workflows that are deterministic, and an audit trail. Because under the hood we are also a ticketing system.

So you say, "Okay, I want my agent to go do X, Y, and Z." Most organizations are going to be very uncomfortable with that at the large enterprise scale. But with Serval, that's going to create access requests that go through an approval process, and all that's going to be documented, logged, and then you can get just-in-time access to be able to run that deterministic workflow one time, and all of it's going to be tracked. Yes, it's a little bit more annoying than the magical personal agent experience we love with Instinct and Muse and all these tools, but it's what has to be true for a large enterprise — especially regulated enterprise — to ever adopt these kinds of technologies.

部署策略：Deployment Strategists、Forward-Deployed Engineers 与 Pro-Serval

Host: This also feeds into the traditional diffusion of this technology, which has been consulting firms — the Accentures and Deloittes of the world — kind of owning a piece of this, doing the implementation for people. You're kind of taking that and putting it in the hands directly of the IT department. Are you also exploring this more forward-deployed motion? How do you actually get this really built out in the enterprise or used effectively?

Jake: Yeah, absolutely. Diffusion is obviously the gap here. The technology can do so much, and enterprises have barely scratched the surface of what's possible. A lot of that is just understanding the people, the process, what workflows actually exist, how you want them to exist in the future — and we think that you still need people for that.

So we deploy both a deployment strategist, as we call them, and a deployed software engineer, that go on site with customers, figure out how we implement this, how we solve all your problems as a business, and then walk you through the implementation.

What we found, though, is that a lot of times after we've got this implemented and deployed, customers then have a long tail of more stuff they want. As we've discovered with software engineering, there's actually unlimited demand for work. We've started to build out a team — we call it Pro-Serval, or Automation Engineering is the field — and we bring in these automation engineers to do ongoing continued support and services, because there's so much that they want to automate and they need the help to figure out what can be automated, what the processes look like, how we navigate all of our systems, and then put it into production with a product like Serval.

"Delusional Plans"：两年半前就立下取代 ServiceNow 的目标

Host: How old is the company today?

Jake: Two and a half years.

Host: And you know, if you just look at ServiceNow as a business — I feel like Serval is one of the only companies that is like, "we are directly attack-replacing enterprise systems of record, including for large enterprises." At the beginning, did you think you were going to do that? How do you eat the elephant, just in terms of how big that product suite is?

Jake: I like to say everything has gone exactly according to our very delusional plans. We set out from the beginning to be the largest enterprise software company of all time. We actually made a list of all the companies. We circled ServiceNow and we said, "we're going to beat them and we're going to build something much bigger." We said that on day one when it was two people in my co-founder Alex's living room, and we just said we're going to do it.

So even though that was crazy, that was always the intention. We didn't grow into that ambition — we set out from the beginning.

为什么不选择"下沉市场"或"上层叠加"策略？

Host: A lot of people would have started with, you know, automation on top of their ticketing system for example.

Jake: Exactly. The way you typically go after these large enterprise startups — they build like the layer, or they go down market. Those are kind of the two common approaches. Let's build a small layer, play nice with the big incumbents, AI agent on top of —

Host: — which, you know, it may be the only one that worked was Veeva or something, right? They started off on Salesforce and they migrated to become their own platform. So they're the only one that I can think of that backwards-integrated.

Jake: It's really tough. It caps you unless you find some niche to kind of expand into later on. The other approach is: we just go down market, service the SMB and mid-market. You see that with a lot of competitors to Workday, competitors to Salesforce — they just say, "we're going to be that, but for the lower end."

Host: This is Rippling or HubSpot the first 10 years.

Jake: Exactly. And we looked at that and we said, why not just go after the big one? It's much harder, but at least the prize is quite big if you win. That was so important for us, because you end up making so many different decisions if you're building for the large enterprise from day one. All the product decisions, how you build your team, how you think about growth — they're fundamentally different than if you go and serve one market and then you hope to expand later on.

为什么是 ServiceNow 而不是 Salesforce？

Host: How did you choose this versus Salesforce — you know, there's a few other sort of canonical giant companies in different categories?

Jake: I think we didn't really understand how we'd beat the other companies and why we had an advantage and what AI unlocked that they couldn't catch up to. What we understood about ServiceNow because of our experience with it is that fundamentally it is a workflow automation platform.

Our belief — my co-founder and I, my co-founder really had this idea early on — that code was the right way to express automation in the enterprise. You should just build all automations in code. These drag-and-drop workflow builders are a painful level of abstraction, because it's too complex for non-technical users and it's annoyingly abstracted for technical users. Code is a better way of building automations.

The problem, obviously, is not many people can write code and do it quickly enough for it to make sense for automation. As AI made this possible, that was what clicked for both of us — that actually, if code is the right way to build automation, and now anyone can write code, we can build a better automation platform. And what is the best market for an automation platform? It's actually taking on these massive legacy software companies like ServiceNow.

两年半前的赌注：Coding Agents 会变好

Host: I guess two and a half years ago when you got started, though, most of the coding stuff was sort of tab-complete.

Jake: It did not work.

Host: Yeah, to be very clear — this is a brilliant idea, but in practice when we started building this... what was the assumption? Was it that the coding would get much better? Was it that you'd build tooling and then you didn't need to because things got so good? I'm sort of curious of that transition.

Jake: The bet was that coding agents would get very good. The theory there was: it's a verifiable domain and it should actually hill-climb fairly well. We believed fundamentally that coding agents would get good, at least for these very deterministic procedural scripts — reset password, get approval. All of these things are just so defined and verifiable that we felt like it would get good at those things. From a workflow automation perspective, we thought it would get there.

I didn't expect them to get as good as they are for just general-purpose software development, but for deterministic workflows, we were confident.

In the early days, it did not work. So what we ended up doing in all our early demos, we would prompt the LLM and say, "Hey, here's a suggested way you might want to build a password reset workflow." We'd seed it with a lot of examples, and over time we'd make that library bigger and bigger. But then the models just got so good that eventually it became hard to break. It became hard for you to give it a workflow that it couldn't automate if the APIs existed.

为什么 Jake 希望模型越来越好——与"权限紧缩"的预言

Host: When you think about where coding agents are today and what your customers want — are you and Alex excited about them getting better from here? Are you nervous? What do you think it looks like in terms of impact on your own product?

Jake: We are so excited for them to get better, because I think it unlocks a lot of the things that we'd love to do around better browser use and computer use and more of an approach to background agents and personal agents that can be really useful in the enterprise. So we're excited for the evolution of the category.

We've always believed fundamentally that we are not building the LLMs ourselves. We are building the guardrails. We are building the boundaries, and the boundaries are the product for us. Because we are the way that a large enterprise with a lot of rules and approvals and process and politics can adopt these tools safely and comfortably at scale.

So Serval is the boundary. Serval is the guardrails. The intelligence getting better just makes our product more powerful, and also makes our customers want to actually clamp down even further on those boundaries, on those guardrails.

I actually think access is going to get more and more controlled for individuals in the enterprise. As access becomes stricter and you let people do less and less and your permissions get more and more narrow — which I think is going to happen —

Host: Why is it going to happen?

Jake: Because if you think about it — I might safely give you more permissions than you need, because I don't actually think you're going to do all that much damage. But if you have access to all these agents, then the damage you can do with any kind of slightly-elevated-beyond-normal permissions expands. And we're seeing this in cybersecurity risk right now.

Host: Absolutely.

Jake: So what I'm actually going to want to do if I'm a large enterprise is shrink everyone's permissions down to truly least privilege. You cannot access any document and you cannot take any action unless you absolutely need to do it for your job. But then you're going to have exceptions all the time.

We are the layer that grants those exceptions and makes it possible for you to set up approval procedures around that, have an audit trail and a ticket associated with that. So by owning how privileges get escalated in the enterprise, we actually become more powerful and more essential the more you clamp down on end-user permissions.

让 Serval 成为"晋升之路"：Fox 的案例

Host: Is there like a story or a win you can share? People would be taking a big risk going with you to replace a very embedded incumbent, right? An investment of their own time, I assume it's personal risk — like why do that? Or is there an experience where people have already gone through to the other side?

Jake: We have to convince ourselves and our customers that Serval is the way you get promoted at work. It can't be the fact that Serval is a risk that you take to hopefully get something on the other side. We have to convince customers that you do this and you're going to make your career. You're not just going to not get in trouble — you're actually going to get a promotion.

This is top down, right? So we sell into the C-level, we sell into IT leadership in many cases, and then distribute into other departments.

The message is: people built their career on ServiceNow — you're going to build your career on this next generation. We're seeing this play out. One of our largest customers is Fox. Fox Corporation adopted Serval company-wide, and the person who led that migration on the ground actually got nominated to be the MVP of the entire company and got an award for his work there.

That is really what we're about — we're convincing our customers that this is the way to not just prove that you're useful to your organization, but to prove that you might be the most essential person to your company because you're leading this change. We're so pivotal to the AI transformation story that I think it's something we can sell really nicely to our customers.

对未来 2-3 年的预测：个人 Agent 与企业治理的张力

Host: When you started Serval, you were very adept at thinking ahead. You knew coding would get better. You knew there was this way of transformation. You kind of identified the good market segment to go after. What do you predict will happen in the next 2-3 years, not only for your company but more broadly? Is there something else you're seeing on the horizon that you're very excited about or a big shift that you see coming?

Jake: I think consumer often gives us a window into what's going to happen next in enterprise. It doesn't always look the same, but I think it's a nice window.

So I'm very bullish on: what do personal agents look like in the enterprise? In the same way that email and Slack and these tools transformed how we communicate at work, I think personal agents will also be a big part of that. Everyone will have their personal agent that does tasks for them, that delegates to other personal agents — so your agent will talk to other agents at work.

But then: how do we secure that in a world of increasing cybersecurity risk and increasing concerns at large enterprises around what's happening with everyone's agents taking action in all their computers and using their browsers? That tension between what employees and consumers want out of their personal agents at work, and what enterprises need from a governance perspective — I think there's going to be a lot of opportunity in that tension.

Host: Do you think there'll be a separate personal and work agent for each person?

Jake: Yeah, I think so. In the same way that I have a Gmail and I have a corporate email.

核心设计原则：引入软件开发生命周期（SDLC）

Host: If there's a premise — there's a bunch of different ideas here — but one is that exceptions or access control is going to get complex and require a different level of scale. Another is that you're just going to have more automations overall, because people, if you make it easy, are going to extend in all different places. Are there core design principles, beyond "code generation should be the actual form of automation," that you have put into the product today that reflect that?

Jake: I think the biggest one is the software development lifecycle. Something that we take for granted in engineering context — there's actually a dev environment, then there's staging, and then there's prod, and there are gates between them, and maybe you've got branches that people can develop on that they're not going to harm the other systems.

Host: And sorry, just to be clear — that's not how IT automation works today?

Jake: It does in some cases, but I think most new AI products are not embracing that. They're basically saying, "Hey, let's build these cool agents and ship to production." But this idea that you have to actually follow an SDLC process — if you're a large enterprise, a large financial institution, you're not just going to ship new agent capabilities without a review and user acceptance testing and all of these —

Host: Exactly.

Jake: So that's something we think about a lot. What is going to convince the largest companies in the world to adopt this technology — not just what is powerful and cool and something we're excited to get in the hands of customers.

Host: It feels like it takes a lot of AI companies, particularly if they're vertically centric, a year or two to figure this out, sometimes longer. It's interesting to watch the whole industry now adopting both the forward-deployed motion, starting to think through software development lifecycle, compliance, other aspects of the enterprise, in a way that was almost missing.

Jake: I think in some cases they never get there. Some companies look at what enterprise software takes and they decide, "we don't really want to build that." You look at the story of a lot of these companies that have gone down market — I think sometimes they do look at the opportunity to go and build for the enterprise, and it requires a whole different set of building principles and products that you have to build, and some just don't choose to do it. They cede that ground to other companies.

We've chosen to say, "hey, give me your gnarliest problems and we're going to solve them and make AI transformations possible in this crazy world — in this world of risk and governance concerns."

平台 vs. 定制：Serval 永远不做"客制化功能"

Host: When you have your deployment in customer environment engineers, and then ongoing automation specialists, and then you have the core platform — how do you decide what is actually brought into the core of platform, or in every individual customer's environment?

Jake: When we deploy these software engineers, what's really important is: we actually never build custom features. We don't build bespoke product capabilities. Luckily for our category, no one asks us to — everything that people ask for is something that every other customer is going to want at some point. Maybe they impact the prioritization, but it's still something we've always wanted in the platform.

Now, because it is a codegen platform under the hood, what you build in Serval is very, very unique. The password reset workflow for one company is going to be very different, shockingly, than the password reset for another. Same with onboarding and offboarding — all these different automations internally, they look very different. But that's just baked into the core primitives of the platform.

Serval almost becomes the IDE for the IT department and other departments to build their automations and manage them at scale.

What we do do is: if we look and see the same customer building the same automations over and over again and having to customize them and build them in the product in the same way, we start to consider — should that be a first-class feature in the product? One example: we saw a lot of customers building workflows to detect knowledge-based articles that were conflicting or out of date, and we said, "hey, we should just do that automatically." We had customers that would set up automations to reclaim old licenses — software you're paying for that no one is using — let's automatically cancel those subscriptions. We just decided to build that into the platform.

So it is a way for us to test the waters of what should be really first-class features versus what should stay as automations in Serval.

Token 消费与 ROI 的证明问题

Host: Customers — as it relates to just general spend on code generation for software teams — have gone through a journey this year, right? They're like, "we're going to let people try it, then we're going to token-max, and we're going to restrict that and figure out who's actually doing this productively." How do you think that reflects for your business, and how do you think about the actual intelligence cost?

Jake: I think we're still watching this. I do see our CIO customers trying to pull back from that initial token-maxing era. But I also think we're so early in the adoption curve that it's not going to be a clampdown in aggregate — it's actually going to continue to be a pretty dramatic rise. Most companies are still figuring this out for the first time, and they're all going to go through this cycle of rapid early adoption and then kind of a pullback of spend and trying to measure and calculate ROI.

What I hear from our customers all the time is not really a concern about the long-term budget impacts. They realize that there's going to be a short-term pullback, but they're still planning on increasing spend. What they need, though, is more proof of ROI. That is what's going to transform in the industry — people looking for "how can I prove that this spend is giving me something?" And that is hard. I don't know that anyone's really figured out how to measure what you're getting from the tokens that you're buying.

But that I think is going to be a huge opportunity for us — to show the work that's being done and try to equate it to work that would have been done in other platforms or with other cost models or by labor. That's what our customers are asking for: help me prove that this was worth it. That's the assignment. That's what we have to do.

We try to price on workflows run, because I think it's a better reflection of actual work being done versus just tokens, which is more like verbosity and inefficiency. But we're all going to figure out different models of proving that what we're doing makes sense.

"SaaS Apocalypse"：是消失，还是重塑？

Host: One of the things people have been talking about is a sort of SaaS apocalypse — the idea is people will just build their internal SaaS software and all these categories will go away. A lot of people, to your point on calculating the ROI and tokens, are trying to sort: is it worth rebuilding these systems and can you actually do that effectively? What is your view on this apocalypse or the shift in SaaS versus AI?

Jake: All the companies I've talked to that tried to vibe-code these tools internally — especially the main system-of-record tools, not the point solutions, but the main system-of-record tools — have discovered that it's quite expensive to build and maintain enterprise software. Even if you can do it, it doesn't make economic sense in many cases, unless your needs are very bespoke and unique in some way.

So buying off-the-shelf for things that are not your core competency, I think, has always been the build-versus-buy argument. I think that is as true now as it has ever been, because it still is hard to build enterprise software. A lot of companies are discovering this — or relearning this — that actually enterprise software is complex and you need people to maintain —

Host: — a lot of use cases and edge cases.

Jake: Edge cases, things that break down, people need to update it. So then you have to staff the team, and then you're paying for that labor, and then no one really wants to work on the internal tools team in many cases. So you have all these problems with doing that.

Where I do see it is in the point solutions. A lot of companies have hundreds and hundreds of SaaS applications — they probably need a couple dozen total. So I do think you're going to have a shrinking of the sprawl of different point solutions, and they're going to be eaten by the core systems of record and the core platforms.

Host: All the middleware too, I think, is just going to go away.

Jake: Exactly. So I think there is going to be consolidation. There will be a SaaS apocalypse, but in that kind of point-solution, smaller market-cap type of company. I don't think that you're going to truly get away from the core systems of record — the ERP, the HR, the ITSM, the CRM. I think those are going to stick around. They might transform — and what we're seeing with Serval is we are displacing those tools. So I think there will be a new generation of incumbents, but I don't see those categories just disappearing.

IT 用户的心智模型：把他们当成成年人

Host: I'm curious as to what mental model or theory of mind you have for the IT user. They're not software engineers, but they understand their business. They understand what they're trying to automate. When you talk about vibe coding, I'm like, "okay, but do you understand security architecture? Do you understand how this is going to integrate with governance?" How do you square code generation and how we think about vibe coding — and what the challenges are with that — with "we want to build robust IT systems"?

Jake: Yeah, absolutely. I think it is really interesting because they're closer to a software engineer than I think a lot of people give them credit for, especially in large enterprises. The IT department is the engineering team in a lot of cases. They don't have the software engineering team. So IT runs all these systems and often does write code and manage the systems.

So we treat them as adults. We give them the tools that we would give software engineers. Now, we abstract away some of that complexity — we make it easier to use in some regards, and we don't just hand them Claude Code and tell them good luck. We actually build a platform that's dedicated to their use case, and we don't expect them to necessarily be able to write code or understand what's being written. But we still give them access to it under the hood. So you can always see the code, and you can always treat this through a full software-driven lifecycle — but you also don't have to.

A lot of the product principles is thinking with a few different personas in mind: an IT engineer who actually can and does write code, all the way through someone maybe in the marketing department and the people team that doesn't want to see code ever, but still wants to have that flexibility of codegen under the hood because they've got a complex workflow that they want to build that they don't want to drag-and-drop their way to.

A lot of it just comes to having multiple personas in your head and also treating it like an adult. A lot of the products out there have actually been kind of pedantic to IT — like "oh, you don't actually understand this stuff, so you need this very stripped-down, more opinionated, simpler version." Actually, IT appreciates the complexity and appreciates the power of these platforms. We want to deliver that to them.

Catalyst：构建自动化的"元 Agent"

Host: You guys built an agent that helps you build automations. Can you explain how that works?

Jake: Yep. One of the things — every company discovered this as they were building the first generation of these AI tools — is that you could build such amazing complicated systems, but then you had to train people to understand all of your product primitives and how these systems fit together.

So the first generation of this is: we deployed all these FDEs to explain to customers, "okay, here's how to build on the platform." Actually, let me just build it for you. Then we realized it would be really nice if customers could just talk to an agent that understood their requirements and then translated that into the product primitives.

So we built this agent called Catalyst that does exactly that. It's an agent for managing the platform. It's an agent for admins to build out all those underlying automations, but also configure the rules around approvals, permission checks, build out different policies, update all these different systems, understand the entire deployment.

Because Serval is all codegen under the hood, having the agent on top of that to help you manage the system just made a ton of sense. It's so powerful because now I don't need you to train yourself on how to use Serval — you can just talk to an agent that actually understands how to use Serval and how to build on it. That is your primary interface into the product.

Host: One thing that's underappreciated — and I think is cool — is that the experiences for agents in different products, and in coding generation agents as well, being able to bring a user along as they are building a product or an implementation, is actually raising the technical competence and ability of a huge number of users, and turning people into more engineers actually.

Jake: Absolutely. You have this blank-slate problem in the old generation of automations — "where do I even begin?" I know I want to automate all these parts of my job, but where do I begin? Products like ours say: where do you want to begin? And they just start making suggestions, and you can iterate with them. You can say, "I actually don't understand that. What are you trying to say? Can you explain this to me?" "Okay, I'm trying to do this. How would I even go about doing this?" And they can give you that information, they can fetch the information, they can explain concepts to you.

So it does become a build partner, and you can achieve so much more than just prompting an agent to go and build something. It can actually walk you through the process and help you explore new opportunities that you wouldn't even have thought of.

背景 Agents：企业软件的"终极登月"

Host: One thing that seems a little bit under-discussed right now is background agents. Could you tell us more how you think about that and what you think is coming in terms of this next wave?

Jake: Yeah, I always describe background agents to the companies like this is the ultimate moonshot in enterprise software. Just these agents that go off and do work for you and magically discover all your problems and solve all your problems. It would be amazing if we could get that deployed and it could work and it could follow our permissions.

I think no one's really figured out how to do this well, because on the one hand, you want these to be very autonomous to go off and figure stuff out and then solve problems without somebody babysitting them. On the other hand, autonomy is very scary in the enterprise. So you do want to see what exactly can they read — this is kind of the OpenAI Hugging Face incidents or other things where agents are given a task and they do something that's unexpected in order to accomplish that task.

Host: So what are the guardrails you can put in place?

Jake: Exactly. Because my best employees — what do you do with them? You say, "here's a general high-level mission, go off, don't talk to me, and go do it, and you'll come back and you'll have done amazing things." I want to be able to trust agents to do the same thing for me, where I can give them this high-level task and they can come back and solve this problem and come back to me. I don't think we figured out how to do that in a way that feels safe in the enterprise.

Host: What do you think is a way to make it safe? People have experimented with different things over time, everything from constitutional AI to certain forms of RL. I'm just sort of curious if you have a solution in mind.

Jake: We think of it in the large enterprise — it's not perfect, but it's an incremental escalation of capabilities. You go off and you do these things, and it comes back and says, "Hey, I would like to be able to do all this stuff. This would help me do my job." And you approve them. All the stuff are deterministic workflows — "I want to call this tool. I want to run this script that does X, Y, and Z. Can I do that?" You just kind of approve these with certain permissions and guardrails around them. You say, "Okay, yeah, that's okay. That's okay. That's okay."

Over time, the agent becomes pretty competent because it has a big enough toolkit that it can solve most problems. It's not perfect, because it's annoying to have to babysit that process, but I think it's what you have to do. Otherwise it could theoretically just start writing code that could take action on all your systems, and that is an unbounded security risk that I don't think anyone's going to be able to take anytime soon.

这是模型问题还是边界问题？

Host: Do you think — to your point of being excited about future capability — we're still missing some model capability here? The reason I ask: the ability to be proactive and then predict what an individual (Jake as a CEO, me as an investor, me as a human being) and get it right is still very hard, right? You need a lot of preference data. Think about an employee working for you — like, "okay, what are Jake's actual priorities when he gives me this high-level mission? What does he mean?" Do you think that's a model problem, or is it entirely a guardrails-and-harness problem today?

Jake: I think it's both. Honestly, I think memory obviously has to be better and better, because you want to understand the preferences. You want the context to be insanely large, because I don't want to have a bunch of different chats with you — I want to have kind of one single chat that goes back all the way to our very first conversation, and you remember the key points of that that are relevant.

And then I think the permissions problem will always remain the biggest thing. Even if I feel like you are a very valuable, smart agent and you can do all these things for me, how much do I trust you to just run wild and not have to babysit your actions? You have to do that with people too, right? Someone that works for you has to come back and check in — "this is what you wanted, and here's three options." It's a very normal process.

组织与运营：从 20 人到 200 人的狂飙

Host: The company's about two and a half years old. You have gone very quickly to at least an enterprise-mature product. How big is the team today?

Jake: We are 200 people today.

Host: 200 people.

Jake: We were 20 in January. So it's been an incredible ramp year.

Host: That's quite a year. One: do you expect to continue hiring so fast, and as somebody who clearly believes in AI, why? And two: you and your team have been part of startups before — what are you operating… how are you operating very differently the last two years than the previous 10?

Jake: The hiring velocity, I think, will increase even from where we're at today. We believe that there is unlimited demand for work and there's unlimited competition and there's unlimited ambition. Even though every single employee does so much more than what they could do a year ago, we have even bigger ambitions for what they could do. Because every employee is so much more productive, we actually want more of them, not less of them.

Host: Given your time at Verkada before, how are you operating differently over the last two years than the previous 10?

Jake: What's so unique about Serval and the category we're in and the moment we're in is: the TAM is unbounded. It feels like the addressable market is really more about the size of our ambition than it is about fundamental limitations on how big this business can get, because we are automating essentially all kinds of work for every single employee in the world. The TAM is as big as we want it to be.

It's really: how fast can we grow and what is our ambition? Making decisions based on that versus, "okay, here's what the market looks like, here's what we think we can actually do." That's a different set of challenges. It's not strictly better, because now there's so much open space and there's so many more decisions we have to make about what we actually want to focus on. But it is really fun to not be constrained and hemmed in by what the market allows for.

组织结构：没有产品经理，工程师直接面对客户

Host: How, given that scope is very broad, do you organize the cadence or the EPD team?

Jake: We are embedded with customers. Even the engineers that are not necessarily deployed, they are in the customer Slack channels. We are talking about customers nonstop. They're hearing from customers every single day. Most engineers are on at least one customer call a week — I think most of them are actually on at least a customer call a day.

What this is, is like immersion in a country to learn a foreign language. You become so immersed in your buyer and your customer's mindset that you understand what they want. You understand how they're thinking about things, and you are adapting to their preference changes in real time. As they are moving with the market and starting to talk about different products that they're trying out and things that they're excited about, our engineers are constantly aware of all this and able to adapt very quickly.

So we've decentralized product development really to the engineering team. We don't have a product function because they're the ones talking to customers every day, and they're able to rapidly adapt to whatever customers are saying today and this week, versus what they were saying a month ago.

Host: That sounds like a really natural way to keep pace with a ripping market and changing priorities for your customers. How do you and Alex and leadership then make sense of it? In a traditional enterprise software company, you'd have an architectural review, a quarterly roadmap, and you'd prioritize the roadmap and train all your customers on the new launches. You'd communicate with your customers that things aren't going to change too fast, because they can only absorb it so fast too.

Jake: Yeah, it's a big challenge. Our product ships and changes faster a lot of times than anyone can keep up — including myself.

We just try to make sure that, one, the engineers we hire are really product-oriented. That's one change we've made — they have to really understand our customers, and we want to put them in front of our customers because they're going to have to make so many decisions at the edge. Not every single product decision can be bubbled up to leadership every single time.

That is a fundamental change: you have to be willing to push a lot of the product decision-making down below, and you have to be willing to move fast and also undo and revert if you go in the wrong direction and kill your darlings. You have to be willing to change course on things that you thought were fundamental to the product and switch gears when your engineers bring you something — "hey, this is how the customer sees things now, and this is what we should do differently."

One of the things I'm proudest of at Serval is how many times we've decided to erase things we've done in the past that we were very committed to, and just say, "you know what, the market's changed, the customer's changed, we're going to do things entirely different." I think that is what's enabled us to keep up — that ability and willingness to reinvent ourselves over and over again.

Host: It's one of the most durable things in this era. Thanks, Jake.

Host: Thanks for joining us.

结尾

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen — that way you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.
