item.title: [Latent Space] Why Agents Love Supabase — with Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：Supabase 把销售团队当作临床试验

视频里几乎被一笔带过、但其实是整场对话最值得解剖的一段是 Paul 描述他们的 "Product-Led Sales" 补偿机制：

  • 每周 1000 个产品信号触发邮件 → 500 人回应 → 把那 500 个不回应的人作为"控制组"。
  • 控制组自然增长 25%／月；接触组增长 125%／月。
  • 销售的提成只计算那 100% 的增量差额。

这是制药行业双盲试验的逻辑被挪用到了销售激励上——他们不是在"卖东西"，而是在用 counterfactual（反事实推断）来定价人类销售的边际价值。多数公司以 ARR 配额激励销售，这会污染数据；Supabase 却选择牺牲归因的直觉性，换取"销售的真实 lift 可被统计证明"。这背后的隐藏假设极其激进：公司默认 PLG 流量会自己长大，销售只是加速器，不是增长的因。这种自我怀疑式的 KPI 设计，在 SaaS 里几乎是异类。

二、意料之外的"时间套利"：AEO 的赢家，是 LLM 诞生之前就存在的公司

Swyx 顺口提了一句——Supabase 在他的 AEO（Answer Engine Optimization）排行榜里几乎垄断"integrated backend"类目。Paul 的反应很有意思："we're very lucky with our timing… it's a complete accident."

但这不是运气，这是一个跨领域的时间套利结构，和 Google PageRank 早期的"老域名红利"是同构的：

  • LLM 的训练语料停在某个时间点。
  • 那个时间点之前，谁的社区博客、Hacker News 讨论、YouTube 教程覆盖最密，谁就被模型"结晶"成默认答案。
  • 这意味着 AEO 的赢家不是今天最会做 SEO 的人，而是 2020–2023 年间最会"喂养语料生态"的人。

Resend 的 AEO 优势也是同一机制。换句话说，2026 年要再想复制 Supabase 的 AEO 地位，几乎不可能——这是一次性的红利，它封装在冻结的训练集里，和化石燃料没什么两样：你可以继续开采（RAG、工具调用），但新的沉积已经停止了。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Supabase 真正的产品不是 Postgres，是"迁移摩擦"的套利

通读访谈，Paul 其实在重复一个被所有数据库公司验证过的黑暗真理：OLTP 从不迁移。他说得非常直白——"you can almost never convince people to migrate"。所以 Multigres、Oriole、Terso（SQLite 加速到 MVCC）——这些看似宏大的技术路线图，都在服务同一个战略：抢占 greenfield。

把这个视角装回去看，Supabase 的产品矩阵突然变成了一张漏斗型抗腐蚀结构：

层级 对手 真正要做的事
Spark (SQLite) Firebase, Neon free tier 让新想法落地到 Supabase 的轨道上
标准 Postgres Neon, RDS 不让客户在 1k 用户时需要换平台
Multigres Vitesse (MySQL 侧) 不让客户在 10M 用户时逃离 Postgres
Compute Lambda, Cloudflare Workers 不让客户为了 "跑一个长任务" 走出去

所以 Supabase 的护城河不是任何单一技术，而是"锁定迁移时刻"的时间轴。这和保险业的策略结构相似：保险公司真正卖的不是保单，是"客户在人生某个关键节点下意识打开 APP"的那一瞬。Supabase 卖的是"开发者在'启动新项目'这个决定性瞬间下意识 supabase init"的那一瞬。

四、跨领域连接：对象存储正在吃掉数据库，就像 CDN 吃掉了 Web 架构

一个容易漏掉的细节：Paul 对 S3 Express、11 个 9 持久性、强一致性的赞美，暗示了一个体系性迁移：

对象存储正在从"冷存储"演化为"分布式状态原语"。

这件事在历史上有过先例——CDN 从"静态缓存"变成"边缘计算基础"，一路吃掉了传统 Web 服务器层。今天的 S3 正在重走这条路：Terso、TurboPuffer、DuckLake 都在用对象存储当"分布式 WAL + 内存"。

Supabase 的 Spark 本质上是在押注：未来的"小数据库"不是数据库，是对象存储上的一个文件格式。SQLite 之所以被选中，不是因为它是数据库，而是因为它是一个被 11 个 9 持久性保证的文件。这是软件工程的"分形重复"：数据库被解构成文件格式，就像容器被解构成镜像层、神经网络被解构成权重张量。抽象的边界每十年重划一次，这一轮重划的刀口刚好落在"OLTP 和文件系统之间"。

五、让我意外的一句话：Gary Austin，20000 个问题里 13000 个在一小时内答完

一个退休的红酒爱好者，六年里在 Discord 回答了 20000 个 Supabase 问题，其中 65% 的问题他在一小时内给出答复——而他不是机器人。

这不是温情故事，这是一个社区的隐藏生产函数：Supabase 的开发者体验，有一个独立变量根本不在他们的工程 KPI 里——它来自一个外部人类的个人热情。公司估值 100 亿美金，但其中有一个百万美元级的"情感应收账款"记在一个退休老人的名下。他们现在用股票偿还，这件事比任何技术发布都更能说明 open-source 商业的底层逻辑：真正的 moat 是"有人愿意为你免费工作六年"，而且他甚至不是你的员工。

这件事和维基百科的核心志愿者结构、Linux 的"仁慈独裁者"模式、甚至 20 世纪初的业余天文学家网络是同构的——专业机构都站在无偿劳动的巨人肩膀上，但大部分时候它们假装没有看见。Supabase 这次至少没有假装。

📝 转录文本

开场与介绍（Swyx 的 cold open）

Hello, it's me again. I hope you're enjoying these little episode intros that we're doing. Hopefully it gives me a little chance to talk to you guys about why we're doing some of these episodes and what you should look out for in the interviews so you get more audio interviews. We're also adding overlays that you can see pop up to keep it visually interesting, to explain things that maybe if you're newer to the industry you don't know because I don't have time to go over every single thing while we're having interviews.

So I was at Supabase Select recently, which is the Supabase company conference. And there's a lot of stuff to cover. In particular, I think I should share that I have a very close relationship with this company. I was an angel investor in a seed round six years ago, and they were my very, very first angel investment. They've done super well. They went from zero to 10 billion in valuation in the last six years as a fully remote open source company, which is enormous — and they're pretty much becoming the standard for hosting Postgres.

So I want to break down what makes them tick. I also want to see why they did so well in my AEO ranking, because it's not a given for sure, and there's a lot of companies that are fighting for what it means to build databases for agents. They were also, I think, our very, very first sponsor for AI Engineer, the very first AI Engineer in 2023. And they're now going to be our first sponsors for Latent Space, because we're open for sponsorships — and who else to do this with, with companies and people that I'm familiar with and trust and can explain very well to our audience.

三大主题：Build、Operate、Scale

And so the main things I wanted to cover — they have a whole recap here on their YouTube, which is very well executed and all that. But they have these three themes of build, operate, and scale. I think the announcements are very much what I kind of look for in a company conference keynote.

Build

So build is basically how they want to improve the Postgres experience for coding engines to set up. And the two that really shot out to me is: one is very simple one, which is that starting Supabase without Docker. That is — the less weight I need in order to start up basic processes to interact with the database, the better. And obviously I can scale it up to a full VM in the future.

But the second thing is Supabase Compute, where you can run compute next to the database. I think co-locating that is super easy. I think this is honestly super underrated — I think it's maybe underselling what it potentially could be. Your app having an MCP server from Supabase is really good.

And… but declarative schemas is so important, right? Like, you want declarative schemas rather than the standard SQL paradigm of "set up a schema and then migrate, migrate, migrate," which is something we cover in the podcast. Like, you want everything to be in Git as source of truth so that your agent can crawl it and figure and set up and fork and whatever from there. It seems so simple, but really when Postgres was not designed to do this, it has to kind of retrofit the events on top of a 40-year-old database.

And really, I kind of see Supabase's momentum now as doing the last mile — like the really frontier of Postgres development for agents to really use them super well. The beauty of it, though, is that it's not actually about agents. We just needed this the whole time. But humans also benefit. And I really like that. I don't like doing things only for agents to be happy.

Operate

So then the second part is operating. So that is mostly just about giving more context, really — whether it's more logs, more checks, more connections, markdown files for your SQL. That's super cool knowledge and skills. Every year they ship some interesting pipeline work from, like, you know, Stripe to other sort of integrations. An operator, for those who aren't familiar — when you run Postgres, you start with a single node, but then with almost any database, you want to run multiple nodes, and you want things like failover, you want it to manage backups. So usually you have this thing called an operator, which can run the entire cluster for you.

So there's quite a few operators in the Postgres ecosystem. And what we had found was that under certain conditions, every single one of them could lose data. And so we decided with Multigres to do a ground-up rewrite of the entire structure of an operator. And so Multigres is essentially — while our initial goal is to give sharding to the Postgres community — what has turned out to be is this entire operating system.

And we actually ran it again through very rigorous testing. And we've done 1,000 sequential failovers, and it didn't lose any data. And we've tested it in basically every way we can, clobbering it to see whether it will ever lose data. So we're very confident now in its stability. And so we're releasing that one as well tomorrow. Product-Led Sales + Control Group 实验

So that's the first thing. So to do that, all we started doing when we did sales was layer on what we call product-led sales. So we look instead for, like, product triggers. It could be, like, a logo, someone who we think is really important. But more importantly, they could be scaling up. They could be hitting some limits, having some errors, paying a certain amount. We've got a bunch of these triggers.

And then AI came along and we're, like, "Oh, we can do some interesting stuff from this." So let's say we have a thousand product triggers every single week. We send off a thousand emails to people who are having problems. And say 500 of them respond. We take the cohort who don't respond and we use them as a control group. Okay. And we measure how much they grow. Turns out they grow 25% month over month.

Then we take all those who do respond, and we say to our sales team, "The only thing you need to do is get on a call with these people and help them." And because we've got all their traffic patterns, we can give them a script. We know what their problem is. AI has been great on this. And we give them a script just to help out. And it turns out just getting on a call and helping people out, their account then grows 125%. So that 100% uplift, the incremental uplift is what we compensate our salespeople.

Traditionally, you'd say, "Get on a call with these people and just sell them shit." And then you get the full quota. But because we know our database grows, our platform grows at 25% month over month on this cohort of users, then we know that our sales force at adding this 100% incremental uplift. So that's how we do our sales function. It's always focused on these logos or very specific product needs.

Split-Brain 风险

Paul: Most of the problem around migrations is actually not rewriting it. And you can do migrations, for example, on the data analytics side quite easily from one warehouse to another. The problem is that usually your OLTP database is powering your most revenue-generating application. So a minute of downtime means that you end up with basically dollars lost. And so then what you end up doing is having to run these two things in parallel. And then the risk of this is that you get this split brain, where you've got some data running on one side, some on another. And if you try to reconcile split brain, anyone who's tried to do it, it's a very hard problem.

So the risks are just so much higher when it comes to OLTP that a lot of the time people just start doing splitting the workloads off and they'll start new workloads. They'll do a lot of operations here and hopefully they'll migrate things over. Yeah. Usually then you've got two problems though.

So if you need to split transaction across two servers, you're basically then going to be fetching it from object storage. Eventually, that will slow down your database.

Now, that doesn't mean that you shouldn't store your data directly on object storage, for example, and then read from it from a different route. Code-First, Git-Native, Declarative Schemas

This year, our big focus is moving to code-first, Git-native. So basically, when you launch a Supabase application, instance inside your local machine, you get the Supabase folder, and it represents your database. It has all your functions, everything.

Swyx: Does this exist today?

Paul: This exists today, if you use the CLI.

Swyx: So it's a virtual file system?

Paul: Like, it's a representation of — it's like infrastructure as code.

Swyx: Okay.

Paul: Yeah. And in fact, what we're announcing tomorrow is, like, we've done our kind of final change for declarative schemas. This was a really challenging one, actually, covering all of Postgres. And so now you can have a full file representation of Postgres — the shape of your database declaratively in your folder.

That's really important for agents, because generally how you operate with Postgres is you have a migration file. Every time you make a change, you add a file to this migrations folder, and it's like a historical log. Okay. So that's great. It's industry standard. But imagine putting an agent across a thousand files and telling, asking it, "Oh, what is the shape of this table?" It has to guess through a thousand files. It has to recompile basically.

Swyx: It has to recompile.

Paul: Or you have to launch the database locally, run the migrations up and then you inspect — introspect the database. But that's too slow.

So basically what we want to do is turn the schemas folder inside our Supabase folder into a completely declarative state of your database. And so we've captured everything from tables, policies, database comments, all inside these files. So we're releasing a new library, pgDunker. You can use it with any Postgres database, but we've got mechanisms for Supabase. And so this is an important step for agents. We know that agents are going to operate mostly on code. They don't want to reach out to anything. They've got to iterate very fast on the file system.

Like, you probably don't need to go to university anymore, because you can probably self-teach and just, like, you know, get your own job done. There's always been, like, this top tier of people that are moving a lot of the needle, and you need to, and they will always find a way to have their own self-interest be satisfied.

Ant: Curiosity in terms of, like, "what is possibly better?" You know, the type of people that take a year off and go to the Recurse Center and just work on cool programming problems, even though they could be making money in industry, and, like, yeah.

两位创始人的分歧（或缺乏分歧）

Swyx: Yeah. What do you disagree on between the two of you? It's rare to have the two of you had — oh yeah, that's a great — on the pod. So, you know, I want to capture this.

Paul: I think one of the reasons we've been so effective, like, working together, is because there are definitely situations when we'll disagree. But as soon as the other person, like, pushes a little bit, yeah, the other person's like, "Yeah, yeah, maybe you're right, let's try it." So we never end up in, like, big bust-ups. And it turns out, like, most of that stuff actually doesn't matter anyway. Like, as long as the general direction is correct, then it's gone okay. But — yeah, I can't think of —

Swyx: You guys are really struggling here. Oh my god. Yeah, yeah.

Paul: Which is why, like, because it's never an important enough thing. Like, we've never had a bust-up because it's never been important enough to actually fight hard enough on it. And also —

Ant: We're fucking busy. So, like, usually, like handling — we're trying to handle different parts of the business.

Swyx: Maybe it's just like, things are growing and obviously you got your domain and you just need to work together.

Paul / Ant: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

EF Singapore 与早期团队

Swyx: It's interesting, you know, so Laura here, all three of us were in Entrepreneur First in Singapore. We were all different, working on different companies. And then you guys stayed back after the cohort. Your housemates after the cohort?

Paul: Yeah, yeah. So we were all — we lived in a house with seven people and we were all doing different startups. Yeah. And so Ant was doing his startup, I was doing another one. This is before Supabase.

Swyx: And so, like, I think somehow your energies, you know, you found that you were suitable working together and working on this —

Paul: Yeah, because traditionally, especially in an accelerator model, you're pushed as a technical person to work with some domain expert, right? But in the house we lived in, it was basically seven people who were all builders, all technical people. And we found that pairing to just be so much more effective, especially when you're building dev tools, because you are the subject matter expert as a developer. Is that we could just get so much more done.

And so then we ended up hiring most of the other people who lived in the flat as well as our employees.

Swyx: Rory was the first employee?

Paul: Not the first, but the first on go-to-market. Like, now he runs all of go-to-market.

Ant: The Postgres guy was first.

Paul: No, Angelico.

Ant: Angelico, yeah, we had an intern.

Paul: An intern from my previous startup. We just dragged him along. Yeah. And then the other, like, first, like, full-time hire was this guy, Steve Chavez, who was the Postgres maintainer.

And the funny thing is — we were in the YC batch and the advice they give you in YC is, like, "Okay, we're going to give you a bunch of money. Don't hire anyone. If the big temptation is to hire a big team." And we went to our partner and we said, "Oh, but we've got this guy, Steve, he's the lead maintainer of Postgres." And he was like, "Hire him immediately." He was like, "Forget the advice, go and get him."

Swyx: Of his reputation or because it made sense for Supabase?

Paul: Well, yeah, both. It just made sense that this was a technology we were very reliant on and we were going to lean in. And the funny thing is, we hired Steve and we said, "Don't worry about Supabase, just keep building Postgres and just making it awesome. And then obviously, if we have support requests or whatever, we can ask them." And the model just worked really well. And then we ended up, when Steve wanted to grow the Postgres team, just hiring more people dedicated to work on that project.

商业开源的未来：Rust 重写？

Swyx: Well, you guys are doing so much for community and open source. One thing I do have in my mind is, like, what is the future of large commercial open source? One, obviously there's a lot of slop and I'm sure you guys are dealing with that. But two, also your dependencies are now becoming optional. Like, you can just vibe-code whatever you want.

Paul: Anything, yeah.

Swyx: Yeah, yeah. So whatever is in your heads about the future of open source, I'd just love to hear it.

Paul: I think the rewrite in Rust is a valid mechanism. I mean, someone came to me on our team and they're like, "Oh, yeah, yeah, I'm rewriting everything in Rust that we're doing." And I was like, "To what level? Are you going to rewrite the database? Are you going to rewrite Postgres?" Postgres is not in Rust, but I doubt down to that level you care. So there's layers upon which you want to get to where things will be rewritten. And then you don't want to be spending your actual innovation tokens — or your actual tokens — rewriting everything.

So there's going to be a collapse of almost every tool probably into, let's say, Rust, if that ends up being the ultimate way of writing things, because it's faster and more correct. And that will happen probably for most open source tools. But then after you've done this iteration and everything's running on this highly effective language, then you're not going to be rewriting all of the things every single time. There'll be a few winners.

A really classic one could be, say, Postgres is written in — Haskell, which is a very unusual language and it's very hard to maintain. Could it be written in Rust now? Yeah, probably it could. And the mechanism, the function is still valuable. And probably there'll be, if that happens, there'll be one Rust fork of Postgres and that will be the winner for that particular category.

Swyx: But you haven't done it yet. And a lot of your stuff is Elixir as well.

Paul: Yeah, so that's the other thing. Then you have to think on the infrastructure side. Elixir is, like, a really interesting language because of the BEAM. So then you start thinking when you're operating things, what is the right mechanism for operating?

Swyx: But now you can change paradigms pretty much easily as long as you fit all your tests.

Paul: Yeah, well, that's a good one. I haven't thought a lot about would we switch Elixir to Rust? It's just an option now.

Swyx: Malte from Vercel is, you know, one of his tweets that sticks in my mind — he's got lots of interesting thoughts. He says, "I have some amount of money and rewrite all of our dependencies at the C level or C++ level into Rust because we just know it is safer, more correct, whatever." And it is a one-time thing — the upgrade of open source.

Paul: Yeah.

Swyx: All the drivers, whatever you use. So I thought that was a pretty interesting call.

Paul: I like that as an idea. Yeah. I don't think it will happen because people love to do it themselves. Yeah. But as an idea, I would — like, we as a company would 100% get behind that.

Supabase 内部的 AI 编程政策与花费

Swyx: Awesome. And then I think closing question, which I should have stuck in somewhere earlier — AI coding within Supabase, right? Obviously, you guys are big beneficiaries of coding agents outside. What is the policy internally? How much are you spending? Is there concern about spend? Anything of that sort?

Ant: Supabase has always felt like a bunch of different startups glued together. So we have the auth product and we've always been very insistent that they should make their own decisions on what tools they use, how they behave as a team, the reporting structure. And the AI policy was kind of no different. A lot of people ask them, "What is the AI coding policy?" And we were like, "Well, it's up to you as your team."

I think we have started to consolidate a few bits, especially around cost. But as much as we can, we'd like to keep that model of, like, let the teams decide how they want to run things.

Swyx: That's it. Very decentralized. I would say I am trying to figure out a number for company leaders to take home with them as, like, what is the market standard?

Ant: And so, what are the data points you can hang your hat on here?

Swyx: People say, you know, the average person is spending, like, $20 a month and then average employee is maybe $200 a month. OpenAI, you know, the sort of 50th percentile is spending maybe 3 to 5,000 a month. And the top percentile is in the maybe hundreds of thousands, right? And so that is the rough idea. I think a good metric is basically, what is your ratio of token spend to human spend? And it's, like, for a lot of people, it's maybe 0.1 tokens to one human salary. And, you know, you can probably go up to one pretty safely. And if you're over 1.5, you're probably in trouble. Something like that.

Paul: So I'll just say, luckily, as a remote company, basically everything that's ever happened is documented. So I can ask our AI how much we're spending. So currently we spend about 300K per month. Yeah, for 600 people.

Ant: No, for 450 people.

Paul: 450 people. Yeah.

Swyx: Okay. It gives people an idea. But what you've said about, like, scaling the cost in terms of related to the number of employees makes sense.

Ant: Also for us, because — we are hiring very quickly. So if we end up getting a lot of leverage out of just, like, actual —

Swyx: You should be, right?

Ant: Yeah.

Swyx: You need a whole bunch of serverless employees that can spin up and down as you need, right?

Ant: Yeah, exactly.

Swyx: Which is, like, yeah, like, you know, I just had a CTO of, you know, another top startup say, like, he was worried about his company's spend. And I'm, like, "Well, actually that's your investment in everyone else." And probably it's very skewed, right? Like, there's, like, two or three people that are super insane in your company and everyone else is, like, probably not using AI enough.

Ant: Yeah, yeah. That's exactly what we see as well. We've got a leaderboard, and people — we put the leaderboard up and usually people are a little bit ashamed. So they're kind of like, "Yeah, because you're wasting money." Probably.

Paul: Yeah. And that's also the wrong focus. Like, the focus shouldn't be on how much you're spending, but, like, how much end-to-end — like, in terms of systems thinking — you should be thinking, like, in terms of how many end-to-end processes are you actually solving where you no longer need a human in the loop, or collapsing down long-running human problems that suddenly become very short problems. So that's where we're spending most of our investment on how we're using AI.

Luckily, you know, as you saw, like, every single thing that's ever happened in Supabase is documented, because we're an async company. So building a company harness, like an agentic harness around Supabase, is basically just formalizing — you can point AI at it and say, "What are our principles?" And it will document down all our decision-making principles for the whole history of Supabase. So that's where we're spending a lot of our time.

招聘：50 个远程岗位

Paul: Before we move on from people, we do have, I think now, like, 50 open roles. And we are fully globally remote. So we don't care where you are, if you're very good.

Swyx: Same salary everywhere, right?

Paul: Yeah, same salary, regardless of where you live. If you're very good at what you do, please take a look at our job board.

Swyx: Yeah, can you, like, one profile, just pick one, whatever is top of mind as your highlight for what you're looking for and why?

Paul: SREs.

Swyx: Okay. Yeah. Why?

Paul: Because we're just growing at a ridiculous rate. We need all the SREs we can get.

Swyx: What is the quality that is, like, you know, you probably get a lot of SRE applications and you don't look at them. Like, what stands out?

Paul: The thing that we really care about is that you actually want to work remotely. This is a strange one, but yeah, it's true. We get a lot of quality people, but to fit in at Supabase, you kind of need to thrive in a remote-first environment, like a fully async environment. It's actually not for everyone. We learned that pretty early on — people would come in and they'd be like, "Oh, this is like, I need to see humans."

Swyx: My typical model of an SRE is, like, this gray beard that's, like, sitting in a dungeon somewhere and doesn't want to talk to humans anymore.

Paul: That's the perfect person. All of those people, please apply it. Hopefully they listen to the podcast. Yeah, we probably do have a lot of gray beards in SRE.

Swyx: As I think one of them, I have been on the record as saying AI SRE is one of the hardest categories for agent startups. I think I might be wrong soon, but so far it's been correct. Like AI has not cracked — sorry, for whatever reason. No, no, no, no, not yet. I agree. Like, building software is, you know, debatable, solved problem. Maintaining, like, keeping things running is a whole different beast.

结尾

Paul: Well, okay. Well, thank you for keeping things running for everyone else. You guys, congrats on your journey, man. I'm so proud to be your friend and investor. Just see the progress. I cannot wait for the IPO, whatever that is. It looks like it's going to take some more time. But it'll be fun. I really want to see you guys do the whole ring-the-bell and building the next great open source company. Right? Excellent.

Paul / Ant: Definitely, man. Thanks for having us.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的发现：Supabase 把销售团队当作临床试验
视频里几乎被一笔带过、但其实是整场对话最值得解剖的一段是 Paul 描述他们的 "Product-Led Sales" 补偿机制：
- 每周 1000 个产品信号触发邮件 → 500 人回应 → **把那 500 个不回应的人作为"控制组"**。 - 控制组自然增长 25%／月；接触组增长 125%／月。 - 销售的提成只计算那 100% 的增量差额。
这是**制药行业双盲试验的逻辑被挪用到了销售激励上**——他们不是在"卖东西"，而是在用 counterfactual（反事实推断）来定价人类销售的边际价值。多数公司以 ARR 配额激励销售，这会污染数据；Supabase 却选择牺牲归因的直觉性，换取"销售的真实 lift 可被统计证明"。这背后的隐藏假设极其激进：**公司默认 PLG 流量会自己长大，销售只是加速器，不是增长的因**。这种自我怀疑式的 KPI 设计，在 SaaS 里几乎是异类。
## 二、意料之外的"时间套利"：AEO 的赢家，是 LLM 诞生之前就存在的公司
Swyx 顺口提了一句——Su

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] The Transistor That Took 34 Years to Ship
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被刻意"雪藏"34 年的终极方案

最反直觉的事实是：Gate-All-Around 并不是"后来才想出来"的新主意，它在 1988 年就被演示过了——比 FinFET 还早一年。可它却整整在实验室里"冬眠"了 34 年才真正进入量产。为什么？Chris 一句话道破玄机："You don't want to tackle something before you have to（除非被逼到墙角，否则不要去动最终极的那张牌）。"

这其实是一种技术期权（technological real option）的管理哲学——与金融学中巴菲特持有现金等待"胖投球"的逻辑完全同构。工程界有个默认叙事："好想法必然立刻胜出"，但半导体史恰恰相反：最好的想法必须被战略性延迟。原因是：一旦打出终极牌，供应链、设备商、材料库全部要同步升级，社会总成本极高；而 strained silicon、high-k metal gate、FinFET 这些"中间牌"虽然不完美，却是把问题分段摊销的"过桥方案"。

跨界回声：这与生物进化中的"间断平衡（punctuated equilibrium）"惊人地相似——物种从不在环境允许时主动采纳所有可能的改良，而是在旧生态位崩塌时才突变式跃迁。晶体管不是"越来越好地解决老问题"，而是在旧 scaling 范式死亡的那一刻才被允许进化。

二、尺度危机本质是一场"维度升级战"

教科书把晶体管进化讲成"越来越小"，这是一个误导性叙事。真正的隐藏模式是控制维度在升维：

  • Planar MOS：栅极从1 个面接触沟道
  • FinFET：从3 个面包裹
  • GAA：从4 个面（甚至是曲面环绕）完全封闭

换句话说，当平面空间（2D）里的物理游戏打不下去（电子会从底部"漏"出去），工程师并没有去发明"更强的电场"或"更神奇的硅"，而是把问题从 2D 搬到了 3D 来重新定义。这是一种拓扑式的解题——不是用力气打破瓶颈，而是把瓶颈所在的维度换掉。

一个让人意外的类比：这几乎是量子力学从一维势阱发展到三维球对称势场的历史重演；也类似建筑结构从砖砌（面受力）走向空间桁架（三维受力）的跃迁。所有在二维中无解的问题，升一个维度往往就自动求解。 芯片业其实是在用拓扑手段逃避物理极限。

三、芯片里藏着 5000 年前的"失蜡法"

转录中最被低估的一句话是："we use a placeholder because the materials in the real gate wouldn't survive the processing that comes after"——真正的栅极材料受不了后续 1000°C 的高温，所以先用一个假的占位材料替身演完整个流程，再把它蚀刻掉，让栅极金属"长"进去。

这不就是失蜡法（lost-wax casting）吗？ 公元前 3000 年苏美尔人铸造青铜像时就在用的工艺——先用蜡做出模型，外头包泥烧硬，再把蜡融化流出，最后浇入金属。半导体工业在纳米尺度上几乎一字不差地复刻了青铜时代的制造哲学。

更深一层的洞见是：最尖端的工程往往需要"用会被丢弃的东西来定义最终形状"。胚胎发育依赖脊索（notochord）但成年个体中它消失；哥特大教堂的扶壁其实是脚手架美学化的产物；现代 3D 打印必须打支撑结构然后再切除。scaffold-and-remove 是宇宙中最通用的建造元算法之一——它暗示一个颠覆性的工程原则：不要试图用一个材料同时满足"制造过程"和"最终功能"两套需求。只要你坚持"一步到位"，你就会被最弱的那个约束锁死。

四、彩蛋式观察：Dennard 死亡 = 创新黄金时代

Chris 把 2000 年后称为晶体管的"golden age of innovation"。注意这个措辞的违反直觉之处：当 Dennard scaling（可预测的性能自动翻倍）终结时，业内本应陷入悲观，结果反而迎来黄金时代。

这暗示一条跨领域的"黑暗启蒙"定律：可预测的进步会抑制创造力；只有当"自动扶梯"坏掉时，人类才真正开始爬楼梯。制药业的专利悬崖之后迎来生物制剂爆发、摩尔定律放缓之后反而催生 TPU/NPU/光计算，都是同一曲线。

所以下次听人说"XX 行业触及瓶颈"时，正确反应不是悲观，而是——准备迎接下一个黄金时代的入场券。

📝 转录文本

导言：晶体管的三维进化史

Modern chip transistors evolved from the planar MOS transistor demonstrated in 1960. The history of transistors since has been the progression from two dimensions into three. Each development that Chris goes on to describe—from FinFET to gate-all-around—is a step in that progression. So it'll help to first look at a basic transistor and how its parts have changed over time.

一、晶体管是如何工作的

A transistor is basically a switch. When it's turned on, it allows current to flow between its two ends, which are called the source and the drain. A piece called a gate sits on top of the silicon between the source and the drain.

Applying a positive voltage to the gate turns the switch on, because the positive voltage pulls negatively charged electrons in the silicon beneath up towards the gate. However, a thin layer of insulation stops them from actually reaching the gate. So the electrons collect just beneath that insulation and form a thin conducting path from the source to the drain. This is called the channel.

Remove the voltage, and the electrons disperse. The channel disappears, and the switch turns off.

二、尺寸危机：当电流开始"偷跑"

As transistors shrank, the source and the drain got so close together that current could flow through the channel even when the switch was supposed to be off. We needed a better way to control the channel and prevent current from leaking through.

The fix was to give the gate a tighter grip on the channel by touching it from more sides.

  • In the original planar transistor, the gate only touches the channel from the top.
  • The FinFET transistor squeezes the channel into a thin vertical fin of silicon. The gate drapes over the fin, so it controls the channel from three sides.
  • The next progression from there was to cover not only the top and the sides of the channel, but also the bottom. This technology is called gate-all-around, and it slices the channel into thin ribbons, each of which gets completely wrapped around by the gate.

三、制造 Gate-All-Around：纳米级的"失蜡法"

But getting gate-all-around to work required new materials and new manufacturing steps. To build these floating ribbons of silicon, you first sandwich them between alternating layers of a temporary placeholder material, which holds the space where the gate will eventually go.

We use a placeholder because the materials in the real gate wouldn't survive the processing that comes after, which involves baking the wafer at around 1,000°C. Once these hot steps are done, chip makers etch away the placeholder, leaving the ribbon suspended. Then they fill the gaps around every ribbon with a thin coat of a special insulator called a high-k material, whose purpose is to let the gate pull more strongly on the channel. And then on top of this material, they put the metal of the gate itself.

四、34 年的鸿沟：想法与量产之间

FinFET was demonstrated in a lab in 1989 and reached volume production at Intel in 2011. A gate-all-around transistor had been demonstrated a year earlier, in 1988, but Samsung didn't begin producing gate-all-around chips until 2022. So these ideas—FinFET and gate-all-around—were developed around the same time, but they reached production a decade apart. I wanted to ask Chris why it took so long to get to this current gate-all-around technology.

问： Maybe you can walk me through the process of getting into high volume manufacturing. I want to understand concretely: once you have an idea that "hey, we're going to make the channel smaller," there are all the other problems of material science and figuring out how to not destroy the gate. How did they actually get figured out? Why does this take so long?

Chris： Gate-all-around's a good example, because back in the 90s we knew of this idea, but we knew there were going to be these problems on how you put this into high volume manufacturing. And at the same time, there's other things like high-k metal gate, there's strained silicon, there's FinFETs that are out there. And so it's kind of like: when's the right time to go and tackle those?

Well, you don't want to tackle something before you have to. And so if you have these other things that can drive performance, you would go and do that. We went through this path where we did strained silicon, high-k metal gate, we did FinFETs, and then it became: well, we need to do things further. How do we get there? Well, gate-all-around is really the ultimate transistor out there. Maybe it's time to go and start tackling some of those issues that you have.

And you're right—now you have to look at how do you put high-k metal gate in with gate-all-around. So it's that innovation that takes time. Sometimes it's: you need new materials. Sometimes it's: you need a different tool in order to be able to do some of the things that you need to go do. And that requires invention from the tool vendor. You have to go to the tool vendor and say, "Hey, I need a tool that can do XYZ. I need a gas that can deposit this particular material that goes into that. I need a heating chuck that has this characteristic to it." All those things take time. And some of it's iterative, where you have to run a gate-all-around transition, you see, "Oh well, that didn't work. Let me figure out what was wrong with my hypothesis and try it again with some different structure."

五、R&D 范式的转折：从"缩小"到"重写规则"

问： How has the nature of R&D changed—from the era of just making planar transistors smaller and smaller and just getting the benefits of Dennard scaling, to the world we're in today? Is it just a totally different kind of R&D process, where previously you just like "let's make things smaller, smaller, smaller," now you do look at all these other facets of performance at the same time, and the improvements in size don't come as easily? Walk me through whether there was some crucial change in the R&D process at that point.

Chris： If you look at the 80s and 90s, yes, it was driven really by Dennard scaling, lithography. We just make things smaller. Transistors got faster, they got more reliable, and it was a very predictable cadence.

When we started to hit the 2000s, what we saw was: that's not good enough anymore. We need to do something different. And to me, it became this golden age of innovation for each technology node. How are you going to provide more scaling? How are you going to provide more performance? And so it drove things like strained silicon. It drove high-k metal gates. It drove FinFETs. It drove gate-all-around. It drove backside power.

These are things that—in the 80s and 90s—you would be like, "Oh no, we're not touching any of that, because we just continue to have the same process flow. We just scale it, scale it, scale it." But for somebody like me who's a transistor junkie, it's awesome, because now the playbook's open. You can do all sorts of things out there. You can bring in new materials.

I mean, just look at the number of materials we used to use in the '90s versus the materials today. It's probably gone up 10x. And there's a lot of innovation there. There's atomic layer depositions—I mean, you're controlling atom by atom this stuff. So it's changed a lot how you approach the process. Before, it was: try to not change anything. Now it's like: take the sledgehammer and start just tearing things up and come up with some new idea.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、被刻意"雪藏"34 年的终极方案
最反直觉的事实是：Gate-All-Around 并不是"后来才想出来"的新主意，它在 1988 年就被演示过了——比 FinFET 还早一年。可它却整整在实验室里"冬眠"了 34 年才真正进入量产。为什么？Chris 一句话道破玄机："**You don't want to tackle something before you have to**（除非被逼到墙角，否则不要去动最终极的那张牌）。"
这其实是一种**技术期权（technological real option）**的管理哲学——与金融学中巴菲特持有现金等待"胖投球"的逻辑完全同构。工程界有个默认叙事："好想法必然立刻胜出"，但半导体史恰恰相反：**最好的想法必须被战略性延迟**。原因是：一旦打出终极牌，供应链、设备商、材料库全部要同步升级，社会总成本极高；而 strained silicon、high-k metal gate、FinFET 这些"中间牌"虽然不完美，却是把问题分段摊销的"过桥方案"。
跨界回声：这与生物进化中的"**间断平衡（punctuated eq

item.title: [Lex Clips] Can AI solve the Riemann Hypothesis? - Mathematician explains | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、认识论的静默颠倒：数学家开始把"确定性"外包给机器

最耐人寻味的，不是 quasi-RH 被证明，而是这位数学家说出的那句话——"Lean 的 sorry-free proof 给我 100% 的信心这个证明是对的"。请注意顺序：他是先相信机器，再去读证明。这是数学共同体中一次悄无声息的权力转移。两千年来，数学的"真"由同行阅读与直觉背书；而现在，一个形式化系统比人类审稿人更先完成了"信任的交付"。

这与航空业有一个几乎同构的历史时刻：1930 年代前，飞行员若与仪表读数发生冲突，往往相信自己的身体感觉——结果是大量"空间迷向"坠机。直到培训文化强制"相信仪表"，飞行安全才真正进入现代。数学现在正站在同样的分水岭：不是 AI 会不会证出 RH，而是人类是否已经交出了"最终裁判"的身份。而且交得非常安静。

二、"七分之八到二分之一"不是距离问题，是维度问题——这正是 AI 时代的本质瓶颈

他轻描淡写地说："这个方法从根本上到不了二分之一。"这句话比它听起来重要得多。它意味着 quasi-RH 的突破不是在"向 RH 推进"，而是撞上了一堵内生于方法本身的天花板——就像卡诺循环再怎么优化也突破不了热力学第二定律，就像古典力学再怎么精细化也到不了量子尺度。

跨领域来看，这是所有"工具-问题"关系的通病：深度学习的 scaling law 终将遭遇架构性瓶颈；心理治疗中的 CBT 对某些人群永远触不到根；传统货币政策工具在零利率下失效。真正的进步从来不是"把方法用得更狠"，而是换一个维度。所以这位数学家说"需要一个新 idea"时，他实际上说的是：AI 若要攻克 RH，不能靠把 quasi-RH 的证明"推得更远"，而要靠跳出该证明所居住的整个概念空间。而这，恰恰是今天的 AI 最不擅长的事——它擅长在既有维度中搜索极值，不擅长制造新维度。

三、一个让人意外的观察：这次突破的"厚度"不在数学里，而在等待时间的曲线里

"这条线七十年没动过。" ——然后突然，不是增厚，而是整条垂直带。

如果你把过去 150 年 RH 相关进展画成一条曲线，你会看到一个极其反直觉的形状：不是渐进逼近，而是长平台 + 突发跳跃。这与科学史学家 Thomas Kuhn 描述的"范式转换"曲线一模一样，但更惊人的是——它也与进化生物学中的"间断平衡"（punctuated equilibrium）完全同构：物种在百万年中几乎不变，然后在短时间内剧变。

这暗示一个几乎令人不安的推论：人类重大数学突破的时间分布，可能本质上是一个遵循幂律的 Poisson 过程，而不是努力的线性函数。也就是说，70 年的停滞不是"因为人类不够努力"，而是突破的到来有其自身的概率结构。那么 AI 真正会改变的，也许不是"能不能证"，而是改变这个 Poisson 过程的参数——把两次跳跃之间的期望等待时间，从 70 年压缩到 7 年，甚至 7 个月。

而最吊诡的"啊哈"在这里：如果 AI 把数学突破的时间间隔压缩得足够短，数学界就会面临一个前所未有的问题——消化不良。Lex 问"你有生之年能看到 RH 吗"，但真正该问的是："即使看到了，人类数学家还有时间去真正理解它吗？" 当证明的产生速度超过人类理解的速度时，数学会不会变成一门我们只能"验证"却不再"居住"的学科？

📝 转录文本

On the Leap from Quasi-RH to the Full Riemann Hypothesis

Lex: Do you think — so the leap between quasi and RH, I presume you think humans will not, in your lifetime, be able to solve without AI's help, the full Riemann Hypothesis?

Guest: I don't know.

Lex: Can AI, I guess, is the follow-on question. Like, how hard is it?

Guest: I don't know. I don't know. I did not think I would see a proof of quasi-RH.

Why the Proof Can Be Trusted: Lean Formalization

Now that I see what the proof is, and there are a lot of technical details that I still have to go through for my own satisfaction — there's a Lean formalization. The Lean statement was already in the library, was already in Mathlib, so the fact that they have a sorry-free proof gives me 100% confidence that the proof is right.

And moreover, having read the proof, you know, at a high level, the ideas that it's using are all completely valid. They're brilliant. You know, to embed the Möbius function, twist it by sextic characters — this is all stuff that's the bread and butter of analytic number theorists, that was chained in just the right way and was absolutely incredible.

The Critical Strip and What Riemann Showed

And so what Riemann showed is that — remember, we were talking about this function that has complex inputs and has these outputs, and we're worried about when the output is zero. So he showed that there's what's called the critical strip, which is a vertical infinite strip in the complex plane, where the real part is — so you can think about the X coordinate lies between zero and one, and the imaginary part, the Y coordinate, can go arbitrarily high or arbitrarily low.

And the hypothesis is that the zeros all lie right at the dead center of that strip, where the real part is a half. That's exactly what Ankur was just saying.

What We Knew Until Tuesday: The Zero-Free Region

And what we knew until Tuesday was a region where there are no zeros of the zeta function — that's like getting thinner and thinner the higher up you go. It goes towards the one line.

The one line is something called the prime number theorem, which tells you the basic distribution of the prime numbers is equivalent to the fact that there are no zeros of this function on the line real part of S equals one. So if the X coordinate is one — as you go up and down that line, you will never find a value where, when you apply the zeta function, it hits zero.

Okay? So we have this zero-free region that was getting thinner and thinner the higher up you go, and that gave us the best known distribution on the prime numbers, the best error term in the prime number theorem — which I can go into if you… you tell me how much math you wanna talk about.

Lex: Let's go.

The Surprise: A Vertical Strip, Not a Thickened Line

But what I could have anticipated is that it would thicken that line a little bit as you — you know, it would still be going to zero. The thickness would still be going to zero as you go up the imaginary axis, but it would be better than what we currently know. That thickness hasn't moved in seventy years, but I could sort of imagine that it could maybe make some progress.

What it did is it gave us a vertical strip — so there are no zeros with real part between seven-eighths and one, an entire infinite vertical strip. That's a quasi-Riemann hypothesis. And if you can get that seven-eighths down to a half, that's the full Riemann hypothesis.

Why This Method Can't Finish the Job

Now, the methods that it used in the seven-eighths proof — and there's a second proof that's about eleven-twelfths, never mind these technical details — that method sort of fundamentally can't get down to one half.

Lex: So a new idea is needed.

Guest: You need a new idea. But quasi-RH needed lots and lots of new ideas, and it came up with that.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [a16z] Mark Cuban’s Plan to Make Healthcare Affordable
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：Mark Cuban 真正在卖的，不是药，是"信任的套利"

表面上看，Cost Plus Drugs 是一家药品公司。但如果你仔细听 Mark 的语言——"trust is still our primary product"——他真正在做的生意是信任的套利。

这里有一个几乎没人谈论的系统性真相：在一个被破坏的市场里，透明度本身是最稀缺的商品。15% 的毛利不是定价策略，它是信任的"票价"。消费者愿意为"我知道你没有骗我"支付溢价，哪怕这个"没骗我"的价格仍然低于被欺骗的价格。

更深层的洞察是：Mark 不是在和 CVS、United Health 竞争药品——他在和它们争夺消费者认知带宽中的"诚实槽位"。而这个槽位在整个经济体中几乎都是空的。这解释了一个诡异现象——为什么 UnitedHealth 的销售会在没有合同的情况下，谎称 Cost Plus 是他们网络的一部分：他们在偷用 Mark 的信任资本来掩盖自己的不信任赤字。这是品牌寄生，但寄生的不是 logo，而是道德权威。

二、跨领域连接：医疗 ASO 合同 = 加密货币的"智能合约悖论"倒影

Mark 讲到达拉斯市的 PBM 合同有 1335 页——他称之为"合同恐怖主义"。这里有一个让人不寒而栗的跨领域映射：

传统医疗合同是"反智能合约"。加密世界的智能合约承诺"代码即法律"——条款被压缩到可以在毫秒内验证执行。而医疗 ASO 合同走的是完全相反的路径：条款被故意膨胀到人类认知带宽无法处理的程度，使得"签字"和"理解"之间永久脱钩。

这揭示了一个被忽视的系统原理——复杂度本身是一种武器。它不是设计缺陷，是定价结构的一部分。1335 页不是律师的傲慢，是精心校准到人类注意力极限之上一寸的信息战。

而 Mark 的"用 AI 读合同"策略，本质上是在做什么？他在把 ASO 合同从"反智能合约"强制翻译回"智能合约"——用算力把语言复杂度压回到人类可处理的尺度。这是一个加密世界从未遇到过的问题的镜像解法：不是从代码走向法律，而是从法律的病理性膨胀反向走回代码。

同样的模式还藏在哪里？税法、劳动合同、服务条款、保险精算表、学区协议——所有"长度即保护"的领域都即将经历同样的 AI 压缩冲击。医疗只是第一张倒下的多米诺。

三、系统性预言：Cost Plus 的"Pod"是对工业革命的反向工程

大家都在听 Mark 说"20 亿美元 pod 业务"，但很少有人意识到他在描述什么。

工业革命的底层逻辑是：集中化 + 规模化 = 低成本。所以我们建了底特律、建了富士康、建了印度仿制药工厂。但 Mark 的制药 pod——$2000 万一个、拖车大小、每四小时切换药品、可以 daisy chain 组合——是对这个前提的根本性反叛。

他真正在做的是把"规模经济"重新定义为"配置经济"。规模经济说："越多越便宜。"配置经济说："越对越便宜。"一个研究医院为某个 N-of-one 病人订制药品的边际成本，比等待印度工厂改线便宜得多——如果 pod 就在隔壁房间。

这里的系统性真相是：AI 不是让制造业更智能，是让它更小、更近、更专。它的真正敌人不是劳动力成本，而是物流和合规延迟。pod 把两者同时折叠到接近零。

跨领域映射：这和 3D 打印、小型模块化核反应堆（SMR）、本地化食品生产系统是同一个浪潮。整个 20 世纪建立的"中心化生产 + 全球物流"范式，正在被 AI + 机器人 + 配置化重塑为"按需生产 + 零距离部署"——医药只是技术成熟度最先触顶的那一个。

Mark 真正的赌注不是药——是赌全球供应链的拓扑结构正在翻转。如果他赢了，印度仿制药工厂不是被更便宜的美国工厂打败，而是被 pod 的地理不可知性淘汰。工厂去找病人，而不是药去找病人。

四、一个藏在对话里的暗线：所有玩家都在"等一个契约时刻"

通读整个对话，有一个被 Mark 反复强调但没有被完整命名的现象——美国医疗系统的失败不是技术失败，是契约失败。

无论是 1335 页的 PBM 合同、EOB、ASO 的 835/837 文件、拒赔和清算、还是雇主对自身账单的无知——整个系统的病理学都发生在"签字那一刻"。AI 的 bot wars、provider 的 upcoding、支付方的 denial——这些都是契约签订后的军备竞赛后遗症。

Mark 的所有干预——cost plus wellness 开源合同、"把你的现有合同喂给 AI 问他们在哪里坑你"、公开州级 RFP——都指向同一个战略支点：把契约时刻变得对称。

这里的洞见是：整个美国医疗 4.5 万亿美元的无效支出，可能可以追溯到不到几千份被少数几家公司垄断了认知权的合同。如果你是风投，这意味着最高杠杆的医疗创业机会，不是做更好的医生、更好的 AI 诊断、更好的保险产品，而是做"合同反恐"——一个解析、比对、谈判支持的 AI 层，服役于那 160M 美国雇员。

这个市场从未被定义过。它的 TAM 可能大于所有数字健康公司加起来。

📝 转录文本

开场：医疗市场的根本失灵

We are not in an efficient healthcare market. The economics are broken.

One of the many ills of healthcare is that it completely lacks competitive dynamics. Just merely by the presence of plus drugs, you've actually forced change in [music] the incumbents.

United Health 3,000 plus subsidiaries, $150 billion in intercomp transfers annually. There's often times when they will increase premiums, increase deductibles, and at the same time force you into a relationship with a company they already own and you don't know they own them. The ultimate mission is to disrupt healthcare so that it's affordable again.

Is there like some area where you're like, why is no one building here? There's no better time to be an entrepreneur than right now. The biggest challenge and where AI, I think, is going to have the biggest impact is...

欢迎与引入

Well, Mark, welcome to the podcast. Thanks so much for joining.

Thanks for having me on, guys.

Julie, what has struck you about Mark's contributions in the space? What have you always found fascinating about what Mark's been up to with Cost Plus Drugs or and just in general, and why you invited him on to the show?

I mean, Mark, first of all, just had the courage to enter into the morass that is healthcare in a way that made such a splash — and that many, many people who, you know, also are in the privileged position that Mark is in to just have such a huge audience have been intimidated to do over many, many decades.

And so I've loved watching the market react to what Mark has done in healthcare. I think, you know, the one thing I know Mark — you and I have talked about this in the past — but healthcare is one of the industries where one of the many ills is that it completely lacks competitive dynamics and competitive forces, free market dynamics, all that kind of stuff.

And what's been fascinating to watch is just merely by the presence of Cost Plus Drugs as one example — and we'll talk about others that you've done too — but just merely by the presence of that entity and what you represent and what you're doing, you've actually forced change in the incumbents that otherwise, even with policy, even with all sorts of other forces, like never changed over the course of many, many decades.

Yeah, 'cause I don't get to see that stuff 'cause I don't talk to those guys.

影子网络效应：没有合同也在被引用

And then I think to your point, like even absent a contract, I think people are recognizing from the demand side of the market that they need to show that there is some pathway for people to get your product, right? And so perhaps even in the absence of a direct contract, I do hear people talking about your solution as part of their network.

Really, it truly does not surprise me when the big three or even the big six use our name as kind of a way to counter the request, you know, in the discussion of pricing — 'cuz they know that our prices are public, that anybody can take our API, and big companies that have half a brain are pulling that data on a daily basis, and they're saying, "You have to beat this price." And so I can see that.

But, you know, I've had at least one company and probably more that have said, "Oh yeah, it's, you know, pick one of the big three has told us that you're part of their network and we get your prices where you're cheaper," and we don't have an agreement at all with any of the big three.

业务版图巡览：四根支柱

Mark, let's zoom out and take stock about where you're at with the business. You launched in 2022 with a few dozen drugs. In April this year, you said you were up to roughly 4,000. You're getting into manufacturing, hospital contracts, potentially AI-based care. Why don't you take stock a little bit of where the business is?

1. Cost Plus Drugs（邮购）

I'll give you the rundown. So, we launched costplusdrugs.com — I mean January 19th of 2022. 111 medications, purely generic, and we didn't know what to expect at all. I went out and started talking about it and it immediately blew up, right?

And then our volumes there led the manufacturers to expand their portfolio with us and we were able to add additional manufacturers. So now, as you said, we have 4,000 SKUs give or take, and our business every week is up and to the right. So our biggest challenge is just keeping up with it. So that's segment number one.

2. Team Cuban Card（本地取药）

Then the obvious response to mail order is "well, I need to pick things up today." And so we created what's called the teamcubancard.com. I did not name it. And it's basically a discount card that allows you to go to any of the 17,000 pharmacies that have affiliated with us and pick up most of our drugs locally — because I'm a big believer in supporting independent pharmacy.

So we pay our affiliate pharmacies a $12 fill fee, which means that's going to make us more expensive for the lowest cost drugs — because if you have a $5 statin plus $12, you're going to get it cheaper somewhere else. But at the same time, if you really want to support your independent pharmacies, you can pick up the cheap drugs. But on the more expensive drugs, the specialty generics, the biosimilars, we're actually much cheaper. And for things like biosimilars and insulin and things that have cold shipping, it's actually cheaper to buy it and pick it up locally through our Team Cuban Card. So that's the second stool in what we offer.

3. 达拉斯制造与 Pod：把工厂塞进拖车

Third is cost plus marketplace. Well, before I get to cost plus marketplace, let me go back to our Dallas manufacturing.

A big part of — Alex, my co-founder, Dr. Oxmanski — his original cold email to me was he wanted to manufacture drugs that are generic drugs that are on the FDA short supply list, because there are pediatric cancer drugs, there are things that are widely used in hospitals — penicillin, oxytocin, epinephrine — this long list of drugs.

And we were able to use AI and robotics to shrink what would have been a football field or more into 5,000 square feet. And not only that, but we were able to turn drugs every four hours. So we can make a six-month supply, turn the line, and then go to the next drug. And we sell those products to hospitals and clinics.

An extension of that — because we've been doing that, we've been working on that five years ago — we've been able to take those same robotics and AI and shrink it into a manufacturing plant, if you will, the size of a tractor trailer. And we call those pods. And those pods can be used for anything and shipped anywhere.

The government was our first customer. We've shipped the first one here recently where we just got an order for a second, and they told us there's more behind that — because if there's an ecological disaster, we can send it to FEMA (if FEMA's around). If there is a weather disaster, military disaster, God forbid, we can ship them there and configure them to make any specific type of drug.

So we can configure a pod for sterile injectables — multiple pods can be daisy-chained together so we can scale, and/or you can have one being a sterile room and another doing the tablet work for generics. I'm not the expert on this; Alex can go into this in precise detail.

But the thing I'm most proud of — and actually Stat News just wrote a story on this yesterday or the day before — is that we can take these pods and configure them to do N-of-one therapies, so that we can ship the pod to a research hospital. These pods cost about $20 million. Ship it to a research hospital, and if they specialize in any types of therapies for those people that are in the N-of-one category, they can make it and iterate very quickly there. And then now we're doing these ASO drugs — and don't ask me what ASO stands for because I can't pronounce it — out of our first manufacturing facility in Dallas. So that's part two.

4. Cost Plus Marketplace

From that manufacturing, we created costplusmarketplace.com. And Cost Plus Marketplace takes those sterile injectables we make, and others that we source from other providers or other manufacturers, and we sell them at a cost-plus-10 or cost-plus-12 to clinics, hospitals, providers — whoever wants to buy them at the cheapest price. And we literally can save hospitals millions of dollars a year.

But our biggest challenge there is we convince the CEOs, but we can't always convince the purchasing people to do it.

5. 直接合同与开源契约：Cost Plus Wellness

You still have to know what the variables are that matter versus the ones that don't. You still have to realize that even as processing costs drop towards zero (hopefully at some point in time), there's still a cost associated with it — even if that cost is only time. And so you need somebody there who's been educated in all those pieces.

医学院课程的根本变革

I think, to your point, Julie, where things might change dramatically when it comes to the role of the doctor is how they'll be trained in medical school. They won't be taught the exact same things. They'll have to learn how to use OpenEvidence or whatever else is available out there, and how to extract information — even if it's just that DNA information — and understanding what's in there, and what the model thinks about it, and being able to translate that to the person.

Because effectively, in order for this to work perfectly, everybody has to have their own model. And that's going to be difficult for everybody, even though there's going to be millions, if not hundreds of millions or billions of models created and supported over the next years.

IP 悖论：信息想要自由，而所有者不想

And plus, on top of that, IP becomes a totally different problem that gets introduced into this equation and process. Because up until recently, it's been publish-or-perish. And if you're a doctor and you create something, you want everybody to happen — maybe you can even license it and make some money off of it.

But now, if you try to patent something, every 12-year-old is saying, "Hey, look at this patent, change it just a little bit, and make my own patent." Or if it's a new procedure in healthcare, you might say, "No, you have to come to my model, and you have to pay me $9,999 every access, or to use inference. You're going to use this software that I require, because nobody's going to give away that IP for free." And that creates a lot more problems.

I think part of the underpinning that a lot of AI entrepreneurs have is that — going back to Aaron, "information wants to be free" — the information may want to be free, but the person who owns the IP feels differently. And so that's going to change how we interact with models.

We can argue about frontends that choose which model is least expensive to answer the question, but we haven't had the discussion on where we find the IP that's needed to either train that model, post-train that model, RAG that model, whatever it may be — if that person isn't making it available, but it's absolutely required.

Does that make sense to you guys? Or do you guys think I'm an idiot?

未来需要更多医生而非更少

You know, I think it's really interesting because it also brings up the point of like, what is the role of the doctor in the future? Number one, I agree — actually, I think we're going to need more doctors in the future, because as care advice becomes more abundant, more people are going to demand healthcare, actual real-life healthcare services. And so we're going to find we actually need more doctors.

And there's something to be said about what you're describing as — the role of the doctor today is very rote. It's kind of like these are the tasks you got to do, these quality measures. You barely need to use your brain, honestly, for a lot of the things that doctors are asked to do in the traditional healthcare setting. And what you're describing is like, what if the paradigm moves towards physicians are actually more physician-scientists? Like it's actually their job is to take the bleeding edge of information that we may not know at population scale yet, but on an individual basis they're at the tip of the spear of collecting novel data, generating novel insights about how people are reacting.

Novel data — by definition, stimulating job description to me.

Yes.

Yes. Because by definition — you're exactly right. Novel data equals person.

Mhm. Exactly. And with data —

纵向监测与可穿戴设备

We're going to have longitudinal monitoring. Like the blood pressure is the one that we always talk about, where it's kind of the same principle as what you're saying. The fact that we take our blood pressure once a year is kind of ridiculous because it changes.

Not me.

I got this s*** right here.

You're — yeah, [laughter] you're cutting edge.

And soon we're going to have wearables that are just measuring it in real time, like every single day. And you'll have a much more precise understanding of how you're responding to different therapeutic interventions, and even diet and exercise, and all that kind of stuff.

新职业：AI 翻译员

And that's going to — you bring up a good point, Julie — in terms of novel information. And that's everybody, in terms of finding jobs. You're going to need AI translators for people who may not keep up with these things. Regular people that are in wherever in this country or in the world who just want to live their abundance life, whatever that may be. And you're going to need people who are going to be the translators for what's novel about this circumstance or this individual, and how do you make it valid to AI and the output of the AI valid to the novel to the individual.

That's going to be a job, and it's going to be very difficult to extract everything from an individual that the AI is going to need. And you're going to need to have a person there to do it. Maybe somebody envisions a humanoid robot that is going to ask you those questions, and somebody's going to be comfortable. I don't think that's going to happen.

关于 EHR：Epic 的世界

By the way, Mark, I don't think I've ever heard you talk about another set of entrenched incumbents, which is the EHR companies. What's your theory of the case there — how that market changes or evolves or doesn't in the age of AI, and what that looks like in the next few years?

Honestly, I don't know. The EHR is dominated by Epic, and it's their world. And so I've just kind of deferred to them and tried to stick where I can have an impact — because we partner with them. We think offering pricing (particularly pharmaceutical pricing) at the point of script, where the doctor is there offering them different options, is a —

Part of that new announcement that they just made about the —

Yeah, exactly. With Epic and Amazon, etc. So I think that's a big plus, and I think that's needed. But in terms of their actual business and where it's disruptable, I'm not really the one qualified for that.

Okay. My problem, by the way, with that announcement was that they announced it and then they said it's not going to be available till May of next year, and I was like, why take so long?

I had nothing to do with that. [laughter]

That's typical in this industry, right?

GDP、生产力与"疾病护理"vs"健康护理"

Do you guys think that in 10 years, healthcare is still going to be a fifth or a sixth of whatever it is now of GDP? And is there kind of this sort of terminal state where there's just way more demand than we can supply, and just as it gets easier, as it gets more efficient, we're still — and as GDP grows even 5% a year, hopefully — at some point our demand is still going to cap at 1/5 of the economy?

I do.

Yeah. But the value that we get out of that spend should be —

Well, the value you get out of the people will increase.

Yeah.

Because they'll be healthier.

Yeah.

So there's a difference when it's healthcare — when it's sick care, as a lot of people refer to — versus when it's keeping people healthy, and they're more productive, and there's less downtime, and they're smarter because it's easier to learn, etc.

So I think we'll get greater productivity that'll more than account for it, which we don't get now.

假如 Mark 是总统：五点医疗政策

Zooming out a bit, Mark, we have a mutual friend who's a very prominent pollster — I won't out him here — but he believes, or he's done some work to indicate, that if you ever ran for office, he thinks you could win. Of course, you've said you'll never run. So, speaking hypothetically now: if you were president or if you were advising the next president, I'm curious how you would think about what is the leverage to most address our healthcare challenges, and then I want to hear your broader policy positions.

It's really easy. It's the same thing I tell states that I've testified for.

One, make all contracts with anybody who takes taxpayer money public. No redactions. Because the minute that happens, you start to have an efficient market and the costs go down.

Two, make it so that anybody who can find a better price for less than their current out-of-pocket with their plan, make it apply to their deductible. Allow it to apply to their deductible. Eight states do that at some level already.

Three, for nonprofit hospitals, require them to publish their entire general ledger down to each detailed entry and all their procurement receipts and requirements — so that everybody gets to see it. It's our money. We're the taxpayers.

Four, instead of current insurance plans the way we have them — 72% of those big carriers' revenue comes from taxpayers. They don't take risk anymore. They offload it. Everything's an arbitrage for them.

So, knowing that, we also have to consider that the one debt we never pay off till the day we die is our insurance premiums. Think about that — whether it's Medicare, unless you're on Medicaid, you are paying till the day you expire. And when you need it, you have to fight for it in the current system, and probably foreseeable systems.

一个替代方案：个人医疗储蓄 + 联邦贷款担保 + 止损

To me, if we were able to create a program where you just deposited what would be — let's just say how much you'd pay for a premium under an ACA silver plan in your state — and we just went and did a deal with the bank and said: "Okay, in Texas for a family of five it's $2,100 at your income, right? So you just keep on depositing $2,100 and it accrues and you own it, but it has to be deposited if you want to participate in this program."

And then if you have a medical incident or pharmaceutical incident — you can take that money. If it's not enough, we've worked out a deal with the bank where two things happen:

One, the bank will loan you money up until a point where stop-loss kicks in — which means we're going to take part of that money you deposit and use it for stop-loss coverage.

Two, the federal government or the state is going to guarantee that loan to you, so that the provider is not out, and we're still going to deduct it from your payroll so that you pay it back.

And if you're lucky and you never have an incident, you get to save all that money when you turn 65 and go on Medicare — you just get all that money and all the accrued interest.

Because if you think about it, the federal government will cover or guarantee your student loans. They'll guarantee SBA loans. They'll guarantee home loans or give you a down payment, right?

Like our internet —

Third-world country.

They'll guarantee all these things, even agricultural things. But the most important thing — covering our healthcare, good luck. You know, you're in a bad accident, good luck to you, and we'll maybe push it off to the hospitals. They have to take you in.

So I would create a plan that says: you have to deposit this money. The bank will have a guarantee just like a mortgage, whatever. We'll loan you this money, and then we'll have federal stop-loss programs above some amount — $40,000, whatever it may be. Now, all of a sudden, bye-bye insurance companies. Now, all of a sudden, you're not fighting back, because it's your money to spend as you choose.

Now, we'll have to set thresholds on where and how you could spend it, so you don't just go give it to your cousin Billy who said he's going to fix your broken toe. But within those constraints, I think now all of a sudden we have a better system. So that's what I would do if I was advising in terms of healthcare.

给 AI 行业的营销建议

What about — one of your gifts is storytelling and marketing more generally. What about the AI industry? AI is uniquely unpopular in the US. If you were advising OpenAI, if you were advising Anthropic, on how to change those numbers — and then there's the whole data center saga. I'm curious what your advice would be to the broader AI industry.

I've had these conversations with them, and I told them they're idiots. Because what controls how pretty much everybody in this country thinks right now? Social media algorithms.

Literally, I was having a conversation with a 23-year-old friend that I work with, and we're talking politics — we're discussing who we voted for yesterday, and how and why. And I said, "What about your friends, the other 23-24 year olds?" And they said that their friends didn't even know (living in Texas) didn't even know who Ken Paxton or James Terico were. Which is insane in my mind, but it reinforces the fact that you get more of what you seek via algorithms.

And if you really have the best AI, you should be able to not only reverse-engineer those algorithms, but put together a marketing program — because you sure tell everybody you can do marketing programs through your bots, or DOT or whatever — and really start marketing there. Because this applies to politics, it applies to AI, it applies to everything in this country, the divisiveness.

We all have our unique AI feed in the social media platforms we use, and those platforms don't give a f*** what it feeds you within some minimal constraints. And so everybody looks at the world differently.

The days — particularly for younger people — of thinking "just buy more ads and ruin our football games and our basketball games and everything's fine" — maybe older people vote more, and that's maybe why — but it's useless when you're trying to change hearts and minds about AI specifically. Even though the irony of it all is that it's the AI behind the algorithms that's ruining everything.

But as long as Section 230 is there, we are where we are. And as long as — unless we take an Australia-type approach or some states-type approach of 16-and-under — my advice to them specifically was: you need to use your AI to segment everything and figure out the best way to put together marketing, promotion, and however else you want to do it. Do it like the Russians do it. It doesn't matter, right? Because that's what's at stake for you.

But people — data-center hate is just a proxy for not being able to understand AI. And not knowing all the pieces there. And I don't blame people at all. Just like employers have been really dumb with their healthcare benefits, a lot of communities have been really dumb with the deals they've negotiated for data centers — they've fallen for the contractual terrorism in a lot of cases.

But educating them about social media, and educating our legislators and whoever's president about social media, because I don't think they truly understand the impact that we don't all read the same newspaper, the same magazines, look at the same websites, watch the same news shows. We all have our own unique TikTok feed.

Your feed is not like mine. The best way to find out about your kids is to just look at their social media feed. My 17-year-old son — it's basketball, basketball, basketball. Now I'm starting to see a little bit of politics pop up, but then hot girl, hot girl, hot girl, basketball, basketball, car, car. And I'm like, okay, typical 17-year-old guy, right?

But until the big frontier models understand completely that they have to figure out how to become part of everybody's feed — they're going to be putting out all these position papers that are useless.

创业的空白地带：所有地方

No, I mean, Mark, we agree with you that this is like the best time to be alive and an entrepreneur. And so many things that again were intractable historically are now all of a sudden addressable. Is there an area of the market — and you meet a lot of entrepreneurs and see people building in all sorts of areas of the world — is there like some area where you're like, "Why is no one building here?" that you think is still a whitespace opportunity for entrepreneurs?

两种公司，两种人

All of them. Seriously. When I go talk to kids, I always tell them: there's going to be two types of companies — those who are great at AI, and those who have gone out of business.

And if you take the time to learn — then there's two types of people and how they use AI: those who use AI to learn anything, and those who use AI so they don't have to learn anything.

And if you're one of those people who uses AI so that you can learn anything, and you realize what type of companies and problems aren't being solved by AI — don't be shy to just talk to your AI.

And I say this not just to kids — to 50-year-old, 60, 70-year-old entrepreneurs. The biggest challenge right now with people, entrepreneurs using AI, is the comfort level of talking to your AI — whether it's by voice or typing, whatever it is — because there's still a lot of hesitancy.

Just like back in the day, those first spreadsheets, people still had their 10-key adding machine, and they would check it to make sure the spreadsheets were right. You still do have to check the output, but you have the opportunity to take the output of Grok and put it into ChatGPT. And the output of — like when I go through all these contracts I was telling you about, I start with one and say, "Hey, one of your peers came out and said this about this contract. What do you think?" And spend a couple hours.

That's all. Young entrepreneurs — so when you ask me, is there one thing? I truly believe it's everything. Everything will change. This is the greatest transitional technology we have ever seen, and I've been around for all of them. And this blows them all away.

The hardest part is just going for it. And that's where Silicon Valley, and kids from the Bay Area, I think, have a little bit of an advantage — because they see their parents and friends and the culture there as "little go." But I think the rest of the country and the rest of the world, once they get that confidence level, you're going to start to see businesses we never imagined pop up — because we're not seeing that yet.

We're not seeing companies where it's like, "Oh, what is that? Why are they doing that? What is the opportunity there?" And then they realized it before we did, right? It's kind of like Napster — first like, "Whoa, what was that?"

So I think the biggest thing to focus on if you're looking for something is: ask anything. I do it all the time. It's just like, "What do you think about this? What do you think about this? What do you think about this?"

I've held phones up next to each other and taken the output and had them have a conversation with each other so I could listen in. Don't be shy about using AI in things that feel really uncomfortable and weird — because that uncomfortableness is probably the path to something that is groundbreaking and game-changing.

结束

That's a great note to wrap on. Mark, thank you so much for coming on the podcast.

It was fun. Thanks, guys. Thanks, Julie. Thanks, Eric.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：Mark Cuban 真正在卖的，不是药，是"信任的套利"
表面上看，Cost Plus Drugs 是一家药品公司。但如果你仔细听 Mark 的语言——"trust is still our primary product"——他真正在做的生意是**信任的套利**。
这里有一个几乎没人谈论的系统性真相：**在一个被破坏的市场里，透明度本身是最稀缺的商品**。15% 的毛利不是定价策略，它是信任的"票价"。消费者愿意为"我知道你没有骗我"支付溢价，哪怕这个"没骗我"的价格仍然低于被欺骗的价格。
更深层的洞察是：Mark 不是在和 CVS、United Health 竞争药品——他在和它们**争夺消费者认知带宽中的"诚实槽位"**。而这个槽位在整个经济体中几乎都是空的。这解释了一个诡异现象——为什么 UnitedHealth 的销售会在没有合同的情况下，谎称 Cost Plus 是他们网络的一部分：**他们在偷用 Mark 的信任资本来掩盖自己的不信任赤字**。这是品牌寄生，但寄生的不是 logo，而是道德权威。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Mathematician explains Navier-Stokes equations | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个颠覆性的观察：Navier-Stokes 其实不是"流体方程"，而是任何有记忆、有惯性、受约束的分布式系统的通用语法

听 Lex 的解释，大多数人会把注意力放在"流体"二字上。但真正令人震撼的是：如果你把这段描述里的"velocity field"替换成"情绪场"、"注意力场"、"资金流向场"、"神经元激活场"——方程的骨架几乎不需要改动。这不是比喻，而是数学同构。

  • 速度场 = 系统在每个点的"倾向性"
  • 压强 = 全局约束（守恒律的"看不见的手"）
  • 动量 = 历史的持续性（为什么系统不能瞬间转向）
  • 粘性 = 内部摩擦（为什么蜂蜜难搅、为什么大型组织难改革）
  • 外力 = 来自系统外的能量注入（加热、重力——或：政策、热点、情绪冲击）

这意味着社交网络的"信息湍流"、金融市场的"恐慌传播"、甚至大语言模型内部 token 之间的"注意力漩涡"，本质上都在跑一个变形的 Navier-Stokes。 这就是为什么 2022 年之后 AI 领域爆发的 Flow Matching、Rectified Flow、Diffusion Models 的核心词汇全都来自流体力学——不是借用术语，是认领了同一个数学现实。

跨领域连接：龙卷风的低压核心 = 爆款内容的"注意力黑洞" = Transformer 的 attention sink

Lex 顺口一句"the core of a tornado is low pressure"藏着一个你可能从未注意的系统性真相：所有自组织的漩涡，中心都是"空的"。

  • 龙卷风中心：气压最低，所以周围的空气被"吸"进来旋转
  • 爆款短视频：内容本身往往极简甚至"空洞"（一个表情、一句口号），但正因如此，人们才能向其投射自己的意义，形成传播漩涡
  • Transformer 大模型里的 "attention sink"（2023 年才被广泛发现）：模型会把大量注意力"倾倒"到第一个 token 这种语义空洞的位置，否则整个注意力分布会崩溃
  • 组织里的"沉默领导者"：话最少的那个人往往聚集最多的信息流

一个让人起鸡皮疙瘩的猜想：是不是所有的旋转结构，都必须有一个"低势能"的核心才能稳定存在？压强的高低差驱动流动——那么在社会系统里，驱动人群聚集的从来不是"中心的实体"，而是中心的"缺失"。流体力学可能是我们理解"为什么大人物往往轮廓模糊"的最严格的学科。

隐藏的系统性真相：粘性 ≠ 阻碍，而是系统能够"记住"自己的唯一方式

人们总把粘性（viscosity）理解为"摩擦力"、"阻力"——负面的、拖后腿的东西。蜂蜜不如水好用，水不如空气轻盈。但从动力系统的视角看，没有粘性的 Navier-Stokes 方程（即 Euler 方程）在数学上会在有限时间内爆炸——速度场会在某点变成无穷大，整个系统失去意义。

换句话说：粘性不是让系统变慢的东西，而是让系统能够存在的东西。

这个洞见可以直接搬到任何系统： - 一个没有任何"组织惯性"的公司，不是敏捷，是会在压力下瞬间崩解 - 一个完全没有情绪延迟的人，不是理性，是失去自我连续性的病态 - 一个没有正则化（regularization，数学上就是加一个粘性项）的神经网络，不会学习，只会在训练数据上爆炸性过拟合

真正的"啊哈时刻"在这里：Navier-Stokes 千禧年难题之所以悬而未决（我们至今不知道三维解是否永远光滑），本质上是在问一个关于所有复杂系统的终极问题——"内部摩擦（粘性）是否足以永远阻止集中性崩溃？" 这个问题在气候、在大脑、在社会、在 AI 训练中反复出现，形式不同，灵魂相同。

你问的从来不只是一个方程。你问的是：分布式系统的记忆、约束与崩溃的边界，到底在哪里。

📝 转录文本

The Building Block: A Velocity Field

What are the different components of the Navier-Stokes equation? Can you — if you — can you dig in? Like, what does it take to describe fluid?

Yeah. So very, very basic: a fluid moves, and it moves differently in different places and at different points in time. And so the kind of basic building block of a fluid is the velocity field. So at every point in space, there is a velocity vector that tells you how that fluid is moving. You know, maybe it's really fast here and slow here, and it creates a vortex.

When Velocity Changes Rapidly: Vortices and Pressure

Um, and it gets more interesting when the fluid velocity changes a lot over space. So like a tornado is a very rapidly changing fluid velocity field in both space and time.

There's pressures that are involved. So again, like the core of a tornado is low pressure. So pressures are, um, kind of forcing this velocity field and causing it to move in the way it does. That's the building block — a velocity field and its pressures.

How the Field Evolves: Momentum, Viscosity, External Forces

And then the equations tell you how that velocity changes in time and in space according to kind of its own momentum. So fluid has momentum to carry itself — that's, you know, gusts of wind.

It has internal friction and resistance. That's viscosity. So honey has more internal resistance than water, has more internal resistance than air.

Um, and then all of the external forces like heating and pressure and gravity and things like that. So each of those can be quantified as a term in this, this larger Navier-Stokes equation.
