item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的发现：Anthropic 的招股书，其实暴露了"模型公司"与"大科技"的角色反转

视频里提到一个被一笔带过、但极度刺眼的事实——Anthropic 上半年自由现金流转正 (+3.4%)，而大科技的自由现金流却集体转负。

这件事如果放在三年前讲，没人会信。传统认知里： - 大科技 = 现金奶牛，印钞机 - 模型公司 = 烧钱黑洞，靠融资续命

但现在镜像翻转了。模型公司开始像"收租的"，而大科技反而变成了"修高速公路的工程队"。原因是：Anthropic 把 CapEx 外包给了云厂商，自己只负责"收入端"；而大科技把全部 CapEx 吞进自己的资产负债表。

这意味着一件更深刻的事：在 AI 产业链里，"轻资产"和"重资产"的位置发生了颠倒。过去是上游（晶圆厂、设备）重，下游（应用、SaaS）轻；现在变成了中游（Hyperscaler）最重，两端最轻——上游英伟达只做设计，下游 Anthropic 只做模型 API。这是一个砂漏型产业结构，和互联网时代的"沙丘图"（CPU + 操作系统两端厚）完全不同。

二、跨领域连接：这位分析师的"钱变贵→偏好现金流软件"逻辑，本质上是19世纪铁路大跃进后的翻版

他的核心论断是：

AI 落地越好 → 大科技砸越多 CapEx → 通胀下不来 → 融资成本上升 → 钱变贵 → 市场只愿意给"现金流稳定、无 CapEx"的软件公司高估值

这个逻辑的历史对照组是 1870s 美国铁路泡沫。当时铁路公司（CapEx 怪兽）疯狂发债建铁轨，推高了整个美国资金价格，结果最终跑赢的不是铁路公司本身，而是沿线的 Western Union 电报（轻资产信息层）和芝加哥的粮食期货商（在铁路网络上做套利的"软件层"）。铁路公司股东基本被稀释光，而电报公司股东赚翻。

今天 Hyperscaler 就是 2026 年的太平洋铁路，而 Palantir/ServiceNow/Datadog 这类软件公司就是那个时代的 Western Union。基础设施建成后，收租的从来不是建设者，而是在上面跑业务的人——这是一个被反复验证的产业规律。

三、一个被所有人忽略的"甜蜜陷阱"：Robinhood 的 Trump Account 不是金融产品，是人口学产品

视频里提到 Robinhood 的 2500 万 Trump 账户，每个账户 250 美元起步，家长可以持续注入。分析师用了一个很直觉的说法："先抓住娃娃的银行账户"。

但更深层的含义是：Robinhood 正在给自己做一张"美国人口学的期权"。

  • 一个 Trump 账户里的孩子，18 年后成年时 CAC（获客成本）已经为负（因为账户里的钱是家长出的）
  • Robinhood 实际上做了一次"反向预售"——不是向客户收钱，而是让客户的父母替未来的客户买单
  • 这和保险业的"终身价值 (LTV)"模型完全一致，但没有保险业的监管负担

这里有一个被忽略的意外联系：Robinhood 正在变成 Charles Schwab + USAA 的混合体，而不是一个券商。它的真正竞品，不是 Interactive Brokers，而是 1920s Northwestern Mutual 的保险代理模式——锁定一代人的"初始账户"，然后在他们的一生里持续抽成。

四、埋在视频末尾最被低估的信号：希捷和西数的估值分化，可能是 AI 泡沫的早期预警

分析师提到希捷 (STX) 和西数 (WDC) 的基本面几乎一致（同样的订单、同样的毛利、同样的 EPS 增速），但希捷的估值比西数贵 20%。

这件事在"效率市场"假设下不该发生——同质产品应该收敛到同一个倍数。

估值溢价的差异，本质上反映的是市场对"故事"的买单能力。当市场愿意为同质资产支付不同溢价时，往往是流动性最充沛、情绪最亢奋的阶段。希捷的"故事"是什么？——它是 AI 存储的首选叙事标的，被更多主动基金持有。

所以当希捷和西数的估值差拉大时，是风险偏好升温的信号；当两者收敛时，是风险偏好降温的信号。这是一个免费的"市场情绪温度计"，但几乎没有人盯它。

类似的现象在 1999 年也出现过——Sun Microsystems 和 SGI 都是服务器厂商，但 Sun 因为被包装成"互联网骨干"而获得了 60% 的估值溢价。那次溢价消失的时候，Nasdaq 顶部出现了。

📝 转录文本

开场

各位观众大家好，欢迎来到一个"分析了那么多，不如直接理发护盘"的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小陶。我们有一句说一句，大家都在留言区告诉我，到底这个理发的威力强不强。

今天我快速地开始，因为有很多的内容和大家分享：

  • 首先我先会聊一下昨天周二的事。周一的时候 Anthropic 公布了招股书，快速地和大家整理一下招股书（昨天我录了一期会员视频，非常详细地聊了里边的细节，今天做一个总结）。
  • 然后我昨天发了一条 X，对于 2027 年自己的一些看法做了些总结。接下去两个月，我认为我们应该利用市场的波动，对自己的仓位进行调整，为 27 年做好准备。
  • 周三会有美联储会议，还有两家大科技财报——微软和谷歌，我自己都有持股，想先做一个比较详细的展望。
  • 还会聊一下周二盘后发布财报的 Robinhood，以及希捷（Seagate）这类公司。

好，废话不多说，马上开始今天内容。开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发，让更多的人可以看到我们这期内容。

一、周一周二市场回顾

周一和周二的这个市场我就不多做展开。主要我们看一下 YTD 倒数第二列：

  • 必需品消费上涨 8.1%
  • 科技板块 QTD（10 月份）仍下跌 3.2%
  • 保险板块上涨 8%
  • 前七大科技股下跌 0.8%
  • 等权指数上涨 4.6%

所以 QTD 到现在，价值股板块仍然是强势的，因为美债收益率出现了下跌——你看 TLT 都上涨了将近 5% 了。而科技板块和半导体相对是弱势的。所以周一和周二半导体和大科技这个反弹，我认为是在期待之内的。

二、Anthropic 招股书八点总结

针对周一 Anthropic 招股书，我们去做一个总结。

很多人认为 Anthropic 招股书让市场稳定下来。我认为要让市场稳定下来，你得有一个 setup——setup 就是市场情绪面是第一位的。setup 是我在周日视频里和大家聊的：整个债券市场里一个利差处在相对高位，接近今年 3 月份水平。这是市场的 setup，然后一个事件进来——Anthropic 招股书显示他们有充足的现金储备——那么对于依赖 Anthropic 现金流的大科技、Hyperscalers、Neocloud 来说，都会是一个利好、一个稳定性或确定性的背书。

第一点：营收增速连续三年翻 10 倍

历史上你从来没有看到过任何一家公司有现在 Anthropic 这个增速。我在上年 8 月、10 月做线下的时候就聊过 Anthropic 未来增速会非常高。一年之前，市场几乎很大多数人其实都不知道 Anthropic 这家公司，当时都在聊 OpenAI 的变现、落地；然后今年年初 coding 这一块落地，大科技的 coding maxing 等等——到现在，Anthropic 过去三年的营收增速非常夸张。以他们现在这个体量，历史上从来没有看见过任何一家公司能有这样的增速。到第三季度营收已经来到 170 亿美金。

第二点：云分销占比接近 50%

他们通过云分销的营收占比接近 50%，来自于大云分销商。所以他们现在的营收其实非常依赖于大云。

第三点：RPO 订单相对小，80% 来自 consumption

RPO 的订单和营收比例相对比较小。80% 的营收直接来自于花费（consumption）。所以他们未来的订单和现在营收体量对比，不是那么稳定——不像大科技未来有非常大的 RPO 订单，起码可以支撑未来一年到一年半的营收。Anthropic 的 RPO 订单其实并不大，80% 营收来自直接花费，和消费（consumption）有关系。所以必须让 Anthropic 保证自己的模型保持在前沿模型、保持在前列，才是他们未来营收的保证。

第四点：未来算力订单达 8000 亿

现在他们营收满打满算 700 亿美金，未来订单达到了 8000 亿。从这块去看，营收和未来算力订单也出现了指数级差距。

当然这 8000 亿不是明年一定要满足，它是未来 5~10 年去满足。另外一点就是——从老黄的角度出发，未来算力就是等于营收。所以他们不断地花钱，比如说明年花 1000 亿美金在算力上，这 1000 亿可以给他们带来 1500 亿、2000 亿的现金流回报或者营收回报。从这个角度去看，他们慢慢滚下去是有可能兑现、或者去履行 8000 亿订单的，甚至订单可以继续扩大——如果他们可以把投入的 1000 亿算力有更好的转化、更好的 ROI 的话。

确实现在他们营收体量和未履行订单之间的差距非常大，是指数级的差距。

第五点：新模型贡献 80%+ 营收

新模型占到了营收 80% 以上。和第三点一样——大模型公司非常依赖自己模型本身保持在前沿模型队伍里，一旦落后，营收就会受到影响。因为大多数营收全部来自最新一代模型。另外也证明了：当上一代模型被淘汰之后，整个市场里的竞争和开源模型之间的竞争就非常激烈了。所以保持模型排在前沿是他们非常重要的营收来源。

第六点：non-GAAP 已盈利，自由现金流转正

Non-GAAP 已经实现盈利，现金流上半年是正的 3.4 个百分点。所以他们现在已经做到了自由现金流为正。

有一点讽刺的是——你看现在大科技自由现金流都变成负的了，反而这些模型公司上半年，比如 Anthropic，已经做到了自由现金流为正。

第七点：近期将租更多短期算力

短租算力可能会影响他们的利润率，但会让营收增速继续往上抬。短期之内保证了营收，但 SaaS 这种模式本身我认为是不可持续的。短期内 GPU 现货租赁价格持续上升，所以短期内这个盈利模式不需要担心，而且短期内也不会上线非常多的算力。

第八点：充足现金储备

Anthropic 本身有充足现金储备 1300 多亿，再加上上市之后筹集的资金，可能能够达到 1600~1700 亿的现金储备。起码足以保证他们未来一年至一年半的算力购买，还不算未来现金流进入。

前段时间市场都在纠结 Anthropic 的 ARR 到底会停在哪里，但其实退后一步去看，他们的 ARR 没有那么重要。重要的是： - 过去几年营收增速确实非常高 - 理解他们营收来自哪、依赖什么 - 最重要的是对于整个市场：市场担心前沿模型下了那么多订单但没办法履行——现在现金流已经正了，有充足现金准备，起码把市场担心的风险往后推一年半到两年之后

未来一年半到两年，整个市场还是在发展，如果 AI 继续往上抬，更不需要担心；如果 AI 增速放缓，那时候再去考虑这样的风险。

三、2027 年前瞻展望

我快速地对 2027 年前做一个展望，不多做展开，以后 12 月底或 12 月初再详细展开。我只是想到了，然后在周一发了一条 X 稍微讲一下。

我认为整个 27 年，一部分会延续 26 年的趋势。有一个确定性比较高的是：AI 的落地越好，整个市场里的钱就越贵。

  • AI 落地越好 → 大科技砸更多钱做资本开支
  • 资本开支越多 → 通胀很难下降，3C 产品通胀很难下降，很多行业零部件价格继续拖在高位，甚至通胀继续上升
  • 同时大科技本身需要更多融资，无论债市也好、股市也好，需要向市场借钱
  • 所以钱只会变得越来越贵

当钱变得越来越贵，就会挤压整个市场里的投机玩家，短期之内有可能出现一些小爆雷事件。至于最后哪家公司爆雷，我不知道，因为整个市场里一定有人承担了没办法经历小波动的杠杆仓位。整个市场不可能一条直线向上，一定会有波动——一旦波动出现、融资成本大幅上升，市场里投机玩家的风险就会浮出水面了。所以"钱变得越来越贵"这一点毋庸置疑。

在这样的背景之下，我认为明年：

1. 现金流软件公司（延续 26 年下半年趋势）

我认为市场会喜欢这类公司： - 有非常稳定的现金流，每年 15%~20% 增速 - 没有任何资本开支 - 即使 AI 存在一定风险、需求放缓——API 和 Token 价格对软件公司是成本。如果 AI 有泡沫，这些成本下降，API/Token 价格下降（Token 价格本来就会持续下降，随着英伟达新 GPU 效率抬升），对软件公司反而是利好，因为他们开发 AI 产品的成本下降。

所以我认为软件公司在 27 年将继续延续 26 年下半年的强势，市场会喜欢这类标的。核心原因：钱变得越来越贵，市场喜欢现金流非常确定、没有资本开支的公司。

2. 医疗板块

挑一些受益于 AI 的。整个医疗板块也受益于 AI——Anthropic 已经把很多精力放在 Life Science 这边。一旦明年又有很多算力上线，Life Science 这一块是会有突破的。而且医疗板块自带防守属性，只是最近走得比较好。等它出现一定回调，可以慢慢布局（11~12 月如果有回调，可以加 15%~20% 的仓位）。我认为医疗板块会是一个 alpha 的来源。

3. 半导体

还是可以布局，但要相对 selective，需要挑个别标的，且自己对标的要有足够信心。半导体的资本开支相对比较低（和大科技、Neocloud 对比），主要我会放在英特尔身上。半导体本身是一个 beta 的来源。

4. 智能体（Agent）

未来 6~12 个月，整个智能体会发展得越来越好。市场不会只有 C 端这一块、不会只有 Meta 的 Muse。 - C 端：谷歌、苹果都会有自己的智能体诞生 - B 端：Copilot——明天周三 Microsoft 采访就可以验证了。Fundamentally AI 做了一个展望，看到 Copilot 席位可能到 5000 万；Q3 vs Q2 环比增 2000 万，Q2 vs Q1 环比增 1500 万，还在加速 - 还有 OpenAI 前段时间公布的 Dots，我认为 adoption 会慢慢上升

智能体会是未来 AI 市场 6~12 个月的主线。

核心逻辑

买花钱的、买获益于 AI 的 这两类： - 如果要买花钱的公司（有 CapEx 的），必须有 risk/reward 要求，且短期市场情绪面偏低才 OK - 不然的话宁愿把钱投资在获益于 AI、现金流稳定的公司身上 - 一定要思考：万一 AI 放缓或出现泡沫意味着什么？API 价格下跌，哪一类公司会获益？

5. 债券——27 年值得关注

从资产配置这个角度去看，债券绝对值得关注。如果大科技的利率（比如 Meta 现在是 6.1~6.2），如果 Meta 的利率达到 7% 以上，投资级两个 A 的债券如果利率达到 7% 以上——增配债券。 - 大科技都能达到 7%，去买其他板块能做到 8%~9% - 标普 500 平均每年回报才 10%~11% - 买 10 年期或 7 年期债券，平均每年可以保证 8%~8.5% 回报，非常有吸引力 - 风险比股市低非常多

万一未来 7~8 年里一定会有衰退，利率下降，如果你买投资级别、信用级别比较高的标的，利差不会扩大太大，价格还会出现上涨。那时你再去捡一些债券然后回到股市里，完全可以。从资产配置这个角度去看，27 年绝对应该关注债券。

我暂时就聊到这边，之后有更新再聊。到年底之前我一定会用一期的时间详细聊 27 年的展望。只是周一想到了就写一下，因为接下去两个月我认为我们利用市场波动可以提前做一些调整。

四、周三财报展望——微软 & 谷歌

微软

关注点：

1）云增速 - 市场预期 44% - 管理层预期 45% - 我个人认为高于这个预期的概率比较大

为什么？微软是能够控制云增速的。两个季度之前市场不满意他们 40% 增速，Satya 马上就改变算力分配，分配到外部，马上在第四季度（财年）变成 42%；到财年第一季度（27 财年 Q1）再次上调到 45%。这个季度 45% 可以观察，最后有可能停在 45.5% 或 46%。

2）总体利润率：市场预期 48%

3）下季度指引：市场预期 44.7%~45%。我个人认为同比增速将继续抬升——比如这季度 45%，下季度非常有可能继续抬到 46% 或 47%。

为什么会出现这种加速？ 几家大云都是一样的： - 现在云这一块的增速完全是因为一年、一年半之前的资本开支投入 - 过去一年、一年半，三家大科技资本开支都是翻倍式增长 - 订单本身又是确定的 - 短期内 on-demand pricing（无论长单、中单、短单）都非常贵，租算力的价格很高 - 所以营收增速可以保证，且会加速——现在看到的营收增速加速，其实就是反映了过去 CapEx 同比增速不断加速的结果

微软估值：周二收盘 forward P/E = 25 倍。26 年年终（6 月份）跌到 20 倍以下，当时我认为是便宜的——但很多人在 20 倍以下不敢碰。

即使经过这波反弹（主要是上一个季度财报之后那一波），现在市场非常强。价格一下子跳涨 20% 之后还能走得那么强，说明很多机构是在那份财报之后开始进场的，不然理论上来说应该会有一部分获利盘；之所以没有看到获利盘、没有看到非常明显下跌，是因为很多人追涨进来之后把那些抛压完全填补掉了。

所以这个季度财报我仍然看好微软。估值这个角度看，微软现在是偏低的。25 倍——我画了一条横线：从 20 到 25 年以来，微软很多次的估值差不多就是围绕着 30 倍左右。当然我能够理解随着利率上升之后，估值相对要往下调一些。所以起码我的期待是：不期待回到 24 年年中的 35 倍，但期待回到 20~25 年中位数的 30 倍。

所以在没有去到 30 倍之前，微软这家公司我是不考虑任何减仓的。 微软是 hybrid——有 CapEx，但软件派发是所有软件公司里最强的。主要关注点就是 Copilot。

谷歌

和微软一样，主要是 GCP。 - 上季度增速同比 32% - 这季度市场预期 42%（原文表述） - 和微软一样，我期待最终结果比管理层预期更高 - 更重要的是第四季度市场预期同比增速 95%，我认为这个速度会加速。原理一样——现在看到的营收增速是一年至一年半以前资本开支增速的反映

利润率：GCP 上季度 35.6%，这季度市场预期 32.5%。利润率可能会有些波动——因为资本开支变成减记变成花费之后会影响利润。

估值：我个人建议看 Operating Profit（运营利润）增速： - 26 年 33%、27 年 29%、28 年 24% - 基本在 25%~30% 之间 - EV / Operating Income 现在 25.6 倍 - 拿这个 multiple 除以 25%，基本得到 PEG = 1 倍

所以谷歌现在的估值我认为就是便宜的。

五、Robinhood 财报分析

Robinhood 这家公司我自己持有，但仓位比较小。今天我听他们财报会议其实没听完，我觉得没必要——因为这家公司首先执行力非常强，而且是非常长期的标的，很长时间里都可以比较放心。

为什么盘后下跌？

从 EPS 体量和营收体量看，Double Miss，看起来非常糟糕： - EPS 市场预期 0.57，实际 0.51

但 0.51 包含了投资上的亏损/调整。CFO 聊到：剔除投资因素后 EPS = 0.60，其实比市场预期 0.57 高。所以从 headline news 看是 double miss，但 bottom line 并没有 miss。

再看 Operating Income： - 市场预期 638 - 实际 685 - 高于市场预期 7%

所以他们的 bottom line 盈利是高于市场预期的。但这些东西不重要——要解释盘后上涨还是下跌，你可以从结果去出发找任何理由。没有一份财报是完美的，财报会议里永远可以找到负面的点去解释盘后下跌。

所以不用去猜盘后到底为什么涨跌。一家公司基本面不可能一条直线，一定会有一两个季度营收或盈利出现一定程度的 miss。但长期来说基本面没变、管理层执行力没变、它在一个非常好的跑道上——这才是最重要的。

财报会议几个关键看点

1）Agentic Trading（AI 智能体交易）

未来很多券商都值得布局。继续围绕 AI 这个角度思考： - 现在聊的是个人智能体帮你打理生活 - 未来在交易层面，有没有可能一部分交易交给智能体完成？ - 交给智能体 = 每个人都变成了一个高频交易（当然不是极高频） - 交易频次一定会上升 - Agentic Trading 会增加所有券商的成交量，券商会获益于 AI

2）万物上链、万物可交易

从财报可以看到： - 对赌市场的营收体量已经超过了股市的营收体量 - 2024 Q4 Crypto 营收 3.6 亿美金，这个季度只有 1.2 亿，萎缩 2/3 - 但总营收体量却比当时高了 30%——因为开拓了其他很多业务 - 比如对赌市场这个季度达到 1.7 亿美金

开发新产品从开发到落地到上线，这个速度行业里你从来没有看到过有第二家公司有这样的执行力。

万物上链可交易和 Agentic Trading 不矛盾：对赌市场 24/7 交易，马上股市也要 24/7 了，每天 24 小时、一周 7 天，随时可以交易。

3）Wallet / Trump Account —— 为未来 10~15 年布局

年底之前他们会推出 Wallet。Trump 账户现在 2500 万个账户，每个账户起码有 250 美金在里面。 - 未来家长可以把钱打入孩子账户 - 孩子成年之后，这些账户是未来 10~15 年的用户基础 - 2500 万 + 未来新生儿如果还和 Robinhood 合作 → 这些新生儿成年之后基本上都会有一个 Robinhood 账户

所以 Robinhood 已经在为未来 10~15 年布局了，先抓住娃娃的银行账户。

这就是为什么在北美，每当落地、每当新生儿诞生时，第一个开户的银行对他们非常重要——他们希望抓到你，会给非常好的福利，送你一个 iPad、送你一个五六百刀的奖品。为什么愿意送？因为他们知道从你身上一辈子可以赚到的钱，绝对比现在的 acquisition cost 高得多得多。

All in Share——他们在为未来布局。

4）Robinhood Chain / Robinhood 钱（新推出） - 成交量已达 $100 billion - 一个季度营收达到 5000 万美金 - 这块增速非常快，公司会花非常多资金在上面

总结

Robinhood 在一条非常好的跑道上： - Agentic Trading - 万物上链 - 24/7 Equity Trading - 未来 10~15 年从账户角度布局 - 新推出的 Crypto 市场喜好度高 - 最最最重要的是管理层执行力和推出新产品的速度——行业里绝对找不到第二家

所以 Robinhood 只要跌下去、估值合理，都可以买和加仓。

估值

好公司也得买一个相对便宜的价格。 - 25 年 6、7、10 月：市场给到前瞻市盈率 70 倍以上，一家券商公司能给 70 倍以上是非常夸张的估值。当时社交媒体有人说"你再也看不到 100 以下的 Robinhood" - 结果从上年 11、12 月开始下跌，1、2 月继续下跌 - 我在 2 月份 70 多块钱加仓/开仓 Robinhood，到现在一直没碰过 - 这次如果跌下来又有机会

周二收盘前 forward P/E = 32.4 倍。盘后跌 7% 后前瞻市盈率可以推到 30 倍。 - 今年 3 月份低点 = 26 倍 - 上一年 3 月份低点 = 23 倍

如果再次能跌到 26 倍左右，Robinhood 的价格又会变得非常有吸引力，我绝对愿意加仓。

六、AI 硬件：希捷（STX）与西部数据（WDC）

希捷（Seagate / STX）

盘后发布财报，财报本身非常好，但盘后还是出现小幅下跌。主要我觉得从估值角度看——

估值对比

两家公司市占基本差不多，还有第三家 Toshiba。

希捷： - 前瞻市盈率 18 倍 - 算上盘后下跌：17~17.5 倍 - 25 年之前估值区间：6~10 倍

WDC： - 前瞻市盈率 15 倍 - 25 年之前估值区间：5~9 倍

从前瞻市盈率看，WDC 和希捷对比，WDC 相对便宜了 20%。

增速对比

未来三年 EPS 增速（上 WDC，下希捷）： - WDC：147%、62%、29% - 希捷：138%、55%、38%

营收增速、盈利增速基本一致，无非是估值上希捷比 WDC 稍微贵了一些。

买点判断

  • 如果前瞻市盈率可以去到 12~13 倍左右，有 risk/reward
  • 未来 2~3 年基本面比较确定
  • 前提：整个 AI 没有非常明显的泡沫、需求没有非常明显问题——这两家公司订单非常稳
  • 在没有看到明显衰退的情况下，前瞻市盈率去到 12~13 倍，这两家绝对有吸引力

七、今天的活动

因为时间关系不多展开。Seeking Alpha 的两个量化选股策略：

  • Alpha Picks：首年订阅立即省 50 美金，还有免费试用期
  • Quant Growth and Income Alpha Picks：集中在价值股身上（喜欢价值股的可以订阅）
  • Bundle：两个加在一起原价 998 美金，现在 719 美金

对 Seeking Alpha 产品订阅感兴趣的，可以在置顶留言找到订阅链接。

结尾

最后提醒：周三晚上 APP 里面会有会员直播，大家不要错过。

今天内容就到这边，我们下期见。

## 一、最反直觉的发现：Anthropic 的招股书，其实暴露了"模型公司"与"大科技"的角色反转
视频里提到一个被一笔带过、但极度刺眼的事实——**Anthropic 上半年自由现金流转正 (+3.4%)，而大科技的自由现金流却集体转负**。
这件事如果放在三年前讲，没人会信。传统认知里： - 大科技 = 现金奶牛，印钞机 - 模型公司 = 烧钱黑洞，靠融资续命
但现在镜像翻转了。**模型公司开始像"收租的"，而大科技反而变成了"修高速公路的工程队"**。原因是：Anthropic 把 CapEx 外包给了云厂商，自己只负责"收入端"；而大科技把全部 CapEx 吞进自己的资产负债表。
这意味着一件更深刻的事：**在 AI 产业链里，"轻资产"和"重资产"的位置发生了颠倒**。过去是上游（晶圆厂、设备）重，下游（应用、SaaS）轻；现在变成了**中游（Hyperscaler）最重，两端最轻**——上游英伟达只做设计，下游 Anthropic 只做模型 API。这是一个砂漏型产业结构，和互联网时代的"沙丘图"（CPU + 操作系统两端厚）完全不同。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Fermat's Last Theorem proved by AI | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、难度等级被倒置了：形式化曾是"硬骨头"，现在"美"才是

这段对话里藏着一个被所有人忽略的反转。十年前，数学界把"形式化证明"（formalization）视为需要几代人才能攻克的苦力活——Kevin Buzzard 拿了百万美元资助，计划用五年时间仅完成费马大定理证明的"最后一步"。而现在，这位嘉宾说出了那句真正爆炸性的话："autoformalization is basically solved"。

但真正令人意外的是——这并没有让数学变简单，它只是把"难"的位置换了一个地方。曾经难的是"能不能证出来"，现在难的是"证得美不美、能不能放进 Mathlib 的架构里"。AI 可以在 48 小时内吐出 1300 万行"能跑通"的代码，但那段代码像一座贫民窟——它成立，但不优雅、不可复用、不可对接。这意味着数学家的职业正在从"证明者"迁移到"美学审判者"。这是一个比表面故事深得多的身份危机。

二、"Jerry-rigging"的生物学真相：AI 复现了生命演化本身的策略

嘉宾反复用了一个词：jerry-rigging（临时拼凑）。这个词值得停下来看一眼——因为它跟进化生物学里的一个核心概念严丝合缝：François Jacob 著名的 "evolution as tinkering"（演化即修补）。自然界从不设计优雅系统，它把眼前能用的零件胡乱焊接起来——人类的眼球是倒装的、喉返神经绕过主动脉、我们的 DNA 里 98% 是"垃圾"。生物的"证明"从来不干净。

那么这里的惊人连接是：AI 现在走的是生物演化的路，而不是数学家走的柏拉图式之路。Mathlib 社区想要的是柏拉图——每个引理有唯一正确的归属，每个定义是"最抽象的那个"。但 AI 用 1300 万行丑陋代码告诉我们：可证明性（provability）和可理解性（intelligibility）是两条独立的轴。我们过去 2500 年把它们混为一谈，是因为唯一能生产证明的那个生物（人脑）同时需要美感来压缩和记忆。AI 不需要美，所以它能把这两条轴分开——而这件事本身，就是对数学哲学的一次釜底抽薪。

三、"KEEP GOING, all caps"——人类角色的静默塌陷

最轻描淡写却最重的一句话是：参与的 2-3 个人，他们的主要工作是打字 "KEEP GOING"，全大写。

把这个意象放到更广阔的历史里：这几乎复刻了爱迪生的实验室分工——爱迪生自己后来承认，他的作用更多是"督工"而非"发明者"；也复刻了现代博士生导师的角色——很多著名教授坦言他们对学生的指导主要是"再试一次"、"你走对了，继续"。换句话说，人类在"KEEP GOING"这种岗位上，并不是第一次被降级，这个岗位本来就一直在。只是过去我们把它交给助手，现在我们把它交给了……自己。

这里有一个让人脊背发凉的推论：如果一个领域的最高成就，可以由三个没有领域专长的人（嘉宾明确说 "there was no domain expertise on the parts of the people"）加上 "KEEP GOING" 完成，那么这个领域里领域专长的边际价值正在逼近零。而 Lex 在对话中那个精明的插话——"公司有动机把它卖成这样"——指向了另一个必须警惕的维度：我们可能正在目睹一场真实的相变，但同时也在被卷入一场叙事战争。两件事可以同时为真。

四、"一个月三次"：相变的签名，不是巧合

最后一个意外观察：FLT、Navier-Stokes、quasi-RH——同一个月，三次世界模型被炸穿。嘉宾说"This was round three"的时候，他其实在描述一个地质学意义上的事件：当板块构造说在 1960 年代被接受时，不是因为出现了一个决定性证据，而是因为一周之内三份不同实验室的证据同时到达。独立事件的高频簇发，不是运气——它是系统进入新稳态前的典型信号。

所以这段 20 分钟的访谈，表面在讲一个定理，底下在讲一件更大的事：一个用 2500 年搭起来的智力生态位，正在以周为单位重新分配。而那位两天前刚在普林斯顿讲"AI 还做不到这个"的教授——他不是错了，他是正好站在悬崖边上做了演讲。他的"错"值得被记录下来，因为它是我们这代人难得的、能精确标记相变发生那一刻的时钟。

📝 转录文本

一、意料之外的 Lean 版费马大定理

Guest: And this is— it's been a month of things happening way outside of my model of what was possible. The Fermat's Last Theorem formalization — I was sure we were three years away, at least, from being able to do something like that.

Lex: So maybe you can elaborate on that. It was in Lean, it was formalized as... how big was the Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean?

Guest: Like, 13 million lines.

Lex: 13 million lines. Okay.

二、Mathlib 的"光环"与 AI 的边界

Guest: So I just — two days before, I gave a colloquium in the Princeton Math Department where I explained in painstaking detail what Lean is, what Mathlib is, but also that AI systems today — you know, there's this Mathlib library where everything is kind of perfectly done, exactly the right levels of generality. There's not supposed to be any code that's reusing code, that's reproving theorems somewhere else. Everything is the most general, the most abstract.

And what AI systems are capable of doing is building, like, one or two layers on top of that. But what they're doing is jerry-rigging. They have not been trained yet — I'm not saying they can't do it, but they're not good at it right now — at what I call canonization: taking kind of sloppy code, refactoring it, figuring out exactly where in the library it belongs, what's the canonical version of this statement, of this lemma. And then every proof should just be a combination of: you apply this lemma from over here, you apply that lemma from over there, put all these things together — there's your theorem. And then it's really clean, it's really beautiful, very elegant. That's what Mathlib is going for.

And what I said in my colloquium is: where we are today is that you can get entire textbooks formalized as long as they're in the Mathlib halo — as long as they're, like, one, maybe two steps removed from things that have already been done in Mathlib. But when you start asking it to do things that are three or four steps removed from the library — the way that it came up with a definition of this object, and the way that it came up with some other definition of the same object (because it was doing it for two different purposes) — then they clash. You can't stitch these things back together. You really need the library, Mathlib, to grow, in order to get to a place where you can do research manuscripts that are really synthesizing tons of different areas of mathematics.

Lex: Which is why you would expect Fermat's Last Theorem to take — because it's so far outside of the halo of Mathlib — it would take quite a bit of time.

三、Kevin Buzzard 的五年计划，与一个被颠覆的周三

Guest: Exactly right. So Kevin Buzzard had a million-dollar grant to spend the next five years — or maybe he's already a year or two into that grant — to reduce the formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem to things that were known in the 1980s. So he wanted to do that last step, those seven years of Wiles' work, and Wiles–Taylor, to finally finish Fermat's Last Theorem, but built on top of things that we knew would be extraordinarily difficult. He wasn't gonna do Langlands–Tunnell, he wasn't gonna do Mazur. There were all kinds of things that were expected to be even much more difficult than what these five years would take.

And everything I said in that colloquium was wrong. My colloquium was on a Wednesday. On Friday, there was a drop of 13 million lines of code from the axioms — Fermat's Last Theorem is proved. The statement of Fermat's Last Theorem is completely elementary. There's no semantic alignment to check. You just glance at it. Yes, that's the statement. It's — Lean says it's sorry-free.

Lex: Can you explain how it was done?

四、"Sorry-free"却不优美：Anthropic 的暴力美学

Guest: How it was done. So it was Anthropic. And how it was done was: AI systems just got really, really good at — it's still not a nice proof. It's not the clean proof. There's still a ton of work that needs to be done to make that proof a Mathlib-quality proof, and I think that's important work and work that we want to do. But in terms of just getting that sorry-free theorem, they just blasted through all of these. They jerry-rigged this, they jerry-rigged that, and 13 million lines later, they had a sorry-free formal Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. It's just absolutely shocking.

五、关于"错话"的插曲：学术话语的新陈代谢

Lex: By the way, it's beautiful to always — because of how rapid everything is, there's going to be a lot of statements that everybody makes, that the world experts make, that are wrong. That's the whole point of it. And that's the fun thing about human discussion — is we have disagreements. And I would venture to say somewhere between 40 to 80% of everything said today will be wrong in five years, because everything's changing so fast. But that's the whole point of human discussion and deliberation and discourse — and even the scientific process is saying shit and seeing what sticks. Over time. Over ten years, over a hundred years, and so on.

六、从"X 倍"到"百万倍"：一个数学家的使用体验曲线

Guest: I was describing my experience. I had a lot of experience with Lean and with using AI. I started doing Lean before AI existed in the sense that we understand it now, and it was very painstaking. And the second AI systems came on — you know, the first LLMs were coming online — they were crap at Lean. But then they got a little bit better, a little bit better, and I was like, "Oh my God, I can do library search." I don't have to sit there looking — I know there's a lemma that does this, but I don't know what it's called, and I don't know which exactly. Is it in the manifolds library? Is it in the algebraic geometry library? Like, give me this lemma. It was great at that, and I was like, "Oh, this is amazing. I'm gonna keep using these systems."

And every bit of my experience told me that they can do, like, X, but not 10X — and this was a million X. It was just completely outside of the distribution in my mind of what systems were capable of.

七、"KEEP GOING"：人类参与的真实形态

Lex: Do you have a ballpark estimate of how many humans were involved in that, and what is the level of human involvement in generating those 13 million lines of code?

Guest: Uh, I believe it was two or three humans.

Lex: Okay.

Guest: And I believe most of their involvement was, "Keep going," all caps.

Lex: Okay. All right, so you think it's really just, like, gentle guidance — not, you know, pathway creating?

Guest: As far as I understand, there was no domain expertise on the parts of the people who were doing this.

Lex: As the meme goes with OpenAI or Anthropic — you know, the prompt is "solve math"... or something.

Guest: Do a breakthrough.

Lex: Yeah, yeah. Do a breakthrough.

Guest: Do a breakthrough. That's the prompt. And it goes and does it.

Lex: Of course, you never know from a company perspective — there's a lot of incentive to sort of sell it as that, even though there might have been a lot of intermediate steps that led — at any stages of the training, or maybe some things left unsaid — even though the final prompt is "do a breakthrough," there could be a lot of groundwork before that that led to it. We don't know.

八、海边的沉思：三轮冲击与"autoformalization is solved"

Guest: So I remember that was a Friday, because I just was completely — like, my mind was completely exploded. And it was Labor Day, and we just took the kids to the beach, and I needed a few days of, you know, I'm not checking my phone, I'm not on Twitter. I'm just throwing my kids into the ocean, and —

Lex: Did you have that moment where you're just sitting and looking at the ocean and contemplating?

Guest: Yeah. Like, what does it all mean? So I had already gone through that a month before. And I was like — so now what that says is that autoformalization is basically solved. It's not solved in the way that I would want it to be solved. And people are still gonna work very, very hard on this. There's all kinds of other things that happen — just like there's all kinds of other things that happen when you prove theorems that are byproducts of that process, for human understanding. There's all kinds of other things when you work on making a beautiful library of mathematics, and that process will continue. That process will be very difficult. It's gonna be, you know, thousands of man-hours of people around the world contributing in this open-source way. But in terms of: can you get a sorry-free proof of something that human beings have written down on paper — I think that problem is done.

九、Round Three：Navier–Stokes 与 quasi-RH

Lex: And so you were standing there with a whiskey, having gone through this a month before, and now again.

Guest: Right. This was round three.

Lex: This is round three.

Guest: 'Cause when I got back from Labor Day, it was Navier–Stokes.

Lex: Navier–Stokes.

Guest: But this one —

Lex: So I was like, "I was just mourning FLT. You're gonna do this to me? Come on."

Guest: But now — I mean, this really hit home, right? With the quasi-RH.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Quasi-Riemann hypothesis proved by AI - mathematician explains | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、黎曼的"降维打击"——他本人就是最早的"AI嵌入工程师"

真正令人震惊的不是 AI 证明了 quasi-RH，而是 AI 用的是黎曼本人发明的那个核心动作：把离散问题（素数）嵌入连续空间（复平面）。这与现代深度学习的所有"几何化""嵌入""latent space"思想，在数学哲学上是完全同构的。黎曼在 1859 年做的事情——把一个数论的、颗粒的、无序的对象，强行塞进复变函数的光滑世界里——就是今天 Transformer 把离散 token 嵌入高维向量空间的祖先。

于是你会发现一个诡异的闭环：素数似乎"喜欢"被这样处理。黎曼留下了一道通往自身证明的秘密通道，而 AI 现在走通了。这不是巧合，这是一个暗示：某些数学对象的本质属性可能是"可嵌入性"本身——它们存在的意义就是等着被映射到另一个空间里显形。素数不是在复平面上"投影"，素数本就是复平面的影子。

二、黎曼假设的物理学真名："素数的热力学第二定律"

Alex 讲到振幅时轻描淡写："每个乐器都以完全相同的振幅演奏。"这其实是个被严重低估的说法。

RH 本质上是一个最大熵声明——它说：素数在"不是合数"这个唯一约束下，是最大程度随机的；没有任何频率占优势，没有任何乐器盖过另一个乐器。换一个说法：素数遵守等分配定律（equipartition theorem）。它们是整数世界里的"黑体辐射"，振幅谱是平的，没有偏爱。

这里有一个跨领域连接，罕有人提：RH 之于数论，犹如热力学第二定律之于物理——它都是在说"系统最大程度地混沌，但正是这种混沌造就了稳定的宏观规律"。素数定理（PNT）就是这个"宏观规律"，RH 则是它背后的"玻尔兹曼公式"。所以我大胆预测一件事：未来某天 RH 的最优雅证明会从统计力学的方向上来，而不是从代数几何。AI 现在"暴力"证明的 quasi-RH，是数学家在未来 20 年才会反过来理解的——哦，原来黎曼在无意识地测量素数宇宙的"温度"。

三、"Jerry-rigging vs Canonization"——人类即将被赶入"美学保留地"

Alex 画出了本次革命最深刻的一条分水岭：AI 擅长"胡乱拼凑可运行的证明"（jerry-rigging），不擅长"把证明净化为最简最美的典范"（canonization）。1300 万行的 Lean 代码就是胡乱拼凑的巅峰。

跨领域看，这个二分从未在人类历史上以如此清晰的面目出现过：

  • 生物学：进化就是 jerry-rigging——DNA 里塞满了"冗余""借用""回收利用"的垃圾代码。而智能设计（如果存在的话）才是 canonization。现在 AI 扮演进化，人类数学家被迫扮演上帝。
  • 艺术史：米开朗基罗的《奴隶》像是"未完成"——但很多人认为那才是完整的。工业时代之后，"finished"和"complete"分道扬镳。AI 让 FLT "finished"，但远未"complete"。
  • 软件工程："it compiles"和"it's clean"的距离，现在变成了"数学定理为真"和"数学定理为美"的距离。

真正让我惊讶的一个预测：人类数学家正在被赶进一个"美学保留地"——AI 负责生产"可信但丑陋"的真理，人类负责"重写优美证明"。而这件事的隐含代价是：人类第一次拥有了没有任何人类真正理解的数学知识。FLT 的 Lean 证明没有人读过全部 1300 万行。这是一种新的认知形态：分布式数学意识。就像 Google 知道许多没有 Google 工程师知道的事。数学正在从"人类集体理解"滑向"系统集体知晓"。

四、被忽略的真正奇观：数学已被"流媒体化"

一个几乎没人指出的小细节：Alex 当时手握威士忌、在博物馆晚宴上、不停刷新手机等待"the drop"——"drop"是嘻哈专辑发布的词汇，是 Supreme 潮牌星期四上新的词汇。数学发现正在被平台逻辑殖民：它有了"发布会""提前泄露""实时震惊""集体 mourning"。

Alex 说："我才刚在给 FLT 哀悼，你又对我做这个？" ——数学家的情感节奏，第一次需要与产品发布的节奏同步。Kuhn 的"范式转移"原本以十年为单位，现在以星期为单位。这是一个前所未有的现象：认知革命的时间常数正在被硬件化。

五、送你一个意料之外的猜想

如果 RH 真的说"素数宇宙是最大熵的"，而 AI 真的能在几天内从 jerry-rig 到 canonization——那么下一个真正会倒下的，不会是 RH 本身，而是哥德巴赫猜想。原因：哥德巴赫比 RH 更"适合 jerry-rigging"（它没有光滑的复分析结构，就是硬核组合），所以 AI 的优势会更大。而数学界几乎没在准备这件事。

记住这一预言——它可能在 2027 年之前兑现。

📝 转录文本

Setting the Stage: What is the Riemann Hypothesis?

But first, we'll have to break if it's okay.

Lex: So Alex, you're a number theorist. Um, maybe it's fair to say the central problem in your field is the Riemann hypothesis, and you showed a lot of excitement on the aforementioned Twitter/X about the quasi-RH, the quasi-Riemann hypothesis proof. Can you explain that? Can you explain what the Riemann hypothesis is, and can you explain the nature of your excitement about it?

Alex: Sure. There's sort of a one-minute version of the Riemann hypothesis — or a five-minute version or a thirty-hour version. I don't know how far you wanna, you wanna go.

Lex: Let's start pulling at that string.

Alex: So we know what the prime numbers are. People are interested in the distribution of the prime numbers, and what Riemann discovered is that there's a function — this is totally crazy — that there's a function that takes complex numbers as inputs and has complex numbers as outputs, and that function governs the behavior of the prime numbers.

It's called the Riemann zeta function, and by the zeros of the zeta function, we mean complex inputs where the output is the number zero in the complex plane, so the, the origin in the complex plane. And the question is, where do these, where are these complex zeros? What inputs, what complex number inputs give you a complex number output of zero when you apply this zeta function?

Why in the world should that — What, complex numbers? Are you — What are you talking about? We have these discrete numbers that aren't divisible by anything else sitting in the natural numbers on the number line, and now you wanna talk about functions from a complex space to a, to a complex space.

The Signal-Processing Analogy: Primes as Music

Um, that was the great breakthrough. The great breakthrough was to figure out how to do signal processing on the prime numbers.

If you think about, you know, the reason people can hear you, your podcast is that my voice box is producing pressure waves of sound. That's the natural space. Then that goes into the microphone. The microphone analyzes it, does the Fourier analysis on it, converts it into amplitudes and frequencies, and it's just a bunch of numbers, stores those numbers or sends those numbers, whatever. The speaker then takes those numbers and reconstructs back out what sounds to people like my voice.

The same thing is going on — that's what the zeta function does for the prime numbers. It takes the prime numbers, you can think of the prime numbers as particles of air molecules wiggling around, and it does a signal processing analysis on it that can recover the same prime numbers back. And the frequencies and the amplitudes correspond to the zeros of the zeta function. The zeta function has that information in it.

And the Riemann hypothesis — so the amplitudes of all of these, you can call them Riemann waves, and the superposition of those waves recovers the distribution of the primes. And all of those amplitudes are supposed to be exactly the same. Like, the orchestra that plays the music of the prime numbers has every single instrument sounding at exactly the same amplitude. That's what the Riemann hypothesis predicts.

Why is it so hard? (And why "hard" is the wrong word now)

Lex: So can you — Actually, we know what the prime numbers are, but maybe going into the space of philosophy and the romantic notions of aesthetics — why are they so interesting and important and central and beautiful at the core of mathematics? And, connected to why the Riemann hypothesis is exciting, is why is it so difficult to figure out if and what the pattern is in the prime numbers?

Alex: Let me start with your second question first. Why something is difficult, I only know how to answer once I know what the answer is.

Lex: Once it's made simple.

Alex: Right? Maybe it's not difficult.

Lex: Okay.

Alex: Maybe it's not as difficult as we thought it was. I did not think I would see a proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis in my lifetime. So the fact that I saw it on Tuesday, was extraordinarily shocking.

The Whiskey Moment: Watching the Drop

Lex: What did you do the moment you saw it, like, in 30 seconds after? Like, what was your — Do you remember, like, what —

Alex: Yeah, I remember where I was — the second I saw the drop. So we were at this National Museum of Mathematics Gala in New York City. And so I had, you know, a whiskey in one hand, and I kept refreshing. I was talking to people, socializing, but I also kept refreshing 'cause I knew it was dropping around six o'clock Eastern Time.

And then the drop hit and, in fact, I was talking to — there was a Quanta reporter there and we were just chatting, "Oh, yeah, they're gonna drop these, you know, 300, 400," — we didn't know how many, 700 it turns out — problems. And I was like, "Oh, wow, that's really cool. It dropped."

So I'm looking at my phone, and, like, the second thing I see is quasi-RH. And I'm like, "What do you mean, quasi-RH? You don't mean, like... For what?" And then I look, and it's, it's the zeta function, and it's all Dirichlet functions, so they've solved no zero, zeros. And I'm like, that can't, that can't be what's in this drop. That just — I, I could not compute in that moment what I was seeing.

Lex: That speed of progress in that little time, yeah.

Alex: It was so far outside my model of what was possible. And this is — It's been a month of things happening way outside of my model of what was possible. The Fermat's Last Theorem formalization — I was sure we were three years away, at least, from being able to do something like that.

The Fermat's Last Theorem Formalization: 13 Million Lines

Lex: So, maybe you can elaborate on that. It was in Lean, it was formalized as... How big was the Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean?

Alex: Like, 13 million lines.

Lex: 13 million lines. Okay.

Alex: So I just — Two days before, I gave a colloquium in the Princeton Math Department where I explained in painstaking detail what Lean is, what Mathlib is, but also that AI systems today, you know, there's this Mathlib library where everything is kind of perfectly done, exactly the right levels of generality, enough — There's no — There's not supposed to be any code that's reusing code that's reproving theorems somewhere else. Everything is the most general, the most abstract.

And what AI systems are capable of doing is building, like, one or two layers on top of that. But what they're doing is jerry-rigging. They have not been trained yet — I'm not saying they can't do it, but they're not good at it right now — at what I call canonization: taking kind of sloppy code, refactoring it, figuring out exactly where in the library it belongs, what's the canonical version of this statement, of this lemma, and then every proof should just be a combination of "you apply this lemma from over here, you apply that lemma from over there, put all these things together, there's your theorem." And then it's really clean, it's really beautiful, very elegant. That's what Mathlib is going for.

The "Mathlib Halo" and Its Limits

And what I said in my colloquium is, where we are today is that you can get entire textbooks formalized as long as they're in the Mathlib halo — as long as they're, like, one, maybe two steps removed from things that have already been done in Mathlib.

But when you start — and this had been my practice, my experience had been — when you start asking it to do things that are, you know, three or four steps removed from the library, the way that it came up with a definition of this object and the way that it came up with some other definition of the same object (because it was doing it for two different purposes) — then they clash. You can't stitch these things back together. Like, you really need the library, Mathlib, to grow in order to get to a place where you can do research manuscripts, you know, that are really using, synthesizing tons of different areas of mathematics.

Lex: Which is why you would expect Fermat's last theorem to take — because it's so far outside of the halo of Mathlib, it would take quite a bit of time.

Alex: Exactly right. So Kevin Buzzard had a million dollar grant to spend the next five years — or I th- maybe he's already a year or two into that grant — to reduce the formalization of Fermat's last theorem to things that were known in the 1980s. So he wanted to do that last step, the those seven years of Wiles' work, and Wiles-Taylor, to finally finish you know, Fermat's last theorem, but built on top of things that we knew would be extraordinarily difficult. He wasn't gonna do Langlands-Tunnell, he wasn't gonna do Mazur. There were all kinds of things that were expected to be even much more difficult than what these five years would take.

"Everything I Said in That Colloquium Was Wrong"

And everything I said in that colloquium was wrong. And I think my colloquium was on a Wednesday. On Friday, there was a drop of thirteen million lines of code from the axioms — Fermat's last theorem is proved. The statement of Fermat's Last Theorem is completely elementary. There's no semantic alignment to check. You just glance at it. Yes, that's the statement. It's — Lean says it's sorry-free.

Lex: Can you explain how it was done?

Alex: How it was done. So it was Anthropic, and how it was done was AI systems just got really, really good at — It's still not a nice proof. It's not the clean proof. It's not — There's still a ton of work that needs to be done to make that proof a Mathlib quality proof, and I think that's important work and work that we want to do. But in terms of just getting that sorry-free theorem, they just blasted through all of these. They jerry-rigged this, they jerry-rigged that, and, you know, thirteen million lines later, they had a sorry-free formal Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. It's just absolutely shocking.

An Aside on the Fragility of Expert Opinion

Lex: By the way, it's beautiful to always, um — Because of how rapid everything is, there's going to be a lot of statements that everybody makes, the world experts make, that are wrong. That's the whole point of it. And that's the fun thing about human discussion, is we have disagreements and I would venture to say somewhere between forty to eighty percent of everything said today will be wrong in five years because everything's changing so fast. But that's the whole point of human discussion and deliberation and discourse — and the, even the scientific process is saying shit and seeing what sticks, over time. Over ten years, over a hundred years, and so on.

Alex: I was describing my experience. I had a lot of experience with Lean and with using AI. I started doing Lean before AI existed in the sense that we understand it now, and it was very painstaking. And the second AI systems came on, you know, the first LLMs were coming online, they were, they were crap at Lean, but then they got a little bit better, a little bit better, and I was like, "Oh my God, I can do library search." I don't have to sit there looking — I know there's a lemma that does this, but I don't know what it's called, and I don't know which exactly. Is it in the manifolds library? Is it in the algebraic geometry library? Like, give me this, give me this lemmas. It was great at that, and I was like, "Oh, this is amazing. I'm gonna keep using these systems."

And every bit of my experience told me that they can do, like, X, but not ten X — and this was a million X. It was just completely outside of the distribution in my mind of what systems were capable of.

How Many Humans? "Keep Going, All Caps"

Lex: Do you have a ballpark estimate of how many humans were involved in that, and what is the level of human involvement in generating those thirteen million lines of code?

Alex: Uh, I believe it was two or three humans.

Lex: Okay.

Alex: And I believe most of their involvement was, "Keep going," all caps.

Lex: Okay. All right, so you think it's really just, like, gentle guidance, not like, you know, pathway creating and —

Alex: As far as I understand, there was no domain expertise —

Lex: Okay.

Alex: — on the parts of the people who were doing this.

Lex: As the meme goes with OpenAI or Anthropic — you know, the prompt is "solve math" — or something. And then —

Alex: Do a breakthrough.

Lex: Yeah, yeah. Yeah, do a breakthrough.

Alex: "Do a breakthrough." That's the prompt. And it goes and does it.

Lex: Of course, you never know from a company perspective, there's a lot of incentive to sort of sell it as that, even though there might have been a lot of intermediate steps that led — whe- at any stages of the training or maybe some things left unsaid, even though the final prompt is "do a breakthrough," there could be a lot of groundwork before that, that led to — we don't know.

Autoformalization "Basically Solved" — and a Trip to the Beach

Alex: So I remember that was a Friday because I just was completely, like my mind was completely exploded, and it was Labor Day, and we just took the kids to the beach, and I needed a few days of, you know, I'm not checking my phone, I'm not on Twitter. I'm just throwing, you know, throwing my kids into the ocean and —

Lex: Did you have that moment where you're just sitting and looking at the ocean and contemplating?

Alex: Yeah. Like, what does it all mean?

So I had already gone through that a month before. And I was like — So now what that says is that autoformalization is basically solved.

It's not solved in the way that I would want it to be solved. I want — and people are still gonna work very, very hard on this. There's all kinds of other things that happen, just like there's all kinds of other things that happen when you prove theorems that are byproducts of that process for human understanding. There's all kinds of other things when you work on making a beautiful library of mathematics, and that process will continue. That process will be very difficult. It's gonna be the thousands of man-hours of people around the world contributing in this open-source way. But in terms of "can you get a sorry-free proof of something that human beings have written down on paper" — I think that problem is done.

Round Three: Mourning FLT, Then Quasi-RH

Lex: And so you were standing there with a whiskey, having gone through this a month before, and now again.

Alex: Right. This was round three.

Lex: This is round three.

Alex: 'Cause when I got back from Labor Day, it was Navier-Stokes.

Lex: Navier-Stokes.

Alex: But this one —

Lex: So I was like, "I was just mourning FLT. You're gonna do this to me? Come on."

Alex: But now, I mean, this really hit home, right? With the quasi-RH.

## 一、黎曼的"降维打击"——他本人就是最早的"AI嵌入工程师"
真正令人震惊的不是 AI 证明了 quasi-RH，而是 **AI 用的是黎曼本人发明的那个核心动作**：把离散问题（素数）嵌入连续空间（复平面）。这与现代深度学习的所有"几何化""嵌入""latent space"思想，在数学哲学上是**完全同构**的。黎曼在 1859 年做的事情——把一个数论的、颗粒的、无序的对象，强行塞进复变函数的光滑世界里——就是今天 Transformer 把离散 token 嵌入高维向量空间的祖先。
于是你会发现一个诡异的闭环：**素数似乎"喜欢"被这样处理**。黎曼留下了一道通往自身证明的秘密通道，而 AI 现在走通了。这不是巧合，这是一个暗示：某些数学对象的本质属性可能是"**可嵌入性**"本身——它们存在的意义就是等着被映射到另一个空间里显形。素数不是在复平面上"投影"，素数**本就是复平面的影子**。

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Are Banks Blocking AI Agents to Protect You or Their Profits?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"受托人悖论"：Anthropic 的 S-1 可能是一份法律上无法被机构购买的招股书

Jim Bianco 提出了一个被所有人忽略的、致命的结构性矛盾——当 Anthropic 在风险披露章节写下"可能终结人类"（existential risk to humanity）时，它其实在法律上自动排除了美国绝大多数公共养老金、州市政基金和保险资金作为合规买家。因为"审慎人原则"（Prudent Person Rule）要求受托人在读到披露文件后做出一个理性人会做的决定，而没有任何一个法官会接受"我读了可能毁灭人类的风险，但 2030 年回报曲线太诱人"这样的辩护。

这里有个让人毛骨悚然的跨领域连接——这是帕斯卡赌注（Pascal's Wager）的金融逆向版本：帕斯卡是用无限正收益证明相信上帝的合理性，而 Anthropic 的 S-1 用近乎无限的负收益证明了买它的不合理性。这意味着一个诡异的结果：越诚实披露 AI 风险的实验室，越只能依赖私募资本和加密货币式的信念投资者；越粉饰风险的实验室，反而越能触及养老金这样的庞大资本池。 诚实在这里是一种资本惩罚。市场上将出现一场奇怪的"风险披露军备竞赛"，但方向是向下的——比谁更会讲一个"安全"的故事。

二、银行屏蔽 AI 代理不是安全问题，而是暴露了金融业的真实商业模式：对"懒惰"征收的隐形税

Jim 一针见血：美国银行系统里躺着 4 万亿美元零利率存款。这不是存款，这是对人类摩擦成本的租金。银行的核心商业模式从来就不是"金融服务"，而是"摩擦税的征收权"。信用卡积分、睡眠账户、每日未扫入货币基金的余额——每一笔都是对"人太懒不会每天登录"这件事的套利。AI 代理的出现，第一次把这个被隐藏了 50 年的秘密揭开了。

让这件事更震撼的跨领域洞见：这完全复刻了 Carlota Perez 的技术革命理论——金融资本在每一次技术革命中都会先经历"狂热期"后进入"协同期"，而旧秩序会把"保护消费者"包装成拒绝协同的理由。你会发现，当银行说"为了保护你"的时候，和 1990 年代电信公司说"长途电话必须昂贵才能保证质量"、1920 年代马车协会说"汽车不安全"用的是完全相同的句法结构。更有趣的是：这一次抵抗者不是律师团，而是风险管理部门——银行主要风控官 50% 的时间现在都投入到 AI 风险上，这个比例两年前是 0%。他们在用合规语言包装自己的租金保卫战。

三、ICBC 的"连接死刑"揭示了一个被低估的金融底层逻辑：金融系统的免疫反应比病原体本身更致命

2023 年中国工商银行纽约清算部门被勒索软件攻击，付了赎金拿回了钥匙——但真正杀死它的不是黑客，而是其他银行拒绝再连接它。连俄罗斯黑客组织的"发言人"（是的，他们现在有发言人，这本身就是一个值得单独写一篇论文的现象）都出来澄清"我们没留后门"，也救不回来。

这是一个绝妙的生物学隐喻——这是医院获得性感染（nosocomial infection）的金融版：隔离机制本身比病原体更危险。但更深的洞见是：金融业的"连接性"同时是它的最大资产和最大脆弱性，而 AI 时代会让这个张力变得极端。当每一次代码库被攻破都可能通过代理网络指数级扩散，整个系统将从"信任默认开启、作恶需要证明"演变为"信任默认关闭、安全需要证明"。这是一次信任拓扑结构的翻转——未来十年金融业最被低估的技术将不是区块链也不是 AI，而是可验证计算证明（verifiable compute proofs），因为这是让"你无法伤害我"从承诺变成数学证明的唯一路径。而讽刺的是：加密货币行业已经为此构建了十年的工具栈。

四、一个意外的观察：真正的"加速主义/减速主义"分裂不是意识形态，而是"已安装资本"的函数

Jim 提到的数据惊人：皮尤民调显示中国民众对 AI 的支持率 80%，美国 37%。日本、韩国、印尼、南亚国家几乎全体加速主义；美国、英国、法国全体减速主义。表面上这被解释为"发达国家更了解风险"。但真实的解释更冷酷：发达国家拥有大量基于摩擦、信息不对称、代理成本构建的高价值行业（银行、律所、咨询、保险、医疗账单管理）。AI 消灭的不是"工作"，而是这些行业赖以收取租金的信息不对称。

跨领域连接：这完全对应 Mancur Olson 在《国家兴衰探源》里的理论——越老的经济体，分配性联盟（distributional coalitions）越根深蒂固，越会把保护自己租金的行为包装成"文化价值观"或"公共安全"。所以，美国"害怕 AI"的本质，不是美国人更有智慧看到风险，而是美国人身处于一个有太多东西要失去的系统中。印尼不害怕，是因为印尼本来就没什么要失去。这个解释比"价值观差异"冷酷得多，也准确得多。而它预测的下一个结果令人不安：在未来 10 年，监管套利不会流向资本最便宜的地方，而会流向"旧秩序租金最少"的地方——这才是真正的 AI 地缘政治格局。

📝 转录文本

Are Banks Blocking AI Agents to Protect You or Their Profits?

Bits + Bips — featuring Jim Bianco (Bianco Research), Ram Ahluwalia (Lumina), Chris Perkins (Franklin Crypto), hosted by Austin Campbell (Zero Knowledge Group)

Cold Open — The Fiduciary Question

Because I've asked the question, if you are the head of a state pension fund or a municipality or some other fiduciary, how do you as a fiduciary read that risk statement and say, "yeah, it might end humanity, but my God, look at these 2030 performance" — that that's really why we got to get in on this thing.

Hey, everyone, welcome to Bits and Bips, where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time. We're here to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto, macro and AI today.

But before we start, remember, Unchained is running a listener survey and it's going to decide some real things — whether there's a weekly recap show, what time are the streams, what goes into premium, all of it's anonymous. Take you a couple of minutes. Everybody who finishes it gets a free month of premium Bits and Bips or Unchained — your pick. Go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. Go ahead and do that. It's open through November 8th.

And before we start, a quick commercial break. This episode is brought to you by Nexo, the premier digital assets wealth platform. Earn daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds all through one platform trusted by more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com. Geo-restrictions, eligibility, and terms apply.

All right, everybody, as always, I'm your host, Austin Campbell, High Scholar of Zero Knowledge Group. I'm here with my usual co-hosts: Ram Ahluwalia, Maester of Wealth, Leader of Lumina; Chris Perkins, the Golden Hand of Franklin Crypto; and a very special guest today, Jim Bianco, President and Macro Strategist of Bianco Research.

Segment 1 — "Black October": AI, PHP Vulnerabilities, and the New Dark Forest

So let's start with something that's been pretty disruptive across the world, we'll call it — Black October. AI-assisted researchers have found critical PHP flaws, which are now being exploited in the wild. The same week, the keys behind eight eMudhra certificate authorities were cracked in under a second — what John Milinovich calls Black October. From crypto, we already have these stress tests to web infrastructure. But for everybody else, they're now learning about the dark forest that crypto has lived in.

So what is broken? PHP. Two critical flaws were patched October 21st, a day early after details leaked. NSA Cyber said if you can't patch, take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated. Exploitation is confirmed in the wild. There's over 5 million hosts that are still exposed. A third flaw may be unpatched. Allegedly, AI found it first.

OpenAI said this is a new phase where AI can find security bugs with internet scale impact. Former CISA director Chris Krebs noted that 3% of all critical vulnerabilities of all time have been found in the last month. And Amazon saw attackers targeting flaws four days before the patch shipped.

Chris Perkins — Max Vulnerability, Max Opportunity

So I'm gonna start here from a human and functional perspective: this appears to be the point of greatest disruption of internet security that we have seen, and the breaches seem more significant on a daily basis. So Chris, I'll actually start with you — having worked in this space, what do you make of this?

Look, if you have security, you've got nothing. I learned that when I was in Iraq, and it's the same thing for the internet and your commerce. Now, here's the good news. I feel like we're at a period of max vulnerability and max uncertainty. Why? Because vulnerabilities discovered are vulnerabilities patched. Ultimately, I feel like we're going to end up with a much more robust ecosystem. We're still going to have threats — deep fake threats will still be there, plenty of challenges — but these vulnerabilities are going to get closed.

And honestly, I earnestly believe that there's this big debate between open source and closed source — I believe that crypto industry, open source, public is going to actually win in the end, because they say sunlight is the best disinfectant. In the crypto space, we've been in the most hostile of environments since our inception. People are always trying to hack us. We're used to this environment. We thrive in this environment.

If only there was a world-class concentration of cryptographers who could solve these issues — it's in the crypto industry. Though we're in max vulnerability stage now, I feel like the crypto industry is going to lead us out of this. Traditional markets, I think, they could hack a lot too — you don't hear about it because they keep it quiet.

Jim Bianco — Industrial-Scale Vulnerability Discovery

Jim, you've been writing a lot about markets lately. You've looked a lot at AI. What do you make of this sudden acceleration?

Oh, I think it could have a significant impact. And it worries me a little bit. Let's remember what it's finding is vulnerabilities, decentralized vulnerabilities written in by millions of different programmers and tens of billions of lines by hand, one at a time. And now we've got industrial-scale AI going through all of this, looking for vulnerabilities — probably more and deeper than all the world's hackers combined.

It underscores the idea that we can't stop. We have to move forward with AI. If the argument out of Washington is "we've got to slow down and look at all of this," China will just continue to move forward and give it to North Korea and let them unleash it on everybody else. But once we're through this, we will have much more robust and we'll have much safer systems.

Markets won't anticipate this any more than it anticipates any other event. The ultimate example we're all familiar with is January of 2020 — there was a virus coming out of China. Markets said "nothing to see here" and they kept going up. Then around late February 2020, markets decided, okay, now there's something to see here — and they went straight down. So markets aren't reacting to this today. But if these vulnerabilities continue, we'll wake up one day and they'll be down.

Have We Seen Economic Damage Yet?

Jim: I don't think we've seen any economic damage from these vulnerabilities. Nor have we seen any economic productivity or benefits from AI just yet. The story came out last week that something like 1% of all companies are using like 70 or 80% of tokens — and most of those are VC-backed companies. I actually look at that as being extraordinarily positive. Your potential universe of people to start using this stuff is enormous.

Ram: Ramp reported that 40% of small businesses are using AI, and Ramp self-selects for a tech-forward audience.

Austin: Yes, I have seen economic damage. One of the things I caution people about is looking at the United States specifically — a lot of our infrastructure is quite frankly harder than some of the others. A good example I was just looking at over the weekend: GMO Internet. Over 70 different brokerages were impacted. Attackers breached servers, stole customer credentials, and executed balance-destroying trades — probably against themselves — across 70 different brokerages. They're now asking the JFSA and the Japanese government for help.

The other part is that with these data breach situations, there are two problems with knowing the economic impact. One, I don't think we've got a great handle on anybody paying ransomware fees. The other part — if these are occurring over the last few months, you're not going to see litigation about that for months to years. There was one major health diagnostics platform that got hacked. With the way HIPAA works, that's $2.5 million per instance of customer data. So the economic damage is real — I'm just not sure it all surfaces at the same time.

Ram: I agree there's a lot of hardening — US banks, brokerage, e-commerce, two-factor authentication. But the market knows all this. Palo Alto Networks stock isn't at all-time highs — the 100x P/E ratio is hard to action on this.

The ICBC Death Penalty — Why Hacks Stay Hidden

Jim: If you recall the story, the Chinese bank ICBC was hacked in late '23 — ransomware was put on it. It was a clearing bank on Wall Street. They cleared tons of trades a day. They paid the ransom, got the keys back, opened up their system. What happened? No other bank wanted to connect with them. They were afraid maybe they left a virus or worm behind.

It effectively was a death penalty for the bank — so much so that even the Russian hackers that hacked the bank came out. Russian hacking is a legitimate business. They had a spokesman. They actually have a spokesman. He came out and said, "no, no, no — we got a ransom, you're cool to do business with them." They actually had to wind up going out of business.

That's why you don't hear about a lot of these hacks. It's a death sentence — especially in financial services — because in finance, confidence matters and you can't have runs.

Ram: I was speaking to the head of risk at a very significant bank over the weekend. He said 50% of his time is solely focused on AI risk. A couple of years ago, 0% of time was focused on this risk. Now it's 50%.

Segment 2 — Banks Blocking AI Agents: Safety or Profit Protection?

Chris: Let's not forget — it's not just hacking risk. As agents come on the scene, they're really good at optimization. You saw the Apollo article: if agents are able to optimize to the basis point, what's going to happen to bank deposits? There has to be an entire array of new safeguards, tripwires — whatever policy needs to get rethought — because we're entering into a new era of risk for global finance.

Ram: I'll tell you the bigger risk than this PHP: it's the harnesses that are used to write code. There was another hack this past week with Light, which is a harness that developers use. The way modern coding is done — you have agents that build, other agents that evaluate and review the code, then agents that publish. Hackers had a poisoned version of the software. If you control the harness, the harness has all the secret keys, the private keys. That is far more pernicious than this PHP issue.

Jim's Bottom Line — Finance Runs on Friction

Jim: We found this out last week that a lot of the banks have now blocked AI agents from accessing — I can't access with an AI agent my Chase account as of this past week. And today in the Wall Street Journal, the same thing is happening with credit cards.

Let me bottom line it for you. A lot of financial services, you know, based on laziness: there's $4 trillion in zero-yielding bank accounts. You don't want to log in every single day and sweep that money into a money market fund. You wanted to have an agent do it.

The banks — a big part of their profit is they'll sweep your money out and they'll invest it for themselves out of your zero-interest account. Now that you're able to do it, the banks are afraid they're going to lose that revenue stream. They offer credit cards with points and other perks. There's a whole cottage industry of people using Reddit subthreads and using AI agents to try and maximize points. The banks want you to sign up for a credit card and pay the $300 a year, but not actually use the points or maximize them. So they're blocking that.

So much of our business model in finance is based on frictions and laziness. And AI is now threatening that. They're obfuscating it by saying "I'm trying to protect you." But the question I ask is: who are you really protecting? Are you protecting me, or you're protecting your own profits?

Ram: The agents here are acting as fiduciaries of the customer. I understand why the banks denied access to Plaid 10 years ago — Plaid was not acting in the interest of the customer. Here, these agents are acting on the interest and request of the customer. So I don't think that is gonna fly, and it's gonna hurt banks like JP Morgan that have a lot of zero-interest deposits.

How Does This Play Out?

Chris: How do we know the direction of travel? Either the banks dig in and create regulatory moats, or some of them break ranks and become tech companies — maybe some of these neobanks. How does this play out?

Jim: We're going to get more regulation. In general, when it comes to technology, what are most people not really concerned about? Privacy and safety. We give away all our private information. We vomit all of our opinions on social media. We don't care that our phone or browser is looking at our private data to serve up ads. Why are we going to put our foot down about this now? If an AI agent can make my life easier, can save me a couple of bucks by sweeping money into a money market fund, I'm not going to lose sleep over safety.

Ram: We saw a preview of this in the 2023 mini banking crisis when SVB and First Republic went down — you had mini runs. But here you don't have a social-media-driven bank run; it's really agents finding these optimizations, and there still are frictions. New bank account opening is a major friction.

The opportunity is that the great disruptor has arrived. If you're a community bank and get in front of it, maybe you can drive scale in a technology-centric way. But the risk is that if agents have their way and margins get compressed, we see incremental consolidation to a point where there's additional pricing power brought back. That's my concern.

Jim: Community banks are going to look at this as a threat because it's going to collapse their margins. A lot of those zero-yielding balances are more at the community banks than at the big warehouse banks like JP Morgan or Citibank. Their business model is a bet on friction leading to laziness. If that goes away, they're going to have to rethink their business model from the ground up.

Chris: AI is learning the lessons of crypto. We were supposed to kill the banks with stablecoins back in the day — now it's the agents that are going to do it. It feels like crypto all over again with AI, except it's going to be eating the banks at their own game instead of inventing a new one with stablecoins.

The Contrarian Take — Crypto Moves Behind the Scenes

Ram: Let me give a really contrarian take. The banks are moving AI. OK, so is crypto stronger for all the hacks that we see every three months? No. The talent moves out of the system. The talent's moving to AI. I was at the FinTech Money 2020 conference — I go there every year except COVID. No one cares about anything but AI. That's where the venture dollars are going. That's where the talent's going.

Which is great for crypto because it goes where it belongs — infrastructure behind the scenes. These technologies are converging very, very quickly.

Austin: How does immutability interact with a customer service dispute around a payment that went awry? There are things like that that are going to be difficult.

Ram: I tweeted about this today — folks are coming to me now and saying "you know what, I kind of like the transfer agent, I love tokenization but I like the transfer agent." It's an additional layer of security which makes sense in the environment we are today. This whole decentralization-centralization thing is a cycle. We're in max regulatory permissiveness, so you can afford to have centralization — but maybe it goes back in the other direction when things change.

Chris Dixon from A16Z just changed the scope of the multi-billion-dollar crypto fund — now it's broader. The backstory, again, I picked up from this conference: there's just not enough good entrepreneurs pursuing great projects and the excitement's in AI.

Global Attitudes — A Divergence

Jim: I'll stick with the AI conversation. In this weekend's Economist, there's been surveys done across the world about AI. The more developed the country, the more skepticism there is about AI. The United States has the most skepticism. But when you get to third-world countries — Southern Asia and the like — they view it as nothing but their path to becoming equal.

But in the US, in France, in the UK — close to them — everybody's afraid of it. But no one's afraid of it in Japan. They're not afraid of it in South Korea. They're not afraid of it in Indonesia. And by the way, they're not afraid of it in China.

Whenever the president gets together with Chairman Xi and Chairman Xi says "we share your concern about this" — no, you don't. Your country's all in favor of moving as fast and as hard as you can on this. It's only our country, and the UK, and France that are the decelerationists. Everybody else is an accelerationist when it comes to AI.

Ram: I saw a survey from Pew — popular support in China is 80%, in the US it's 37%.

Chris: Ukraine took out three of Russia's data centers two weeks ago, and the spam bot traffic on Twitter and other social media declined dramatically. How much of the current public opinion is being shaped by foreign adversaries?

Generational Shift — SoFi vs. the Majors

Austin: Let's throw a stat out there. Over the last few years, SoFi opened more accounts for 35-and-unders than all of Chase, B of A, Citi, and Wells Fargo combined. The banks are already losing young people. They are going to internet-native platforms that allow agents — SoFi, Robinhood. All these protective measures by the banks remind me of the early days of e-commerce in the early 2000s, when you were told by the banks "don't you ever put your credit card on the internet because it was dangerous." Dangerous for who? It was dangerous for the banks.

Ram: I'll challenge a little bit — back then you did have a lot more fraud, and PayPal grew up in that environment by being one of the first to do fraud tooling, then Visa rolled out zero-liability protection a few years later. But overall the point stands: technology is going to be a rug pull for incumbents that can't advance.

Commercial Break

What if your crypto could do more than just sit in your wallet? Nexo is a digital assets wealth platform where you can generate daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds against your assets. Today, Nexo serves more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com.

One more thing — we've got a listener survey open. It takes just a few minutes. It's anonymous and it changes what we make next. Use the QR code on screen or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. The link is in the show notes.

Segment 3 — AI Jitters, Vendor Equity, and Wall Street's Forced Mutation

Let's continue on the AI thread — the flip side. Tech led a sell-off last week. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq had a second straight weekly loss. Meta's capex, Lam Research's info on supply constraints, revived AI spending fears, and Jensen speaking of a scarcity of capital. Today the Anthropic S-1 came out at the exact same time Elon Musk is telling everybody debt markets are locking up for the neoclouds.

Scoreboard: Nasdaq fell 2.6% on Thursday — worst day since June. Bitcoin itself is down — I saw it trading under $80,000 today. Meta fell 7% on Thursday. The financing bottleneck is real — Jensen is out there, Elon said the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.

Jim — Why Volatility, Why Mutation

Jim: When you get a new technology, two things tend to happen at the same time. The future is very uncertain, so it's very hard for Wall Street to properly price this stuff — nobody knows where we'll be in six months or five years. So you get a lot of volatility. It's never a straight line.

Second, I'd argue a lot of Wall Street incumbents are nowhere. One of the biggest problems Wall Street has is its regulator, FINRA. Basically FINRA's job is to protect the big incumbents against startups — if you have 50 lawyers in your legal department, you've got no problem following the law. But if you want to be a startup with 10 people, good luck.

FINRA's rules on AI are: do anything you want. But if you screw up, we're going to use you as an example against everybody else. So they scared everybody away from really developing AI internally. I go to a lot of money managers, investment banks. They're nowhere. AI to them is a glorified Google search. So you tend to get that TradFi argument about AI like we heard about crypto: "oh, it's nothing."

Third — and I'll write a piece on this soon — whenever you get a transformational technology like this, it is so big it causes Wall Street to mutate. - 11th century Venice needed to bring up warships to protect themselves from the Byzantine Empire — they invented the secondary bond market to finance it. - 14th century, when we had multi-currency trade because of the spice trade, we invented double-entry bookkeeping. - 16th century with the Dutch East India Company, they needed more financing — they invented public equity.

I think we're going to have to do something like that today with AI. You're seeing it with how we're financing data centers, with power agreements, with vendor financing — because traditional tools of public equity, public debt and bank loans are just not going to work for the kind of build-out we have.

Vendor Equity — The New Instrument

Ram: It's absolutely a transformational technology and we're all underestimating it — including me — in a big way. These agents are going to drive a lot of compute demand.

Where we're going from now is vendor financing to vendor equity purchases. It was announced today in the Journal that AMD, NVIDIA, and Broadcom may be buying up to $5 billion of Meta stock. The bigger story is the handing over of free cash flow from these hyperscalers to capex receivers — the semiconductors. I'd rather own the semiconductors than these Mag 7 companies that have given up their free cash flow.

AI will bend the reality of markets. It's not a bubble, though — sentiment is so dour. Meanwhile, fundamentals, when you look at earnings, are still quite strong. Goldman came out with a report saying we're going to see 40x token growth in the next few years. The real issue is who's going to capture the value from that. Semiconductors will. The frontier labs have a lot more difficulty ahead from competition from open-weight models.

Chris: Elon's tweet around financing drying up — who benefits if the neoclouds go bust? Elon definitely does.

Ram: I was in Silicon Valley last week. There are seed rounds getting done for half-a-billion-dollar valuations where if you have the chips from NVIDIA and a power source, you can rent them out, your costs are below that, you get some kind of leverage. NVIDIA is trying to spread around and diversify their concentration risk away from the hyperscalers.

Gavin Baker referred to NVIDIA as the Federal Reserve of AI. There's a lot of truth to that statement.

Jim: The traditional rails we have — Series A, Series B, Series C, IPO, borrowing in debt markets — that has to mutate for this new technology. It's a square peg in this new technology's round hole. Wall Street is forced to mutate all the time when there's a new technology, and it will again.

Chris: Let's not forget — ledger started 3,000 years ago in Mesopotamia, and that's when a lot of economic progress kicked off: algebra, et cetera.

Ram: As Anthropic goes public, it's going to flood its allocators and the venture capitalists with a lot of DPI, a lot of distributions. Where does that capital go? Back into AI. The last 10 days — seven days on the road, Money 2020, then Silicon Valley — it's all AI. All DPI is going right back into the AI stack. It's going to go buy compute. The no-brainer's own compute — and the expression of that is semiconductors.

Austin: You're sure it's not going to go into Pac Heights real estate in San Francisco?

Ram: It's going to go there too. Early Game. Also Santa Cruz, right? The price per square foot beats Manhattan.

Jim: I've heard the price per square foot of the average house in the US is about $180. I hear it's pushing $4,000 or $5,000 a square foot in Pac Heights right now.

Segment 4 — Taking Apart the Anthropic S-1

Austin: Let's drill in on something that came out today — the Anthropic S-1. A couple of interesting things:

  • H1 revenue up at $16.3 billion, way up year-over-year (full year 2025 was $4.6B).
  • Q2 was technically positive operating income — but they have on a forward basis over $400 billion of apparently pretty non-cancelable compute commitments.
  • The FT reports a $1.5–1.75 trillion valuation is expected.
  • Governance: Founders' Class F shares have 50.1% of the vote. There's a long-term benefit trust that elects a board majority — and future board members and trustees are picked by the previous ones. So there's no real method of outside intervention in governance for regular shareholders.

Jim — The Pharma Analogy and the Fiduciary Problem

Jim: It was interesting that they compared themselves to pharmaceutical startups — big investment up front, and hopefully on the back end is a product, a drug, with long-tail cash flow.

The other thing I got hung up on, being a financial type, was the risk section talking about an existential risk to humanity. Because I've asked the question: if you are the head of a state pension fund or a municipality or some other fiduciary, how do you as a fiduciary read that risk statement and say, "yeah, it might end humanity, but my God, look at these 2030 portfolio formulas"?

And you also have to be careful — because if you buy it and it does something like Facebook did after its IPO, or even what SpaceX has done — the typical tech IPO comes in and deflated valuation, sells off 50% — you're going to get a lawsuit. They're going to throw that risk section in your face. "What part of ending humanity didn't you like?" So there might be some pushback against public fiduciary money going into this thing. But there might be enough private capital that can overwhelm that.

They'll raise money. There's so much hype. But $175 to $200 billion — that's the question.

Ram — The Opacity and the Open-Weight Threat

Ram: A few observations.

One: there's no gross margin in the S-1. A few weeks ago there was leaked financial data indicating a gross margin of 85%. The way you measure gross margin — cost of revenue vs. revenue. They've lumped it all into one big pool. You cannot differentiate the cost of training, the cost of inference, and the cost of R&D. It's very opaque accounting — that's not going to inspire much confidence.

Two: open-weight models are taking more and more share of compute, and I don't see that stopping. DeepSeek released 4.1 Flash. DeepSeek is from China, but you can run their open-weight models in the US — your traffic is not going to China, it's 90% cheaper, and about as good. And "about as good" means good enough — you can just run the token three times and it's going to be better.

Three: there's always a primary desktop. In financial services it used to be the Bloomberg Terminal. For coding it was Claude or Codex. But now the primary desktop is the harness, which allows multiple agents to interact. Claude doesn't have a harness. Their harness biases to Claude — it's not agnostic. So their positioning with developers is diminishing over time.

Austin — The Three Taxonomies of Model Consumption

Austin: I want to pile in. It's not just DeepSeek — you're starting to see real fragmentation. If you look at the model landscape and people actually adopting these models, I think you're seeing three taxonomies:

  1. Direct Frontier Consumers — People consuming the frontier models from the labs themselves. There are significant numbers using Claude in enterprise developments or through the API. Credit to Anthropic and OpenAI here.
  2. Frontier-at-Best-Price via Open Router — People who want the best model for the best price, using open router. DeepSeek Flash is a very good model — I think their most recent one, 1017, is on par with Grok High but significantly cheaper. Meanwhile, you've got MiniMax, Qwen, GLM — all roughly comparable, dirt cheap. And Moonshot just dropped Kimi K2 — right up there with the Claude models, significantly cheaper, open weight.
  3. Self-Hosters — People who want to throw everything into their own AWS Bedrock instance or host themselves and train their own models. Coinbase for example was doing that with a version of Qwen for anti-fraud, all internally.

For Anthropic, I'm paying close attention to: is your revenue curve exponential up, or is it starting to bend because of all these other deployments?

Ram: It's bending up — because they drop their token prices. Open Router will flow traffic to whoever's cheapest and most productive, so they get a spike. They dumped the bad news first through leaks, then dropped the S-1 with the good news on tokens. Open Router has first-class position with engineers.

Ken Griffin from Citadel said it well — the analogy is airline business models. Marginal revenue is high margin, marginal cost is low, and they're fueled by debt. If you see a drop-off in revenue and fixed costs stay in place — and they will, because it's debt — then you're not in a great spot.

Anthropic and OpenAI are best in the world at what they do, so they can command that premium. But you're seeing more proliferation of specialized niche models — for example, a video model came out today that's a quarter of the cost of Higgsfield. They're going to get picked off by specialization. Open Router is going to deploy that token capital to the lowest-cost provider — until regulation pushes out some of the competition. And it's coming.

Segment 5 — Midterms, Labor, and the Reshaping of Work

Chris: Midterms are coming. If there's one thing Republicans and Democrats seem to be aligning on, it's this.

Jim: I'll push back a little. Democrats have the DSA crowd — definitely decelerationists. But the other big part of the Democratic Party is labor unions, and they're accelerationists. They're seeing tremendous job opportunities in continuing to build data centers. Congratulations Tuesday night when the Democrats do well. Wednesday morning they're going to have two powerful parts of their constituency base battling each other over this topic.

Ram: The data center growth is creating a proliferation of blue-collar jobs. It's been inflationary. But the thesis is that medium term, once we're through this, it's going to be deflationary and everyone's going to lose their jobs — which I don't buy personally. When I heard Jeff Bezos say "we're going to have a three-day work week," I don't know — the more technology comes out, the harder I find myself working.

Jim — Channeling Marc Andreessen

Jim: I'll channel my inner Marc Andreessen and say: a job is a series of tasks, you put enough of them together and it's a job. What we're talking about is automating tasks. We're not going to automate every task — some jobs maybe, like driving. But we're going to automate some of the tasks of your job.

If your attitude is "oh, so now I can go home at 1 o'clock every day because some tasks are automated," you're going to be unemployed pretty soon. But if your attitude is "now I can do higher-function, more revenue-producing, more cost-saving ideas with the rest of my day because I've got the drudgery out of the way" — you'll be just fine. Your job will be different in 10 years. Your job will be different, but you have to allow it to be different.

Ram: The doomers are saying "why would anyone study math?" Probably because it's the most exciting time to study math — foundational problems have been solved. It's a question of what's next.

Jim: I'm old enough to remember before the internet, people saying "why does anybody need to learn how to write? Nobody ever writes." Then we invented email, and now we made it incumbent on everybody to learn how to write a paragraph. That's probably been the best thing. Kids in the 80s and 90s were not very good writers because they had no one to write to.

Ram — The Hollowing Out of Low-Skill White-Collar Jobs

Ram: I do think low-skilled white-collar jobs will be at risk — that's a change in my thinking in the last few months. I talked to a partner at Latham & Watkins — they're using Harvey. He said, "Rob, I don't need associates anymore. I just interact directly with the AI. I'm closer to the customer. I'm more responsive." That's happening in different areas: Rogo in financial analysis, Basis going after CPA firms. We're doing this a little bit for the wealth management category at Lumina.

AI services is huge. SaaS is a $300 billion revenue market. The revenue pool in legal, in CPA, is multiples of SaaS. For the first time, you can actually have AI service workers that do the job better, faster, cheaper. If you're the best at what you do, you're going to love AI because you're going to make even more money. But there will be a hollowing out of the lower ranks.

Jim: The associate job as understood in 2025–2026 might go away. But there will be an associate job in 2030, 2032 that will look very different. There will still be a need for associates — they're just not going to do the same thing.

Austin: Chris and I have both worked on trading desks and we damn well know you don't let the analysts trade anything. But that doesn't mean you don't need analysts. You do need to train them, develop them as the next generation. If law firms decide "we don't need associates, we're just going to do all the work ourselves" — that works fine until the partner retires and then you need somebody to take their job. You're killing your own recruitment funnel.

It's going to transform the work that analysts do — make them look truly more like apprentices versus "hey, go read documents for 700 hours so we can bill a client." Knock on wood, that improves their lives.

Chris: One thing won't change until the Optimus comes around — those first-years still have to go get me coffee.

Ram: You'll need less of them — that's the issue. Of course they'll still be around, repurposed. But now whoever lands that apprentice shop can do really well. That's the sharpest associate in the pool, and number two and number three don't get hired.

A Capitalist's Caveat on Inequality

Ram: Overall I agree — upskilling will happen. But look at technology teams, they're smaller. Inequality will go up. I'm a capitalist, I'm not in the AOC camp at all. But if you own capital and you're indexed to AI — and your human capital is into AI — you're going to do well. Unfortunately, the average person will not be indexed to that. We have to think about what that means.

Austin: You also have this interesting demographic where all the old people — the Boomers — have the capital. The youngsters have the technological sophistication, but none of the capital. So I'm bullish for the young associate. I think they're going to be just fine. I don't worry about it.

Lightning Round — The Fed

Austin: Fed this week. Jim, do you think anything interesting happens, or is it BAU?

Jim: They're not going to move. What's going to be interesting is if they're going to make the case that they will hike rates in December and into 2027. I think they should. It wouldn't slow the economy at all — it would actually make it healthier to get interest rates at their appropriate level.

No, they're not going to hike on Wednesday. But is the door left open? The last thing — Warsh is not into forward guidance, kind of telling us what they're going to do. But the rest of them are. So they'll start talking again on Friday, and we'll have to see whether they open the door towards the December hike.

Austin: Yeah, I concur. All right. Well, on that note, we are at 5:30. Thank you everyone for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips.

All: Thank you everybody. Thanks Jim. We'll see you next week. Thank you guys. That was fun.

Thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember — nothing we say here is investment advice. Please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

## 一、被忽略的"受托人悖论"：Anthropic 的 S-1 可能是一份法律上无法被机构购买的招股书
Jim Bianco 提出了一个被所有人忽略的、致命的结构性矛盾——当 Anthropic 在风险披露章节写下"可能终结人类"（existential risk to humanity）时，它其实在法律上**自动排除**了美国绝大多数公共养老金、州市政基金和保险资金作为合规买家。因为"审慎人原则"（Prudent Person Rule）要求受托人在读到披露文件后做出一个理性人会做的决定，而没有任何一个法官会接受"我读了可能毁灭人类的风险，但 2030 年回报曲线太诱人"这样的辩护。
**这里有个让人毛骨悚然的跨领域连接**——这是帕斯卡赌注（Pascal's Wager）的金融逆向版本：帕斯卡是用无限正收益证明相信上帝的合理性，而 Anthropic 的 S-1 用近乎无限的负收益证明了**买它的不合理性**。这意味着一个诡异的结果：**越诚实披露 AI 风险的实验室，越只能依赖私募资本和加密货币式的信念投资者；越粉饰风险的实验室，反而越能触及养老金这样的庞大资本池。** 诚
