💡 创造性洞见

一场被低估的"身份转置"：Anthropic 其实已经悄悄从模型公司变成了云厂商

人人都在谈 Opus 5.5 的智能、价格、写作风格。但这期访谈真正让人头皮发麻的转折不在模型层，而在财务物理学的切换：一年前每赚 1 美元亏 1.29 美元，今天每赚 1 美元赚 2 美元；人均营收从 140 万美元飙到 660 万美元。这不是"AI 公司做得好"这种描述能解释的——这是一次身份转置：Anthropic 对外还在被叫做"模型实验室"，但它的 S-1、它的客户结构（10 万美元+客户里 50% 在用 Cloud Platform）、它的 CPU 焦虑（而不是 GPU 焦虑！）全都在说一件事：它已经是 hyperscaler 了，只是外界还没反应过来。

一个让人意外的信号：Caitlin 全程最焦虑的不是模型、不是对齐、不是 safety——而是 CPU。"你没法再按需扩 CPU 了，必须提前做 capacity planning。" 这句话如果你是 2010 年代的 AWS 架构师听到会浑身起鸡皮疙瘩——它意味着云计算的"弹性契约"（elasticity contract）正在倒退 15 年。GPU 紧张大家都知道，但 CPU 居然也成了零和博弈，这是外界几乎没在谈的"二阶稀缺"。沙箱、CI、训练、推理在同一个 CPU 池里打架，这才是 Opus 5.5 定价能大降的真正底层原因之一：他们必须把客户的集成往更省 CPU 的方向推（prompt caching、preserved thinking、Rust 重写），不是单纯让利，而是生存。

跨领域连接：Anthropic 的产品哲学其实是 Nassim Taleb 的"反脆弱"工程化

Angela 在访谈最后说她最爱的书是 Taleb 的《Black Swan》——这不是一个无关的个人趣味，这是整个产品路线图的隐藏操作系统。她原话："我们已经从 deterministic 产品规划变成 deeply probabilistic……build a portfolio of bets……take hedging scenarios。" 翻译过来就是 Taleb 的 barbell strategy：用大量冗余的、看起来"过度设计"的通用原语（trust grants / 认证系统 / 单按钮回滚），去对冲你根本预测不到的黑天鹅。

Fable 被政府以意想不到的方式使用，就是他们自己遭遇的黑天鹅。他们的回应不是"下次预测得更准"，而是"把每一个 primitive 都做得比直觉上该做的更通用"——Caitlin 原话："从传统产品管理角度看，这不合理，我们应该聚焦。但选择泛化之后，我们发现自己越来越频繁地伸手去拿这个解法。"

这里的跨领域连接是：这跟免疫系统的工作方式一模一样。你的 B 细胞不是预测会遇到哪种病毒才生产抗体，而是提前随机生成几十亿种可能的抗体受体，等真正的抗原来了，匹配上的那一支就被克隆放大。Anthropic 的 trust grant 系统、通用 verification program、"单按钮回滚一切"——都是在生产抗体库，而不是在诊断具体疾病。这是生物演化用 40 亿年验证过的策略，而大多数创业公司还在用"精确 roadmap"的牛顿力学思维做产品。

最反直觉的洞察：distillation 是商业问题的伪装，真正的恐惧是"去安全化的克隆体"

表面看 Anthropic 投入巨大工程量防止模型被蒸馏，所有人（包括 Twitter）都默认这是商业护城河问题。但 Angela 说了一句被很多人忽略的话："如果你从我们这里蒸馏，你其实付钱给了我们，所以商业上我们是赚的。"

那他们到底在怕什么？答案藏在一句轻描淡写里："如果有人蒸馏模型但不运行 safeguards classifiers，世界上就可能出现坏结果。" 他们怕的不是克隆，是"去安全化的克隆"——不是竞争对手，而是绕过良心的自己。

这把整个"API 作为产品"的概念推翻了。传统 SaaS 的定价逻辑是"价值 - 成本 = 利润"。但 Anthropic 的真实定价公式其实多了一个负项："价值 - 成本 - 外部性风险 = 利润"。他们愿意为了降低第三项，牺牲掉一部分 UX、一部分开发者好感度、一部分可集成性。这是第一个真正把"负外部性"内生化（internalize）进 API 产品设计的技术公司。

跨领域连接：这跟核能工业监管的发展史完全同构。核电站不怕被仿制，怕的是没有安全壳的仿制品。所以 IAEA 的核不扩散机制不是在保护专利，是在保护人类的下行风险。Anthropic 正在把自己变成算法领域的 IAEA——而它居然还同时是全球最大的算法生产商。这个双重身份本身就是一个未来几年会反复炸裂的张力点。

彩蛋级的意外观察：他们"用 Rust 重写整个 API"的操作，暴露了"研究式工程"的真正含义

团队零 Rust 工程师，一声不吭 fork 了整个 Python monolith，用 Claude 写 Rust 代码，shadow traffic 验证两边输出一致，然后切流。CPU 省 40-50%，延迟改善 10-20%。

这件事在传统工程里不可能。它需要几年时间、专门招聘、分阶段迁移。但 Caitlin 一句话道破了新范式："真正重要的是 plan 和 verification。实现是 Claude 写的。"

这里有个被埋得很深的洞察：当 AI 把"实现"降为商品，"计划"和"验证"就暴涨为稀缺资源。但更深一层——"验证"本质上是研究方法论，不是软件工程方法论。Shawn 后半段说的"treat engineering like research"直接呼应了这一点。所以未来十年工程团队的组织结构会出现一次权力转移：传统上在工程 org 里，Staff/Principal engineers 的地位最高（他们"写最难的代码"）；未来是懂实验设计、懂假设验证、懂控制变量的"研究型工程师"地位最高。这跟学术界 PI vs 博士后的分工会越来越像。

而讽刺的是，Anthropic 作为训模型的研究机构，是最早被迫把这套方法论下沉到应用层的——因为他们的工程师每天都在跟研究员打交道。这是他们相对 OpenAI、Google 的一个隐性结构优势：文化上的研究-工程融合，而不是"研究员发论文、工程师部署"的分工。

Chain-of-thought extraction 与 UX 的权衡

— Yeah, exactly. We've known for a long time that chain of thought extraction is one of the most powerful ways that you can distill models. And actually something like how do we preserve thinking blocks across turns and make that something that's more required is something that we've explored back for a while. And where we were at was we always have this really, really hard trade-off that we have to make between user experience — like user experience changes that are maybe painful for users of the API — versus protection against distillation.

And so how do we kind of walk that line and say: we're preventing distillation... and maybe just take a step back. The reason we don't want distillation is because the entire point of why Anthropic exists is because we want AI to create positive outcomes in the world safely. And we run a lot of safeguards classifiers on the tokens that we're producing in order to make sure that they're safe. If someone distills our models and they run those models without safeguards classifiers, there could be bad outcomes in the world, and that's something that we don't want to have happen.

We don't want people to distill the model specifically for the sake of just using them for malicious reasons or for bad reasons. It's always an interesting trade-off: for all the people who are using the models for good, right — like we don't want to make them have a harder time getting the intelligence out of the models — but we have to make some trade-offs in order to prevent that distillation.

And so we had been working for a while on how do we prevent that chain of thought extraction? Like, what do we do about preserving thinking blocks in a way that wouldn't be too painful for people?

And we kind of think about user experience hits in like two layers. One is just like, you have to make an integration change and it's annoying, but you could still accomplish all the same things that you otherwise would have been able to accomplish. It's just a little bit annoying. And then two is like actually you can't accomplish the same things that you could have accomplished previously. And that's the one that we're really, really, really trying to not have happen.

And so where we landed with the last couple models is a few incremental changes to have like enforce these preserved thinking blocks across turns. And now like starting to be more about across, you know, like if you're using multiple accounts and things like this, right — like how do we make sure that we're ensuring that you aren't able to take advantage of this chain of thought extraction with the models. And so we shipped a couple additional features to help with that.

We worked actually with a lot of open source harness maintainers. We reached out to them, we talked to them, we were like, "You're going to have to make these upgrades within your harnesses. Because in traditional product management, I guess, you can be like, "okay, these are the set of things I hypothesize to happen. They will have a certain sequence, a certain ordering." But you are picking bets in a way that are much more concrete versus, you know, the deployment of Fable, for example. And so from this form of thinking, it's become deeply probabilistic actually from a product management standpoint, of like: so should we prioritize this? What are the chances of it ever happening again? When we look at things like that, we're like, okay, if we are to imagine the most crazy set of possibilities, we probably actually have very little certainty as to where things will go. And so we actually just kind of need to hedge and build a portfolio of bets. And so more often than not, we will take hedging scenarios of like: okay, we don't think it would happen again, but in the event that it does, we would actually want that hedge or have the ability to be able to do that very well. And so we will prioritize things like that. And then we have increasingly found that more often than not, by taking that strategy of product development, most of the time, we actually find ourselves being like, we actually do use the thing.

Dreaming as "Managed Agents all the way down"

— Some of the previous conversation here — we do a lot of this ourselves — but the harness that we provide is very simple in a way. It's intentionally simple. Now, the interesting part on top of that, though, is once you get that base layer, there are these hill-climbing strategies that we construct. And Dreaming is actually one of them. So Dreaming under the hood is a multi-agent system that we hill-climb on top of CMA. And it's actually CMA on top of itself, basically.

CMA on top of itself? It spins up another...

— Yeah. The way Dreaming works is that we spin up another Managed Agent that then can expect the previous Managed Agent and then write memories to that Managed Agent. So it's Managed Agents all the way down.

And this is a bit of a thing by design because we envisioned that you could probably put together a lot of these modular components for something interesting. And Dreaming is just like an example of one of the more interesting things that we were going after. But we have been looking at this as being like, there's actually a ton of other stuff you can do. You can do best-of-N as a type of multi-agent strategy. You can do a verifier agent — that goal thing or outcome thing. There's a bunch of other stuff in there. And we've seen people do some pretty funky, crazy stuff. There's been a harness that shares crazy memory across everything, and they spin up tons of parallel agents.

And we're like: we should actually just probably enable you to do that. In the same way that we built Dreaming — that's like Managed Agents all the way down — there's an update that we'll make relatively soon where we're updating the underlying primitive. We'll expose it to allow users to kind of construct harness strategies maybe, or however you want to call this stuff — like multi-agent strategies — that allow you to kind of build your own version of this. Sandboxing、Brain/Hands 架构与安全默认

Then related to the compute problem is the sandboxing problem. People have trouble containing agents inside boxes. They keep breaking out. What's going on there? What's the state of the art?

— Yeah. The state of the breakout recently. Yeah. It's interesting. One of the things that we did with Cloud Managed Agents specifically is the way that we architected it. We put out this blog post at the time of launching where we talked about: we have the brain separate from the hands.

And what that means is like the harness runs on a durable server — really ours, right?

Oh wow, nice quote. Yeah, that's good.

— And the hands are an execution environment, like a sandbox or some sort of container, right?

Part of the reason why we did this was for latency and reliability and these things. If the harness is just running on a durable server and it's only spawning a sandbox or a container to execute when it needs it, that means we can get you tokens back really quickly on your initial request. It means that your sandbox can die, but your whole agent doesn't die because the harness is durable and over here and the agent storing state separately also.

And there was a whole product development journey that we went on to get there because our first iteration of an API for agents was just like "throw a Claude Code in a sandbox and shove an API on top." And the reason why we didn't launch that as our durable, scalable solution is everything that I just said. It was like, you've got to boot a sandbox and boot Claude Code before you can even get a token back, right? The sandbox dies and you lose your whole agent. And so reliability wasn't where we wanted it to be.

安全比可靠性更重要：Credentials 与 egress 控制

— So we architected this way mostly for reliability and latency. But the interesting thing, there's actually a product manager who worked on this from the very beginning was like, "the most important property of this architecture is security." And everyone's like, "yes, yes, yes, but latency and reliability." And like now, no. I literally yesterday apologized to this person. I was like, "I'm now like telling everybody who I meet about what you've been saying for months that nobody was as excited about as this person was."

One of the more important properties of this architecture is: you have credentials for any work that the agent needs to execute. If you're going to go talk to an MCP server, or if you're going to go use a CLI or call some API — whatever you might want to do — you need to authenticate those things. You need to store those credentials somewhere so that the agent can use them. The way that we architected this was we have a totally separate vault where those credentials are getting stored. And once the agent decides "I'm going to go and call out to one of these services," the agent only ever sees like a placeholder, right? And on egress, we have a proxy that goes and pulls the right credential out and injects it and lets that out.

And so what's interesting about that is: the agent is never in the same place where the credentials are, right? Because in the old world of "just boot the agent in a box and let it run," you had to send credentials in there. And then you're doing some sort of like, "ah, how do we scrub this and that and make sure that the agent can't take that credential and go do something that it shouldn't be doing?" It's just literally a literal infrastructure wall that says the agents can't access those credentials and can't do anything bad with them. So that was one thing that was really great.

The other nice thing is on that sandboxing infrastructure, we can make sure that we have really great egress controls. So we have like domain allow lists and things like that, or you just totally shut off network access so that you can't say, "okay, agent wrote untrusted code, that code executes in sandbox, and that code can reach out to the internet." Now it only can reach out to where you say it can reach out to.

So there's a lot of really great properties around all of this within the architecture and within the way that you can configure your sandboxes, make it so that you end up secure by default.

One of the things that's starting to happen is as we're talking to customers who are like, "I want to run agents either for a product for my customers or internally, but I'm hearing about incidents where agents are breaking out of sandboxes and bad things are happening. How do I think about these things?" I think the two most important things are: architecture so that it's literally impossible for an agent to do something that isn't okay. And the configuration that you have on those sandboxes.

And so one of the really, really nice things about Cloud Managed Agents is you just get that out of the box. 收尾问答一：如何对抗 Slop

We're going to go into a few closing questions, which I thought would be fun to sort of bounce back and forth between the two of you. How do you fight slop on your teams?

— So we actually, this has been an interesting debate within our team. We're no different than anybody else, right? I think plenty of teams are talking about this. And what's interesting is what we're trying to figure out is: if you're producing a document, you're producing something that you want other people to consume — code, documents, whatever, right — you should use Claude to help you, of course. But if you use Claude to totally generate a thing, you didn't spend any time on actually reading it yourself and making sure that it was something of high quality, then you're putting a whole extra burden on the consumer of that document or of that code or whatever to spend a whole bunch of time trying to parse it, and that's just insane and totally unfair.

But what's funny is we, you know, we push back, we push on our team, "you can't do that, right? Like, if you're producing something, use Claude, sure, whatever, but you have to make sure that it's a high-quality thing."

Yeah, you as the human are still responsible for the quality.

— Right, you're still responsible for the quality, but then you get into this really funny thing where because of the Claudisms, even just like silly — I don't know, there's like an em-dash in the middle of the thing right — like people's brains trigger on this like, "oh no, I'm reading something that was written by Claude and not a human, and I'm annoyed because I want to be reading a thing that was fully produced by not necessarily fully produced by a human, but like that has the quality bar that the human would hold."

And so then we get into funny situations where maybe actually the person did spend a lot of time making sure the thing was high quality, but they use Claude to help them. But there's those little hints of Claude and then the reader is like turned off, you know, like that's unproductive as well.

And so we're — what we have kind of tried to do is set a bar within our team that's very much like: use Claude to help you because it would be really silly if you didn't use this hilariously powerful agent to speed you up in your job and in your life or to just help you produce better things. But it has to have a certain bar. And then for the consumer and the reader, if it really actually is just slop, send it back. Just say no, just send it back. You're not going to waste your time on this. But also don't be too nitpicky about the little Claudisms, right? Because we have to find the right balance here.

And so it's just really funny because we're, you know, we're going back and forth on this stuff within our teams, and just like so is everybody else in the world right now. We're just not any different.

But you have free tokens.

— Well, sure. But I mean, that doesn't tend to matter quite as much when it comes to...

So you have more than anyone else in the world. You probably see a lot — you guys use a lot, you see a lot more people doing a lot more.

— Yeah, it's totally fair, but it's definitely heavily discouraged.

Engineering slop?

— Yeah, I mean, it's the same thing, right? But I do think that where we've gotten to is a pretty good spot where humans play a large role in making sure designs of systems are good, right? And implementation tends to be Claude, right? And we're in a pretty good spot where for a lot of the code that gets written, all you really need is just a quick stamp and you can keep going. And you don't necessarily have someone deeply reviewing every single line of the code because you care more about the overall plan, the overall design is in good shape, less so than the exact perfect implementation. And obviously, you rely on a whole bunch of verification to make sure the thing that you're going to ship is high quality. And so it's actually been less of a conversation these days on code quality being slopped, in part because Claude's just gotten better, but in part because we have a lot of the right verification in place to make sure that we're holding a high bar.

I see. Trust your tests.

— Yeah.

Any product PMing slop? You can ship features a lot. You can put stuff out in a day. So he said this to me recently. Do you remember what he said to me? Tariq tweeted this. The right way to use model capabilities is not to ship 10x more features into prod. Spend more time understanding your users, trying experiments, building whatnot. But basically, you know, you could very easily just keep shipping random slop, but you should actually think about it. You should spend more time kicking off that first prompt. I know now today he's like, "kick off plan mode, we don't need it anymore." But outside of plan mode, you should think about what you're doing, right? It's very easy to put out a lot and you can get products solved.

— Yeah, I mean, I tend to kind of go on this rant about: there's a lot of just like fundamentals about how software gets — like, and products get planned and shipped and otherwise — that doesn't need to change just because agents are helping speed up certain parts of the process. But there's this inherent laziness is starting to come out from a lot of people where it's like, "oh, I don't have to think about some part of the process at all because the agents are doing it and helping me or whatever." But those are still incredibly foundational parts of the process that should be things that you're spending your time and energy on.

And I think that's kind of the spirit of what he's getting at here. It's just like as a founder or creator, let's call it as well: it just feels like because the cost of experimentation or exploration is so low now that I should be doing more of that. And he's basically saying to not do that, to use it in service of a very intentional goal that I start from the start, which like I obviously am coming around to. It's just hard. It's like you have this toy that does everything. It's just like, throw it at the wall.

Yeah, there is scope too. Like the blog post of today was two weeks to make Cloud AI faster. There were 12 things. We had — there were 13 things. We hit 12 of the 13 targets in three days, right? Well, you could just stay, okay, it's a two week sprint. We'll do the 13, but instead there's 20 things you push down. This is not product slop. It's not new products. It's refactoring. But still, you guys do a very good job at outputting a lot, but keeping high bar quality.

— Yeah.

收尾问答二：Angela 的 Tweet Corner 与阅读

Nice. Okay. Part two of three. This is going to make Angela very uncomfortable. This is Angela Tweet Corner.

— I will tell... nice. I don't know. I will tell people nonstop to...

I'm pretty sure you've deleted stuff.

— Mm-hmm.

Because I'm like, there's stuff in your deletions that I'm like, still...

— Yeah, I know.

They really like, altered my DNA.

— Oh, I appreciate that. Wow.

What do you think about the most? What do you refer people to the most that you want to sort of bring up? And I can pull it out for you if you want, but...

— I actually don't think I have a favorite, honestly. No, I really don't.

Okay, I guess maybe I like the one that you say where it's "half doing something is an expensive way of not doing it."

— That's very on topic for us today.

I guess, you know, obviously, you're in a different job now. You don't do this anymore. But like, I think this is a power tweet. This is like a Naval Ravikant. Naval knows you — that do this. And like, what mode of, what framework of mind, frame of mind are you in?

— That's a good question. Yeah, this was a very long time ago. I went through a period of my life where I was like reading constantly actually. I found myself like very bored of the stuff that I was doing and I felt like I was just like not being intellectually challenged. And so I actually went on this a bit of a bender where I think I read something like 200 or so books in like a year.

And I was just curious about — I just wanted to read everything. And I was missing a little bit of the kind of intellectual, like, I don't know, muscle building you get when you're in school where they're like, "this is a new topic you got to learn, it's tough, it's not super fun actually, but you are really stretching yourself." And I felt like after just working for a couple years, I just stopped doing that. Like, yeah, the job's interesting, and yes, it's challenging, but it doesn't have that intellectual bit to it.

So anyway, I went on this bit of a bender, a reading bender, and I read like 200 books in a year. It was great. I had a really long commute, so it was a good use of my time. Very long Caltrain ride. But I ended up coming out of that and being like, I was just thinking a lot as a result of that.

And at the time, it really wasn't to build a Twitter follower or anything. I was just tweeting into the abyss. I had no followers. These were tweets for myself, and I was practicing a little bit of: how would I try to compress the idea that I have in as few words as possible? It was kind of like the personal test I had for myself. And then I guess people just started liking it. And so I just kind of just kept going at it. And then I got too busy with work and I stopped doing it.

I got to ask, after all the reading, any book recommendations, blogs, long articles?

— My favorite one still is probably The Black Swan by Nassim Taleb. That was like one of those — like, to me at least — it was like a bit of a life-changing philosophical book where I was like, "that's a completely different way to look at the world."

And, you know, I was thinking of Black Swan when the Fable thing happened. It's a thing that you didn't know could happen. Now that it happens, it permanently changed your framework of how things work.

— Exactly. And the idea is so simple, but I think he did a great job of just really hitting it home and articulating it and how it's a common property of so much of the world. So I really love that book, and that's probably my favorite.

And for listeners, if you're bored with that one, you do Fooled by Randomness, also by Taleb. Did you like Antifragile?

— Less so.

The more famous he got, the more intolerable he became.

Also, question for Caitlin. Do you have a similar "this is a book I recommend to everybody"?

— No, that's a good question. I didn't think about it.

— It is funny because I do think we have very different styles on this front. Like she's no longer in fortune cookie tweeting mode.

But I do think that like you stop that. But I do think a big part of how you work and how you work with other people is like, philosopher mode sometimes, you know?

— Do you drop fortune cookies in Slack?

— Oh, I do actually. Not intentionally. I think it might just be somewhere kind of articulated.

I think that's the core success of succeeding in topic is like you have to be very good on Slack. Yeah.

— Oh, you do have to be very good on Slack. Right? It is — it's a pretty intense place, but I think I'm a little — so I'm kind of psycho about inbox zero on both email and Slack. It's easier on email these days than Slack, but I pretty aggressively prune: here are the channels that I'm actually in and paying attention to versus the ones that are muted below the line sort of thing. And I'm always making sure that I'm on top of the ones that I need to be on top of.

But it is — it's basically it feels like a full-time job. Like there are days where I'm like, "I could cancel all my meetings and write no documents, do no work," right? And literally just sit there like on Slack the entire day. And I would have done what felt like an entire day's worth of work just by engaging on Slack with all the things. It's pretty wild.

— No, but that's horrible. So that's exactly how I feel. I feel like you do all this, you put in all this effort and yes, like you met the mark on responding to people and getting certain things over the line. But you didn't actually produce the output that you wanted to. And that's personally a very hard thing for me to deal with. So I try to be like, I need to dedicate time to actually thinking and actually trying to produce something in order to feel like I'm actually...

And ignore and drop stuff, right? You're going to drop stuff.

— Yes, I have gotten a lot of feedback. I'm a little hard to reach on Slack.

— Yeah, pretty terrible thing that happens now is I get a lot of Slacks saying, "can you get Angela to respond to this?" And I'm like, "I'm like really trying to write a doc here."

Wait, wait, so you guys don't have like a personal Cloud, like assistant something that I don't know if it's going to help you. There's got to be a mobile email, but there's obviously... I have no one written in a personal EA for each of you.

— Yeah, well, so we do have — we have a human one also. We also have plenty of Cloud help in Slack for sure. But I do think actually the types of Slacks that I'm like, when I'm sprinting through and getting are often just like our team is blocked on something because there's some hard decision that needs to happen or whatever it is, right? And it is just like a form of — whether it's in Slack or some other way — a form of getting the team unblocked, executing in high quality. That is my job anyway. And it happens to happen a lot in Slack.

But I do agree that it ends up feeling like, what did I even produce when you get through a whole day worth of literally just going back and forth with people and trying to solve problems.

You produced a functioning team. That's unblocked. So I will give you applause for that. As a former manager, that is — yeah, you don't feel like you produce anything, but like you produce the team.

— Yeah.

收尾问答三：DevRel Corner 与招聘

Speaking of your team, I was going to go to you next, Caitlin. DevRel Corner.

— Oh, nice.

I know you're really hiring DevRel, so I'm going to give you a call out for developer relations. You hired Addy Osmani recently.

— Yeah. Great get.

Lance, you still don't have a team. What do you guys want to hire for? This is it to talk about it. And I'm happy to trade notes.

— Yeah, well, props to you, because I will say when I'm the outsourced Anthropic recruiting... Caitlin recruiting team. Literally. It's fun. And it's actually not even just recruiting.

Like, I'm going to toot your horn a little bit. So when I joined Anthropic, we're a small team. We're all things considered, we're an extremely small team. And so we run the platforms, the API business and all of our product infrastructure. And we had a very nascent DevRel function within Anthropic that was, you know, not necessarily within the product engineering org. And when I joined, we were like, "okay, we need to grow up a little bit and need to figure out how to engage with the community, engage with the world. And we need to really invest in this DevRel function."

And we ended up spinning up a DevRel team within platform and a DevRel team within Cloud Code, in part because it's two pretty different developer ecosystems that we're trying to engage with across the API business and agentic coding, right? I ended up doing it as like two separate teams, but kind of like dotted line to each other and spend a ton of time together.

But it was something that I was going to be responsible for — DevRel — which I've spent plenty of time with DevRel before at Stripe or otherwise, but it was never something that I was responsible for. And I was like, "I have no idea what I'm doing." And you were like, "I got you. Here are the three pillars of DevRel. Here's how you think about it," which is really great. Across like product, content, community. And then now I can rattle that off to people and they're like, "wow, you really understand DevRel." I'm like, "no, somebody stop me."

You're like, "I copied that."

— Yeah, that was not a rich drop off. That post is apparently like the default reading for Google when they onboard new DevRel.

Yes. It's really funny.

— Yes. It really helped me because I had no idea what I was doing. But then on top of that, we've — I don't have a manager for the DevRel team within platform right now. And so that's one of the things that I'm hoping to hire. Our DevRel ICs report to me directly, in part because I think it's a really, really, really hard problem right now, but also in part because I find it really fun and I'm having a lot of fun working with the team.

But really specifically what's hard on platform: platform in some sometimes in our public narrative, our platform business is a really large business, but it can kind of get lost in between research and policy and all this work that we're obviously doing — that's like our most frontier important work — and then our applications like Cloud Code and CoWork and all the things happening over here. When you think about Anthropic and you think about our public narrative, those are some of the things that often come to mind and less so that we're running this massive developer platform business that's really important and so many people are building on top of.

And so a big goal that we have with our DevRel team within platform is figuring out, not only the really classic "how do we better engage with product, what people are building and how we get feedback back into the product and these sorts of things," but a lot of it is just finding our voice and finding what our brand needs to be and what our narrative needs to be and who we even are going to be in the community and not kind of get lost in all of the things that are happening.

And so that I think has been interesting because I think the brand that we've started to spin up for our DevRel team — in part because actually Lance joining our team was you connecting me with Lance — but Lance is highly technical in the way that he goes about DevRel is very much like teaching, right? Like he writes a lot about memory and managing costs and these sorts of things. And he goes really deep. He builds evals. He has a lot of really technical content that he puts together.

And I really like that idea — like that idea of our DevRel team being kind of like thought leaders for people within what is a really nascent, really hard, really evolving space.

Master Builders、Cookbooks 与 Skills

Educators, thought leaders, explainers of things. There's another version of this I really like called the master builder, which is: I will build the things with the platform to show you what's possible and then you'll be like, "oh, I didn't know that was possible with the Cloud Platform." And then you just go. And this is a thing stolen from Lego. Because Lego — how do they sell Legos? They have master builders, they build things with Legos and you're like, "I want to do that. I want to be like this person." And then they do that.

— Nice. That's awesome. Yeah. And CJ, the other person on our team, who's really great as well, I think he also does a lot more of that sort of writing cookbooks and putting out examples and really engaging with the community on X.

Cookbooks is funny, right? When APIs launched in 2023, let's call it, for LLMs. Very important. Now, I don't know.

— Yeah, well, it's interesting because you're less in the spot where you'd copy-paste the code and use it, right? But I do think it shows the art of the possible for people. And just like, what even is the use case, right? And how can you go about accomplishing it? But I hear you that, you know, the code itself is maybe less — like we for the longest time had this: there's an engineer on our team who wrote our cookbook on computer use. And it haunts him to this day because it was massively complex and kind of a beast of a thing that I think, you know, a lot of people got use out of at a time when it's like "I'm going to build a computer use implementation and I'm going to deal with all the screen chatting and all the things, right, that are happening between the messages API."

Yeah, we're there for the hackathon that you guys launched in the office. Yeah, yeah.

— And like that was the era when you needed to have that sort of thing. And now, you know, it's much more about: we have a skill, like the Cloud API skill. It's really, really excellent at helping you either within Cloud Code or any other coding agents to build a really high quality integration. And now these sorts of things, like "I'm going to build a computer use integration, how do I go about doing that?" — very few people, I think, slash hope, are reaching for the big gnarly cookbook, and more so they're loading up the skill and a coding agent and working.

Yeah. Or they're just putting it to a reference architecture.

— Yeah, it actually does much better. Like increasingly we're seeing that for a lot of the things that you might want to have different implementations on, typically at the harness layer but there could be other variants, you just point Cloud at it and you say, "this is the reference architecture I want."

Fun fact: the Cloud API skill that helps people build against the API is owned by our DevRel team.

— So that was built by Lance.

DevRel 的"前台-后台"拆分

Exactly. This is the most high leverage form of DevRel is to distill everything that is best practices that's going to go into those agents.

— Yeah. One of the reasons it's weird because I'm regarded as this DevRel person or authority, but there's some part of me that just wants to tell you don't need DevRel. Get so good you don't need it. Right? Or you turn the engineers, the leaders into the public faces. Because all you really are trying to do is public faces and like, here's how we do things here. And then that's kind of it. You're Anthropic. You don't need, you know, people will hear about you.

— So I think to me, when Boris burst onto the scene, it seemed like a very like, "hey, I'm Boris and the creator of Cloud Code, blah, blah, blah. That's how we do things." And you're like... yes, he has the day job, but he's also doing that functionally. So why doesn't everyone just do that?

— Yeah, I mean, it's really a good question. And there are teams that have done this really well. Like, I think the Cloudflare team is a really great example. They're all pumping out stuff. They're awesome, right? Nonstop. Yeah.

And to me, that's actually a very visible sign of a good manager, is that they're all happy with their jobs. They're all publicly identifying. They're not quitting.

— Yeah, totally. It's interesting because I think this is actually something we are trying to do more of with the platform team and with our team and folks who can kind of just get out there and be part of the community and be speaking and be on X and be wherever they are, right? I think the problem for us is just having time and kind of knowing the right way to do that stuff at high quality. So I see the DevRel team in some ways as just being the experts in doing this sort of stuff at quality. They can do it all day, every day, and they can help enable the rest of the team to think about how to do this with the small amount of time that they are able to spend on this sort of stuff to do it at high quality too.

Yeah. So I call this kind of the unbundling of DevRel into a front office and a back office. So a typical person who does this job does the whole thing, start to finish, they're kind of autonomous. But actually you can sort of build up this back office that lets your product leads and engineering leads actually take the spotlight with a simple contract of like, okay, you sit down with me for 30 to 60 minutes and we'll do the brain dump and then you're done, you go back to work. And then we'll ghostwrite for you, whatever. But that team of production people, writing people, whatever, provides the service to the rest of the people.

And I think that, to me, that's kind of the future of this stuff, to be honest. Because people don't actually really want to hear from DevRel. They want to hear from Lance. And, you know, and you have like lots of — Tariq, you have Tariq, and Lydia, you got Lydia through Bun.

— Exactly. But he does the job. He does the job.

And so like that, you want more of those. Because people want to hear from people in the product, not like who are like paid shows, paid spokesperson. Which I get a lot of. And I guess fine, that's a job. Somebody has to do it. Then reasonably you can expect people who are working on engineering to not be good at it. So you should pay someone who specializes in it. Specialty is a skill.

— I think there is a back office, front office separation that can emerge.

Yeah, that is really cool. Yeah. And my analogy would be like everyone hires, but you have an HR department. HR department enables you to hire.

— That's true, indeed. You hire. Makes a ton of sense.

结语：在 Opus 5.5 上尝试 Multi-Agent

Cool. That was my soapbox. Closing questions. You've been very generous with your time. Any parting thoughts or calls to action?

— Build something cool on Opus 5.5.

What's something people should try to push the bounds with new Opus 5.5? You guys have been using it for the longest.

— Yeah, I mean, it's really cost efficient. It's less verbose. All the things we mentioned, the vibes are really, really high. It's been fun. Yesterday was a really fun day for us because, like, finally again, I got a whole slew of texts from friends and people who were just like, "amazing model, thank you." Like one of my old bosses messaged me and he was like, "Opus 5.5 just saved our butts in an incident," right? And it's like, okay, great. Like we're back is really the energy that we feel. And so I think things that like, maybe you wanted to experiment with something and like cost was something that was front of mind for you, right? And like token efficiency and these sorts of things, like that kind of might've held you back from really firing it off and letting a model run. I think those are the sorts of problems you should return to now with Opus 5.5, because I think you'll be able to get just a lot further than you maybe otherwise would have been able to with models that were less cost effective.

— I think you should try something with like a multi-agent setup. I think you will find it to be very good.

Any other hints, by the way? I mean, multi-agents are very broad.

— Nope. I think we're very curious to hear what people build. But yes, it should be extra good.

Yeah, including, let's say, roles that are not strictly defined, but they are assigned among themselves. Right? Which is, to me, the new thing. You can assign roles. You can always assign roles. You can give tokens jobs. But this is like they're giving themselves jobs. I guess, say more on multi-agent, right? Like should we use sub-agents? How should people think about multi-agents?

— This is pretty good in a sense of like basically generally you want to have one lead and you want to split up a bunch of different stuff. And as long as you can have a task that you think could be generally parallelizable and they share uniform context across it, I think you will get a lot of gains. Now, of course, it depends on the problem that you're pushing at, but increasingly, this is a very superior way for us to handle a lot of these things. And especially if every sub-agent is — or whatever you'll call these sub-leads — they are asynchronous and they're not blocking of each other. That is the only two bits I would say you should care about in your architecture. Other than that, let it rip and see what Cloud designs for you.

And increasingly, I think a lot of this architecture stuff will fall into this direction. Cloud will get smarter and smarter. It's going to learn how to figure ways to split itself, clone itself, adjust itself to the architectures that make sense. You just need to make sure it can parallel process. So it needs a shared state and it needs to not block its sub-agents. And as long as you contain those two principles, honestly, I think people should experiment and probably try some really crazy stuff. And I wouldn't be surprised to see some really interesting things on top of that, that maybe they felt like there was some intractable problem that was really annoying and they'd keep pushing for, that something like this could actually probably just crush in maybe one shot or something.

Excellent. All right, everyone go build.

— Cool. Cool.

## 一场被低估的"身份转置"：Anthropic 其实已经悄悄从模型公司变成了云厂商
人人都在谈 Opus 5.5 的智能、价格、写作风格。但这期访谈真正让人头皮发麻的转折不在模型层，而在**财务物理学的切换**：一年前每赚 1 美元亏 1.29 美元，今天每赚 1 美元赚 2 美元；人均营收从 140 万美元飙到 660 万美元。这不是"AI 公司做得好"这种描述能解释的——这是一次**身份转置**：Anthropic 对外还在被叫做"模型实验室"，但它的 S-1、它的客户结构（10 万美元+客户里 50% 在用 Cloud Platform）、它的 CPU 焦虑（而不是 GPU 焦虑！）全都在说一件事：**它已经是 hyperscaler 了，只是外界还没反应过来**。
一个让人意外的信号：Caitlin 全程最焦虑的不是模型、不是对齐、不是 safety——而是 **CPU**。"你没法再按需扩 CPU 了，必须提前做 capacity planning。" 这句话如果你是 2010 年代的 AWS 架构师听到会浑身起鸡皮疙瘩——它意味着**云计算的"弹性契约"（elast

item.title: [Lex Clips] Humans vs AI: Can AI develop math we can't explain? | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

被忽略的事实：我们早就活在"看不懂的黑盒"里

Tao 把"AI 给出我们理解不了的证明"当作一个未来时态的担忧，但有一个更尖锐、被几乎所有人回避的事实——当代数学家从未亲手验证过他们所引用的绝大多数定理。整个现代数学运行在一张巨大的"社会信任网络"上：每个人都在相信别人相信过的东西。从这个角度看，LLM 的黑盒证明并不是一个新的认识论威胁，它只是把这条本就存在的信任链上的某一个节点，由人换成了机器。真正发生变化的，不是"能不能理解"，而是"能不能追问"——同行可以被追问 "你为什么走这一步"，而当前的 AI 回答不了 "你怎么想到的"。所以未来数学的分水岭不在证明长度，而在可被盘问性（interrogability）。

教学倒置里藏着一条认知科学的隐藏法则

Tao 把实分析课"倒着上"——先用实数，再构造实数——这不仅是教学技巧，它触及了一条被哲学家长期忽视的规律：人类对数学对象的直觉理解，几乎总是先于它的形式定义的发明。牛顿-莱布尼茨用了微积分 200 年，epsilon-delta 才被写下来。这个结构与儿童语言习得完全同构：先流利说话，再学语法。更惊人的跨域连接是维特根斯坦晚年的"梯子"隐喻——你爬上之后必须踢掉梯子。形式化不是通往理解的路，而是你事后用来验证"已经抵达的理解"没有逻辑漏洞的拐杖。AI 极其擅长建造梯子，但人类是先登顶、再回头造梯子的物种。这意味着：如果我们训练 AI 只会从公理往上爬，我们可能永远不会得到会"直觉先行"的数学家。

"问题会反击你"——创造的物质阻力定律

Ankur 那句 "when you fight with a problem, it fights back" 听起来像励志口号，实则揭示了一条跨越数学、艺术、工程甚至神经网络训练的普遍规律：没有阻力，就没有新结构的生成。木匠讲"听木纹说话"，小说家讲"角色开始自己走"，雕塑家讲"石头告诉我哪里凿"，神经网络的 loss function 本质上就是模型在"顶回来"。由此推出一个反直觉的结论：一个过于"听话"的 AI 数学助手，可能永远产生不了真正的新数学——因为它不会反击你、不会让你撞墙、不会在你走错路时沉默。真正的突破需要有东西在抵抗你，这是信息论意义上的必要条件，不是美学上的修辞。

顺便一个小揭露：Alex 用 Bach "平行五度" 当作"数学不是音乐"的反例时，其实无意间瓦解了自己的类比——艺术史上几乎所有伟大作品都诞生于"违反规则"的那一刻。所以当他说"数学不是音乐，你不能破规则"时，他可能把音乐讲错了。而这个"讲错"，恰好证明了他前面讲对的那件事：故事的力量，长远来看会盖过规则。而这或许正是未来人机协作数学的真正形态——AI 负责守住规则，人类负责讲出那个值得破例的故事。

📝 转录文本

The Thought Experiment: An Incomprehensible Black Box

  • So this is where I'll just take the tangent, and the thought experiment may be a bit philosophical at this moment, but what if you have that black box that gives you proofs that you can't understand? Let's say the more interesting case where, not because it's so big, but because the ideas just don't make sense to you, to any of the world expert mathematicians in that field. What do you do with that?

  • So the only way, sort of almost by definition, because the logical rules of inference are written down, and there, there's only a few of them. There's a handful of them. The axioms, there's a handful of them. So the only way that you have mathematics that's not understandable is scale.

A Contrarian Take: What Would "Unformalizing" Math Look Like?

  • Let me add a contrarian take.

  • Yeah, please.

  • So one of the things I also wonder is what would unformalizing math look like? You know certainly formalization helps tremendously that we have confidence that the results are correct. But much of the way that we understand the results ourselves is really at some unformalized level. You know, what is an interesting special case? What, you know, where does this come from, you know, this technique you're using, right? And, you know, maybe that's what that world would look like. If we have these black boxes, we would try to tease apart and figure out how to ask them easier questions to develop some kind of system of understanding of how they actually got to the answer.

Engineering a Proof vs. Communicating It

  • Yeah, so there are really two different things that we conflate when we write a paper. One is the engineering of the proof, and the other is the communication of that to someone else, and they're almost at odds with one another.

I had this experience—so I taught real analysis last fall, and you open up any real analysis textbook, and this was my experience when I took real analysis. The first couple of lectures are what are the real numbers? You know, we have to define them or construct them as equivalence classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals, whatever the hell all that means. It takes, like, two weeks for a first-semester course in real analysis to get there, and then we have the real number line, and now we can start doing calculus, you know, with formal epsilon and delta definitions, yada yada.

And it always struck me as bizarre that we do this because before the class, I knew what the real numbers were. It's this number line, and then we spend these two weeks talking about Cauchy sequences of rationals, and then on week three, they're, they're a number line again. What the hell was the purpose of that?

Teaching Backwards: Intuition Before Construction

And so it's because the way things are written or had been written were very engineering. You need to construct the real numbers before you go start using them. But the real numbers, human beings used the real numbers long before we understood that they needed to be constructed formally.

So what I did in my class is I jumped straight into epsilon delta calculus. We did, you know, six weeks of calculations until we got to a point where wait a second, you know, if here's a theorem, it's true in the real numbers. There's some convergence, something called Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem. You have a sequence of real numbers that are jumping around, but in a fixed range. There has to be some subsequence that converges to a real number. Well, that's not true in the rationals.

Why is it true in the reals? What are the reals? So you don't start asking that question until you hit a problem that needs to be solved. So the way I taught the course was sort of backwards from how it needs to be taught if it's an engineering project, 'cause you can't just start talking about the real numbers until you've constructed them, until you know what they are.

Building the Theory vs. Telling the Story

Well, that's correct if what you're doing is building up the theory. But if you're telling a story, then you absolutely can just start with the real numbers. You have an intuition for what that is, and until your intuition breaks, you don't need the resolution of how you actually construct them.

So I think the way that we write papers in the future is gonna be very different, where we spend a lot more time just talking about the story of what have I learned in this process, what are the interesting—uh, here, here's, you do the standard thing here, here, and here, but then here, you're sort of stuck, and where do you go? And here's an idea for why you go left and not right and not up and down or whatever. And there's a Lean formalization that accompanies this story that lets you know that the engineering actually works out.

'Cause you can't just tell stories. If you just tell stories, you know, math is not music where you can tell a beautiful story, and it's okay that you have parallel fifths moving somewhere, and, you know, you've broken some rule, but Bach does it all the time, so.

Mathematics Is Not a Rising Tide of Theorems

  • So I think that's a very important point, just to sort of emphasize the point that Alex is making. You know, there's this view of mathematics which I don't believe in, where it's just this rising tide of theorems. You know, how can AI be bad? It's contributing to this rising tide.

But, you know, really, mathematics is not just about the number of theorems we have, far from it. It's also about that story of fighting with problems, because when you fight with a good problem, it fights back at you, and you learn something about it. It's really about the system of beliefs and abstractions you come up with en route to, you know, when you're fighting this problem, you discover some more general meaning that applies more broadly.

And I think it's a great opportunity to sort of disabuse ourselves of this idea that we're just you know, axiomatizing things until we get to the next theorem. You know, telling that story of how we actually got to these problems, what the parallels are to other problems, is now, at this pivotal moment, more important than it ever has been.

We Want Stories, Not Just Verified Lines

  • Yeah, so to get all the way back to your question about, you know, is it a matter of scale, well, Yes, it's just a matter of scale, but exactly to Ankur's point, the way that we think about mathematics is about stories, and it might be that we don't understand the story of this. You can follow a proof line by line and not understand what's really going on.

You might say, and you just ask some other LLM to explain to you the story if it can come up with such an explanation. But that's what we want. We want stories. We want understanding.

Coda: The Problem Fights Back

  • When you fight with a problem, it fights back. I think there's a deep truth to that about all the great pursuits that humanity has taken on. And on that topic,
