item.description:
## 一、整段对话最被低估的洞察：数学家刚刚公开承认——自己就是那个门童
"门童谬误"真正令人毛骨悚然的地方，不在于它适用于AI时代的数学，而在于**它是整个数学学科的一次集体自我识别**。几百年来，数学家把"证明定理"当作自己的核心产品，把"深度思考"当作副产品。而AI在五秒钟之内把这个关系颠倒过来：**证明是开门的动作，深度思考才是真正的工作**。嘉宾那句"If I don't signal brand value, I don't know what I'm doing"是全场最尖锐的黑色幽默——数学家终于意识到，自己卖了几百年的根本不是真理，而是"**对真理的品味**"。
一个让人不适的推论：如果证明只是门童动作，那么从高斯到陶哲轩，整个数学史的"产品说明书"都需要重写。数学家从未真正生产定理，他们生产的是**可被社群采信的审美**。
## 二、跨领域连接：这正是1839年发生在绘画界的事，但数学家还没读过那段历史
当达盖尔的摄影术在1839年公布时，巴黎的学院派画家们并没有立刻失业，但有一件事瞬间改变了：**"画得像"不再是一种能力的证明**。写实技巧从"稀缺的智力标

item.title: [Lex Clips] A crisis moment in math explained by mathematicians | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这不是"数学的危机"，而是"数学作为选拔机制"的崩塌

Terence Tao 哀悼"PhD 学生多年耐心努力被随意打断"，Ankur 用了一个很罕见的词——"intellectually lonely"（智识上的孤独）。表面上他们在悼念研究路径，但如果把两段话叠在一起读，你会发现他们真正在哀悼的根本不是问题，而是难题作为社会筛选函数的失效。

过去一个世纪，学术数学界的运行逻辑近似于一种"认知劳动价值论"：Fields Medal、终身教职、学派声望，全都挂钩于"独立攻克过一个足够难的问题"。难题从来不只是数学对象，更是一种信用货币——用证明的稀缺性来给人定价。AI 没有摧毁数学，它摧毁的是数学界的贵族制结构。

一个几乎没人注意到的证据：三位数学家的焦虑程度，恰好与他们的工作在多大程度上依赖这套社会结构呈正相关。应用数学家 Steve 最乐观——他的价值从未来自难度稀缺，而来自流体、心脏、飞机这些可触碰的问题；Ankur 最撕裂，因为他把 mentorship 视为职业核心；Alex 则用"手电筒"的隐喻把危机重构为机会。真正令他们痛苦的不是认识论，而是社会学。

二、Tao 的"剧透比喻"暴露了一个秘密——数学其实是一门叙事艺术

Tao 用"剧透电影"来比喻 AI 公布证明带来的伤害。这个比喻在哲学上有爆炸性，因为它只在一种条件下成立：真理必须有时间性。你无法剧透"2+2=4"，你只能剧透一段有悬念结构的体验。

这意味着——数学家嘴上说的是追求永恒真理，但他们的真实工作体验，其实接近读一部长篇小说：铺垫、伏笔、顿悟、高潮。证明不只是逻辑结构，更是一种叙事形式。AI 的真正威胁，不是它算出了答案，而是它跳过了叙事。

跨领域连接：这与录音技术出现后古典音乐演奏发生的转型几乎同构。乐谱（真理）始终存在，但现场演奏（叙事体验）的价值反而因录音泛滥而上升——因为人们意识到自己消费的是"过程"而非"结果"。未来十年数学界将发生类似分裂：证明的"生产"将被 AI 商品化，但证明的"演绎"——讲授、推导、品味的选择——将成为稀缺的人类溢价。数学家会越来越像钢琴家，而不是像工程师。

三、Steve 的"传送门悖论"推翻了 Tao 的剧透论，而两人其实都对

Steve 讲了一个几乎没被注意的反例：如果你知道另一个国家发明了时间旅行，你会在五年内复现它。知道答案存在，反而是终极激励。这与 Tao 的"剧透杀死好奇心"看似矛盾，但用 Roger Bannister 四分钟一英里的案例就能调和：1954 年之前没人跑进四分钟，之后 46 天内就有第二人破纪录，一年内多人跟上。

两种直觉的分裂点在于问题是否有外部价值： - 有外部价值的问题（Navier-Stokes 的工程含义、传送门）→ 知道可解 ≈ 加速 - 纯粹的智力游戏（数学作为审美对象）→ 知道答案 ≈ 剧透

一个让人不安的推论：纯粹数学家在未来几十年会越来越像诗人——不是因为他们没用，而是因为他们工作的价值将不再由"是否解决问题"衡量，而由"是否选择了值得被解决的问题、以及是否以优雅的方式呈现"衡量。数学将从生产函数转向品味函数。

Ankur 感到"intellectually lonely"的真正原因，可能是他隐约意识到：从今往后，数学家最重要的能力不再是推理力，而是问题审美力——而整个学科的训练体系对这件事几乎毫无准备。你可以培养一个会证明的 PhD，但你不知道怎么培养一个"能一眼看出什么问题值得活一辈子"的 PhD。

跨领域连接：这与围棋在 AlphaGo 之后发生的事惊人同构。李世石一度抑郁退役，但五年后围棋没有消失——它变成了一种人类"学习如何学习"的艺术。今天看职业棋手复盘，他们谈的不是"胜负"，而是"美感"和"创造性"。数学也会走这条路，只是比围棋晚了大约十年。最讽刺的是：Tao 所哀悼的"路径的消失"，很可能恰恰是路径真正开始成为路径本身的时刻——当它不再通往任何必须到达的目的地时。

📝 转录文本

An Emergency Episode on the State of Math and AI

All right, so this is a kind of emergency episode — I think it's fair to say — about the state of mathematics and artificial intelligence. A kind of crisis moment in the history of mathematics.

Over the last few weeks, machines claimed to have solved some of the hardest problems in the history of math: Navier-Stokes, the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, the unique games conjecture, and hundreds of other results.

Meet the Guests

So here with me, we have Steven Brunton, a mathematician and fluid dynamics expert at University of Washington, who can speak to Navier-Stokes, turbulence, all things fluid, and many other topics.

Also here is Ankur Moitra, a mathematician and theoretical computer scientist at MIT, visiting the Institute for Advanced Studies in Princeton this year, who can speak to many things — unique games, conjecture, complexity theory in general, and the mathematics of how AI learns and all things theoretical computer science.

And Alex, a mathematician and number theorist at Rutgers, who can speak to very many topics including the Riemann hypothesis and Lean, the automated proof and the automated verifier and checking, and so many other topics in mathematics.

All three are brilliant. All are very kind to show up this early morning and talk to me, assembling this kind of multi-agent mini swarm of human brains to try to interpret what happened in this very moment.

A lot of mathematicians — brilliant mathematicians, including Terence Tao and others — are freaking out. It's a mix of awe, terror, dread, and a few inklings of light, of hope also. So I apologize to start with a question about feeling, but what have you been feeling about this historic moment?

Alex: A Golden Age, Not a Crisis

Maybe Alex, do you wanna go first?

— Yeah, I don't know if I would call it a crisis. There's a lot of opportunity in that crisis. It's a chance to rethink what it is we're trying to accomplish, and it's the chaos of opportunity that some people are reacting negatively to, some people are reacting positively to — and sometimes those reactions are happening in the same person.

And so I think we're entering, if we're not already in, a period of some kind of golden age of mathematical knowledge. After millennia of having a candle that we are walking around the woods, and this is as far as we can see — now we have a flashlight.

The Magnitude of the Moment

— I think we should comment on the magnitude of this moment for people who are not aware. So maybe to quote you, something like, "Holy shit, if a human did this, it'd be an instant Fields Medal." Maybe you didn't say "holy shit," but basically saying, "This is an incredible result."

So a lot of people wouldn't have expected this amount of progress in this amount of time — so this is truly shocking. So you're now speaking as a person who is dealing with the feelings you've felt over the last couple of days, having found this out.

So maybe also it'd be useful to go back to the feeling you were having when you first saw the report that, in this case, OpenAI dropped. And the two of you happened to be on camera loosely on the same day, maybe a few drinks in, because it was a conference or a get-together.

Ankur: Pulled in Two Directions

Maybe, Ankur, can you speak to what you were feeling?

— It was an interesting night when the results dropped. Now, it was not entirely unexpected because for weeks there'd been rumors about the two biggest problems in my areas that were in that collection of results — so the unique games conjecture and RL equals L. There were even rumors about matrix multiplication.

So really my first reaction was, "Wow, it's all true. Thank goodness it's finally out there, because now people can actually go through it and process what's happened and figure out what to do next."

Now, as to your earlier question — you know, what are we feeling? Well, for me, it changes on a daily basis, but I think the biggest, most overarching feeling is really feeling like you're getting pulled in two very different directions.

My work has always been about asking the right questions, and to that extent, these tools are amazing for me because, you know, they increase my ability to learn about other fields. It's like having a world expert who's there to teach you about things in your own language. Your ability to make connections is just magnified.

But, you know, one of the parts of my job that I really love the most is the mentorship aspect — not just training grad students and postdocs and seeing them do great things, but having them come with me on these journeys.

So the part that pulls me in the other direction is the recognition that, you know, the playbook and the blueprint for success that we had for so long is now thrown out the window. So it becomes a lot harder to advise students and postdocs about, you know, what are things they should be working on that are gonna make an impact, are gonna make a name for themselves.

So I feel very excited, but maybe more intellectually lonely than I felt before. In part because, you know, a lot of times great results come from asking very humble questions — at least for me. And now there's so much anxiety and dread and feeling that, wow, you would have to do something really momentous to stand out in the sea of AI results, that it feels like we've lost some of that patience in terms of planting the seeds from which the great oak trees grow.

Terence Tao's Lament

— Terence Tao, Fields Medal winner, wrote:

"I am horrified by the many person-years of ongoing patient and deliberately slow research efforts, particularly by graduate students and postdocs, toward many motivating problems in mathematics being casually disrupted or destroyed by such a release. Much as one cannot unhear a movie spoiler or a crossword clue, one cannot explore a problem as profitably and richly once one is aware of an existing solution, and I mourn the path not taken and the opportunities lost in the frantic race to develop the technology."

So I mean, if we're being realistic, it's more dramatic for a PhD student and a postdoc than maybe the way you've articulated. I mean, you're saying it quite calmly, but if I was a PhD student right now, I'd be in a state of, like, shock. Like, my whole life —

I was going through some of this. I know a lot of my friends are programmers. They're going through this state of shock in last December when basically most of the programming world switched to AI writing most of the programs. So I would approximate it to a feeling of kind of a loss of meaning, kind of terror, like dark stuff. Um, we'll keep exploring that.

Steve: The Hopeful Engineer

Uh, Steve, what do you think? What were you — what are you feeling?

— I would say most of my feelings are pretty hopeful. I think I'm an engineer. I like solving, you know, problems that make technology more realistic for humans — artificial hearts and airplanes. And our ability to solve real applied problems is going to get much, much better. Our scope and reach is gonna increase, and so for that, I'm extremely hopeful.

But there is a lot of uncertainty, and I think, you know, some of this fear of meaning, of losing control, of just being kind of cut out of the process that we all love being a part of — it is a little scary.

And I don't think any of us would be surprised at either of the kind of two paths that might take place over the next five or 10 years, where we really are just dwarfed by, you know, other intelligence — or it kind of levels off, and this becomes an incredible tool that we use for our curiosity, for our human problem-solving. And that uncertainty is massive. Those are two very different worlds.

And so uncertainty is difficult for humans. I think it's also difficult for those of us who have chosen math. We chose math, you know, probably because we liked rules and formalism — and, you know, uncertainty is uncomfortable.

On Humility and Purpose

The humility aspect is really important, though. This is a really good opportunity for us to remember why we're doing this. Like, what is human purpose? It's not to be famous. It's not to have a Fields Medal.

You know — solving interesting problems, helping other people, being curious, just wanting to understand the world — those are really good things to kind of get back. Like, what do we need to be satisfied humans? And I think that's a really interesting moment for us to think about. I've been thinking about it a lot lately.

Um, it is more difficult for young people, right? Like, figuring out how to find their way. But I actually have more faith in them than us, in a sense.

Spoilers vs. Teleportation: The Path and the Destination

— Do you think there's something to what Terry says about it's harder to be motivated when you know a problem has been solved — to explore that space when a problem's been solved like this by an AI system?

— Yes and no, in the sense that I do very much agree that the path is as important as the destination. Like, if you go on a road trip, the road trip is usually just as fun as getting there.

At the same time, if we found out that another country had invented teleportation or time travel, I guarantee we would reinvent it in the next five years. Like, if you knew it was possible, and you could reverse engineer a little bit, we would be curious, we would dive into it, and we would figure it out. So knowing there's a solution also is an incredible motivation to get there much faster.

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Chipmakers Can Only See 4 Years Ahead
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"四年可视距"：被误读为短视的物理常数

Chris 轻描淡写的那句"我们对技术缩放只有四年的能见度"，表面上像是行业的保守告白，但真正令人意外的是：这不是认知局限，而是一种结构性物理现象。四年之外看不清，不是工程师想象力不够，而是技术栈的每一层都在为后续层施加约束——下一步选什么材料、什么结构，取决于当前这一步选了哪条路径。这与气象学里的"洛伦兹预测极限"惊人相似：不是算力不够，而是系统自身的敏感性让远期预测在原则上不可能。半导体行业其实在运行一个滚动的技术事件视界，这个"4"几乎是物理常数——它每向前推进四年，就暴露出下一个四年的轮廓，但永远看不到更远。

二、热才是真正的天花板——而生物学早已验证过这堵墙

节目里被一笔带过的那句"热是最根本的限制"，暗藏了一个跨领域的宇宙级规律。请注意这个惊人的对应：CFET 把 N 型和 P 型晶体管垂直堆叠时遇到的散热困境，与鲸鱼大脑为什么无法无限变大、恐龙为什么必须冷血，是同一个问题。 生物学里的 Kleiber 定律告诉我们：代谢率随体积的 3/4 次方缩放——因为散热依赖的是表面积（二维），而产热依赖的是体积（三维）。3D 芯片正在重走这条路：NAND 可以堆叠因为它"代谢"低（静态存储），逻辑芯片"代谢"高（持续开关），所以散热上限就是堆叠上限。这不是工艺问题，这是几何学对一切三维计算实体的终极约束。硅基计算和碳基大脑撞上的是同一堵墙。

三、蝴蝶振翅之问的隐藏分野：物理必然 vs 历史偶然

访谈开头那个"60 年代一只蝴蝶振翅"的提问，被回答者在不经意间拆解成了两类技术：

  • Gate-all-around、铜互连：这是"物理必然"的——即使改写历史，物理定律的收敛性会把工程师推向同一个解。
  • 背面供电（Backside Power）：这是"历史偶然"的——90 年代没人认真预测它，它是在特定路径依赖下涌现的奇思。

这个二分有一个相当颠覆的推论：技术路线图里真正能被预测的部分，恰恰是最没有创造力的部分；而让行业惊喜的突破，本质上不可预测。任何试图用"趋势外推"预测 AI 硬件未来的分析师，其实只预测了必然的那一半。

更深一层——这个"必然 vs 偶然"的分野，和进化生物学里 Simon Conway Morris 关于"趋同演化 vs 偶然演化"的著名争论是同一个问题。章鱼的眼睛和脊椎动物的眼睛独立演化出几乎相同的结构（必然），但语言和意识可能是偶然。芯片技术的演化史，正在悄悄重演生命演化史的核心悖论。

四、一个让人回味的反直觉观察

最反直觉的一点：存储器（NAND、DRAM）在 3D 化上领先了逻辑芯片十多年。按照"CPU/GPU 是高端产品走在前面"的直觉，这个顺序完全反了。为什么？因为低功耗的后进者反而更自由——约束越少，越能先走出维度升级的路径，然后反哺给约束更多的地方。

这暗示了一个被严重低估的创新论法则：先锋往往不是领先者，而是约束最少者。它同样适用于：先在玩具项目里验证新架构，再搬到生产系统；先在小国做政策实验，再推广到大国。半导体行业正在无意中为所有创新组织验证一个通用定理——边缘的自由度，才是维度跃迁的温床。

📝 转录文本

The Butterfly Question: A Counterfactual Tech Tree

If a butterfly flapped its wings in the 60s, could you imagine a world where gator all around is not even a word people have heard of, an idea people are familiar with, but people are thinking of an extremely different branch of the tech tree? And how far down the tech tree do you think things could be totally different? Could it be like we're not even using copper? If you look at uh say transistors and interconnects —

What Was Inevitable: Transistor Structure and Copper

I think uh where we've gotten to, you know, as far as the transistor and gate all around and it being the ideal transistor structure that I have, I think was somewhat inevitable. As I said, in the '90s, we were already talking about these type of things.

Backside power — that one's pretty out there. Uh, I think even in the in in the 90s, the idea that you're going to strip off the entire silicon substrate and put lines on the backside — uh, you know, that one is probably, you know, something that's a little bit out there.

Um, copper — of course copper wires are the best. So I don't know how you would end up somewhere else besides copper. I think for some of the very tightest pitches, you know, I think it's inevitable that you will replace copper. And so that's a good example of where you will have another material that will come in there. But for the larger lines, I think copper is about where it's at.

From Backside Power to Full 3D Logic

I think that once you start to do gate all around transistors and you do backside power, now you start to enter a very different regime — because now you see it's not, "hey, there's just some substrate and you stack everything on top." Now you've got a transistor which is floating in interconnect, and you're like, okay, well why don't I have transistors, interconnect, and more transistors, more interconnect — you know, this whole 3D stacking that we now do with just discrete chips that we stack on top of each other. Now you're like, why can't I just build an entire structure like this?

You see it with, you know, memory — NAND, DRAM — you know, they have some incredible 3D structures. NAND already does it. DRAM talks about it. But I think that DRAM inevitably is going to go there.

The Four-Year Horizon

So, a lot of people say, "Oh no, we're not going to do this because, hey, we can't do it in the next 5 years." Well, come on. Let's put a larger time scale on this. Let's put 10 years, 20 years — in 2045, do you think you could do it? Uh, and now you start to say, "Oh yeah, I could see us having some pretty exotic structures at that point."

So we limit ourselves by what we see as possible in the next four years. Because, you know, as I've always said, when people say, "Hey, you know, how do you see technology scaling going?" — yeah, we have visibility about four years. And then you get out to the four years and you go, "Yeah, I think there's something we can do another four years out of that." And you get to that four years and you're like, "Yeah, I think you can do something." But if you start to talk about 10 years, yeah, it becomes hard to say what it's going to be.

[Narrator] CFET Explained

Chris's idea of building upwards could start with the transistors themselves. Chips use two types of transistors called N-type and P-type, which work the same way, but with the charges reversed. Nearly every circuit is built by pairing them up. Today, chipmakers build them side by side. The next step is to stack them directly on top of each other in order to save space. In principle, that fits twice as many transistors into the same area. This design is called a CFET, short for complementary field-effect transistor. But every extra layer adds manufacturing steps and cost, and also leads to heat building up that doesn't have a clear way to escape.

The Thermal Problem

Because logic consumes more power than memory, you can't do stacks of DRAM that make HBM, or, you know, 3D NAND, as easily with logic — because of the heat issue.

Is that the fundamental issue then over the long run — how you [handle] thermals?

The Three Limits of Compute

Yeah. So there's three things that you have when you try to say, hey, what limits compute. Okay.

  1. Frequency — How fast can you do the switch? So the frequency of the device.
  2. Power efficiency — How much power does it take in order to do that switch?
  3. Thermals — How do you dissipate the heat that was generated by doing that switch? And that's the thermals piece of it.

And I think the thermals piece — and these are not new problems. You can go back 20 years and you can see articles on these three things. And so the question is, yeah, thermals — how do you deal with that, particularly when you start to talk about these 3D type devices?

The Next Frontier: System-Level Simulation

I think that there is a need for that sort of system-level analysis and simulation tools. I think we're at its infancy, because we've just started to look at this. Uh, but it is a limiter, and it will be a limiter. But, you know, again, these are problems that we can go solve.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

### 一、"四年可视距"：被误读为短视的物理常数
Chris 轻描淡写的那句"我们对技术缩放只有四年的能见度"，表面上像是行业的保守告白，但真正令人意外的是：**这不是认知局限，而是一种结构性物理现象**。四年之外看不清，不是工程师想象力不够，而是技术栈的每一层都在为后续层施加约束——下一步选什么材料、什么结构，取决于当前这一步选了哪条路径。这与气象学里的"洛伦兹预测极限"惊人相似：不是算力不够，而是系统自身的敏感性让远期预测在原则上不可能。半导体行业其实在运行一个**滚动的技术事件视界**，这个"4"几乎是物理常数——它每向前推进四年，就暴露出下一个四年的轮廓，但永远看不到更远。
### 二、热才是真正的天花板——而生物学早已验证过这堵墙
节目里被一笔带过的那句"热是最根本的限制"，暗藏了一个跨领域的宇宙级规律。请注意这个惊人的对应：**CFET 把 N 型和 P 型晶体管垂直堆叠时遇到的散热困境，与鲸鱼大脑为什么无法无限变大、恐龙为什么必须冷血，是同一个问题。** 生物学里的 Kleiber 定律告诉我们：代谢率随体积的 3/4 次方缩放——因为散热依赖的是表面积（二维），

item.title: [Latent Space] An Eval for AI Scientists That Knows the Answer Key - Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的隐喻：Leash Bio 其实在做"科学界的 Atari"

当 Ian 轻描淡写地提到他们的图表"看起来有点像 Arc AGI 2 的分布"时，一个巨大的秘密其实已经被泄露了——他们正在无意中构建生物学领域的第一个"Atari 时刻"。

回想一下 DeepMind 2013 年的突破：Atari 之所以关键，不是因为游戏本身重要，而是因为它提供了一个反事实稠密（counterfactually dense）的环境——每一步都有即时反馈，每一次选择都能回滚重来。真实世界的科学恰恰相反：实验昂贵、延迟巨大、路径依赖、无法回放。Ian 用一句"lab in the loop with amortized latency"把这个核心矛盾一笔化解——他们不是在加速实验，而是在把科学从"连续时间问题"转化成了"离散博弈问题"。这是一个比 DNA 编码库本身更深刻的范式转移。

出人意料的观察：聪明模型的"放弃能力"才是真正的智能信号

绝大多数人会以为更强的模型是"更会找到好分子"。但 Ian 的数据揭示了一个令人毛骨悚然的反转：更强模型的核心优势不在于"坚持"，而在于"放弃"——它们更早识别出糟糕的化学邻域并撤离，而弱模型则像赌徒一样在失败点位附近做无意义的微调（"这两个分数低但我感觉不错"）。

这跟心理学里的沉没成本偏误惊人地同构。弱模型 = 认知受损的人类赌徒。而且更深一层：我们一直把 LLM 的"坚持推理"当成能力的标志（long chain-of-thought、test-time compute），但在真实的开放世界探索中，"知道何时切断自己的思路"可能才是更稀缺、更难训练的能力。这意味着当前主流的 reasoning benchmark 可能系统性地激励了一种错误的智能——它们都在封闭问题里奖励"钻下去"，没有一个在奖励"跳出来"。

跨领域连接：药物化学 × 蒙特卡洛树搜索 × 投资组合理论

最让我拍案的是 Ian 在最后一段轻飘飘说的："我需要去找更多做决策学（decision science）的人聊聊。"——他意识到自己构建的根本不是一个化学工具，而是一个通用的"有限预算下的序列决策"训练场。

想想这个结构的同构性： - 医药化学家 决定接下来合成哪 100 个分子 ↔ 风投合伙人 决定下季度投哪几家公司 ↔ 临床试验设计者 决定下一阶段招募哪种队列 ↔ 强化学习研究员 决定下一个 rollout 探索哪个 action space

它们都是稀疏奖励、高维搜索、不可逆决策、预算约束。而 Leash 的巧妙之处在于——因为分子-蛋白结合是可以预先穷举测量的，所以它成了唯一一个你事先知道全部答案的决策环境。这正是标题"knows the answer key"的真实含义：这不是化学的 eval，这是人类决策理论的第一个"全知环境"。

还有一个几乎没人提到的隐藏含义：当 Ian 说"我们可以把这个游戏化"时，他低估了自己。这个环境可以反过来成为训练人类医药化学家的"飞行模拟器"——第一次，一个新手化学家可以在职业生涯中经历 10,000 次完整 SAR campaign，而不是传统师徒制下的 20 次。生物医药的 10x 工程师可能不会由 LLM 产生，而是由 在 Leash 环境里打了一万小时的人类 产生。这才是真正的 "AlphaGo 让人类围棋手变强" 效应。

一个讽刺的脚注

Ian 吐槽前沿模型发布太快导致论文永远发不出来（"每 11 天来一个新的 stupid model"），这件事本身恰好证明了他的方法为什么重要——在一个模型迭代速度已经超过论文周期的时代，唯一还能稳定存在的科学资产，是不随模型变化的"客观测量过的世界"。模型会过时，答案钥匙不会。

📝 转录文本

开场与嘉宾介绍

Hey there, welcome to Lab and Space Science. This is Brandon and RJ joined with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio.

We recorded an episode earlier this summer with Ian where he talked about the cool things Leash is doing with DNA encoded libraries and how they could screen millions of compounds against thousands of proteins in a high-throughput way.

Around this time Ian realized that they could do fun things with this data. It essentially allows them to create like a virtual sandbox where agents can explore and make decisions in real time as if they were medicinal chemists and get instant feedback but with like a huge amount of exploratory rollouts.

Since that episode Ian has and Leash have developed this idea much more fully and since then they have — and they're now releasing a paper and a dataset and a blog post along with the episode that we just released. We wanted to sit down with Ian, talk a bit more about what he's done and, you know, hear about the updates.

Anyway, welcome to the podcast.

Thank you, Ian.

从"沙盒想法"到完整的 Agent 探索环境

Yeah, so last time we talked to Ian you were saying that you had some agents exploring a sandbox and you're like, "Oh, this is just a fun idea. We don't know what we can do with it but it's an interesting idea." I think you've since fleshed this out into a full environment for agents to explore, maybe do RL on, you know, scientific reasoning. Can you talk a bit more about that?

Yes, so the thing that I talked about last time was this idea that we had these large collections of screens and that they were big enough environments and counterfactually dense enough that you could take agents and drop them in there and then give them tasks and they could go do those tasks on a limited budget in this landscape that we had measured completely.

And so the flagship problem that we spent a lot of time over the past couple months on is a structure activity relationship problem. And the idea there is like, okay, I've got some molecules and I know that they bind — maybe they bind to this protein that I want them to. How do I change them to make them better? This is a very common task for medicinal chemists to do.

And SAR, as it's sort of abbreviated to, also includes other stuff like certain drug-like properties, you know, does it get metabolized? All these things. We're not doing those right now. We're just doing, can we find molecules that bind better to the thing that we're interested in?

And so what we do is we take an agent like a language model and then we say, "Here's a catalog that you could look at. You have a budget of 100 molecules. We're not going to tell you anything except the target, and go find the best binder you can."

And so different agents tried different stuff. They have different search policies. They have different ways of wanting to spend their budgets. And what they'll do is they'll put out in readable language SAR hypothesis about why they think these molecules are working or not working. And then they'll go in and with this limited experimental budget, they'll test this hypothesis. And because it's all pre-measured, you can roll out a lot of these. We're up to about 90,000.

预印本与模型差异

So you started doing these on foundation models. I think you have like a preprint or something at this point that you can share. Do you want to share that or talk about it?

Yeah, so the preprint will probably be out at the same time that this episode comes out. It is pretty ready.

And what we show in there is that we get great separation across model families and that kind of levels and that kind of stuff. But another thing that's really interesting is because we have not just the results that you could use as an eval for how the agents are doing the job, we also know the results of the entire measured landscape or world. And so then you can start to interrogate how good is the agent at making scientific decisions.

Because maybe it only got to the thing that's half as good as the best thing in the entire environment. And so there we see all kinds of interesting behaviors like agents that give up early, ones that find molecules that don't agree with the rest of their hypotheses, ones that keep retesting the same molecules over and over despite having a limited budget. And also when it's good to explore versus exploit.

And it turns out that more performant models are much better at abandoning unproductive neighborhoods. And that was actually a really interesting surprise for us.

Yeah, and so when the paper comes out, we're going to release a bunch of these environments as Harper packages and then many thousands of transcripts for people to go play with and see how their science is doing.

聪明模型为何更早放弃坏区域

That's super cool. So do you have a feel for why the smarter models are able to figure out that they're in a bad part of the landscape and move?

We don't know that at all yet. All we know is that they're abandoning these crappy neighborhoods more quickly. And we definitely see a progression — a more willingness to jump around overall for more performant models, but they especially abandon the lousy places fast. And then the really poor ones stick around.

It's not just that they jump more, it's that actually they're figuring something out and saying, "Hey, this is not good. Let's get out of here."

Exactly. Exactly. Yeah, and what happens with the dumber models is that they'll just keep running little subtle changes on molecules that aren't ever going to go anywhere. Right? Like, "Oh, these two, they have a low score, but I feel good about them." And so I'm going to keep trying stuff. And then the smarter models will abandon the entire process. We're going to go somewhere.

Rollouts 中的"医药化学叙事"

Have you looked at the rollouts to see what it's thinking about?

Yeah, they think about all kinds of stuff. When we release all these transcripts, like — one of my favorite things to do is just take large numbers of transcripts and just dump them into LLMs and have a look at the different failure modes and stuff like that.

But you'll see — yeah, "I think that this ring is good and I think that this particular nitrogen is painful," or whatever, and they'll say these things and then they're very plausible medicinal chemistry narratives. So it's pretty fun.

That's amazing. I'm curious, have you given humans these same questions?

I have to have them look and evaluate it like, you know, not a ton. But because we have a large number of them, when we get medicinal chemists to look at it, they're like, "Yeah, no, those are very plausible thoughts about how to conduct this particular part of the SAR campaign."

游戏化的可能性

I don't know, maybe I'm overthinking — could you make a game out of this? It's sort of a game, right? And then medicinal chemistry becomes the video game, and you can put people in these environments and give them... yeah. Do the medicinal chemistry capture.

[laughter] Yeah, that's your business model. I like this plan.

We did do a game a little bit like this for "Name That Chemist." We would have to probably boil it down to have a smaller number of building blocks. Because right now to have a chemist go in there, you can imagine that if you're a medicinal chemist, you might have this suite of things that you might want to try over time — like put a methyl here, move this around — and when we have these pre-measured environments, we are going to be restricted to the things that we did actually measure.

And so then we would have to be asking the medicinal chemist, "Oh well, you can't do whatever you want. You can just do a lot of stuff." And figure out a way...

And they have to know what the stuff is.

They have to know what the stuff is, yeah. So we'd have to figure out a way to surface it to them in a meaningful way, but I kind of like where you're going with this. Like we could shrink it down to a smaller number of options.

前沿模型排名

What model is best? Of the frontier models, what are the best ones?

Let's see. I was looking at the plot a minute ago. It's kind of embarrassing — I forgot already. Right now, the champion is GPT-5 (after six).

Nice, nice.

Not a big shock.

Not a big shock. Sonnet 4.5 is actually pretty good, too.

Okay. Yeah, and Sonnet 4.1 is also pretty good. And everything 5 is just a racing pilot trap, right? [laughter] Yeah, so GPT-5 is both very expensive and not very performant. Yeah, I think 5 will be long considered a big mistake by Anthropic. 8.5 are pretty good.

Do you have Opus 4.5?

We don't yet, no. That's one thing that — as you guys can appreciate — has actually been a little infuriating. So when we talked last two months ago, we started these rollouts to see what happened, and then there's been a new frontier model drop like once every 11 days.

Eleven days, yeah.

Yeah, so every time I'm like, "Oh, we're going to ship this, we need to drop this public stuff," and then a new stupid model shows up and like... yeah, they ship faster than Anthropic.

[laughter] Right, good luck Ian.

开源模型表现

So yes, we are excited to put more in here, and we also have run a large number of the open source ones as well. So we've thrown a bunch of smaller Qwens in there, and GLMs and Kitty and DeepSeeks and that kind of stuff. So there's a lot of these.

How do they do?

They're not — DeepSeek V4 Flash is pretty good. Not that bad. Yeah, maybe I should just send you guys the full chart of how things are going.

Yeah, we can just put it in the show notes.

I can say it kind of looks a little bit like, you know, like the Arc AGI 2 plots. Where you've got some crappy models.

Right, right.

It does kind of look like that, and that's kind of why we made it like that.

SMILES 语言与模型的化学理解

And then one thing that has been very interesting to us — about this time last summer, we had started an internal project to do supervised fine-tuning on some of these language models to get them to understand SMILES. Because none of the existing frontier models were any good at it. So like none of the Anthropic or OpenAI models at the time could even convert SMILES to non-canonical SMILES very effectively.

So just for non-chemists, SMILES is a string language that you can use to accurately describe a chemical, right?

Yes, that's right. I think we mentioned it a little earlier when we recorded last, but it's a string, and molecules can be forks or circles or both put together. These different things.

And so a SMILES is basically a graph traversal across the molecule written down into a one-dimensional string. And so you can imagine starting the graph traversal at a different point in the molecule. And so there's multiple SMILES ways of representing the same molecule. And so it's nice to be fluent in transferring from one to the other.

There's a couple open-source packages people use like RDKit to do this. But we wanted the language models to do it just because it would go faster and they weren't good at using tools on their own back then. And nobody could do it.

And then around February, like a lot of other things, it became clear that they could start to actually work with chemistry in a meaningful way, which is a reason we started going in this direction.

That's really interesting because that means that it's internalizing some understanding of the physical nature of molecules.

I think a little bit. Yep. Like these are the tasks that we're having these things do right now — they're iterative tasks where they're looking at molecules and they are learning something about those molecules to make choices to make better molecules next.

And when we remove the information about the molecules, these decisions really suffer. So they're learning something. Or at least they're using it — I guess that's a better... we're not changing weights here, but they're definitely using the information to make future choices.

贝叶斯基线？"地形太崎岖"

You mentioned all these little models that you tried. So I wanted to ask — have you just used like one of these Bayesian hyperparameter algorithms as a deterministic baseline for your problem?

We think it's too spiky of a landscape and it's very high-dimensional. We don't do that, but we mostly think it's not going to work. I think that's the party line.

发布内容清单

You plan on releasing all this, so I guess we'll put — wait, what are you releasing? You said you're going to have a preprint, blog, and then some data rollouts and everything, so we can put all this in the show notes. Is there anything else?

Yeah, that's it. I think that's the big thing. What I would probably say is: we have built this thing where if you've got scientific agents and you want to know how they're behaving, what mistakes they might make, how they might learn from physical feedback — you know, if a new training recipe improves scientific decision-making — we've got the capabilities to measure these things at scale.

更多问题 & "带有摊销延迟的循环实验室"

That's really cool. Do you have plans for other similar problems for this same kind of thing?

We do, yes. Broadly, the way that we think about this is it is a lab in the loop with amortized latency. So it's like go out, you record the thing once, and then you can have a huge number of rollouts through that thing — effectively infinite rollouts.

And we are thinking hard about other types of biological or scientific questions that you could transmute into these kinds of environments. Because if you're doing conventional lab in the loop, it does take a long time, and because those things themselves have limited budgets, it's also not counterfactually dense. So you've got to keep running it and do different choices with every rollout to make the agents learn.

Right, but with your multiplexed strategy, then you can just amortize.

You can just amortize. So it's not quite accurate to say it's a lab in the loop with zero latency, but it's pretty close.

This is the same thing that Lyra's doing — I mean, it's not the same thing, but they also do experiments and then they use that in their rollout, but they're not doing them live.

Right. They are doing it in the rollout one step at a time, which offers a lot more freedom because you can choose almost anything. And here you're restricted to the number of choices that we made when we pre-measured the environment. That's definitely true. But it's still a pretty big number of choices.

扩张计划：目标每天 20 个新环境

Right now we've screened about a thousand proteins against a couple of these chemical libraries since we started Leash, and we're going to start to grow that. I think we're going to try to get to maybe 20 of these new environments a day. That's a plan for us to try to get to the beginning of maybe '26 or '27. We're doing two a day right now. I think we could probably get to 20 a day without too much lifting. So we're pushing — we'll see if we can do it.

Wow. And so you're going to have this huge RL environment.

Yeah. [laughter] It seemed like the thing to do.

Informally it seemed like where a lot of these agents are making the best and the fastest progress is where there's instant feedback that's very scalable. It's really hard to do that in the physical world, but we think that there's probably a handful of biological questions that you could rebuild in this way and go after them.

And yeah, we don't yet know if we're able to take reinforcement learning progress from these kinds of environments and move on to new biology yet, but we're trying. We're going to find out.

终极目标：决策能力的迁移

That's the obvious goal — how does this transfer to other biology? You can imagine if you did it for some sort of covering set, that you might be able to get things in between that you could transfer to pretty well.

Yep. And then also one thing that I need to do is talk to some more decision people, because a lot of this is about how do you spend a limited experimental budget, and then what can you do to do better at that? Beyond just medicinal chemistry, right? When do I stay? When do I go? How do I get better at that?

Interesting. Yeah, you can imagine if it knows how to connect a decision at that point to a knowledge that it has, then it could learn that skill for other problems.

Yes. Yes. We are incorporating more and more structural tool calls and things like that with this as well. So it's a pretty fun time right now.

结束语

Yeah, we'll be sure to link to all that cool stuff you have coming out. Thanks for taking the time to chat.

Cool, cool.

Thanks for taking the time for a follow-up chat.

Yeah, yeah.

I think this will actually appear back-to-back with the rest of the episode.

Okay. This was great.

All right, guys.

All right. See you.

Always fun. We'll see you later.

[music]

观看原视频 →

item.title: [a16z] Why OpenAI Is Racing to Make Computer Use Superhuman
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

隐藏的系统性真相：当"看"变成"做"的时刻

一、意外观察：这不是关于AI的，而是关于"软件已死"的讣告

表面上这是一场关于计算机使用代理的对话，但如果你把访谈倒过来读，会发现一个被埋藏的秘密：OpenAI实际上在宣告"软件作为交付物"时代的终结。

注意Ari那句看似随意的话："任何软件默认都会与agent协同工作。"——这不是功能描述，这是一个存在论宣言。过去40年，软件的本体是"人类通过UI操作的程序"；而computer use把软件的本体悄悄替换成了"可被任何智能体像素级操控的接口"。你的ERP、CRM、财务系统，它们的用户群在一夜之间从"员工"变成了"员工+无数个agent实例"。这意味着所有软件的产品经理，正在失去对自己用户是谁的定义权。

更惊人的是：当James说"广告商的商业模式与agent访问其产品不一致"时，他实际上在描述互联网原始契约的崩塌。整个Web的经济基础（广告、点击、曝光）建立在"人类注意力的稀缺"假设之上。Computer use不是绕过广告——它是在彻底否认广告存在的前提。

二、跨领域连接：计算机使用 ≈ 工业革命前夜的"机床"

这里有一个被完全忽视的历史平行。1770年代，蒸汽机本身并不改变世界——改变世界的是让蒸汽机能驱动任何机器的通用传动装置。Computer use就是数字时代的"通用传动装置"。

单独的LLM、单独的API、单独的MCP连接器，就像19世纪早期每台机器都需要专用蒸汽机。而computer use做的事情是：它让"智能"这种能量可以无差别地注入任何已存在的软件躯壳。这就是为什么James强调"legacy software that doesn't have MCP tools"——这不是技术债，这是价值千亿美金的"机械能转化介面"。

跨到另一个领域：这个访谈其实在描述生物学中的"内共生"事件。线粒体曾经是独立的细菌，被古细胞吞噬后不仅没被消化，反而成了细胞的能量工厂。Computer use agent正在被所有现存软件"吞噬"——但真正发生的是反向的能量转移：legacy software成了agent的能量来源（上下文、工作流、合法性），而agent成了软件的新代谢系统。

再看一个让你意外的角度："Codex cursor很可爱"这个细节。为什么OpenAI要给代理一个"可爱的光标"？这不是UX糖果——这是对人类前额叶皮层的驯化工程。当你看到一个带表情的光标在你的屏幕上移动时，你大脑的镜像神经元会把它编码为"社会性他者"而非"自动化工具"。这意味着OpenAI在用动画社会学解决一个心理学问题：让人类下意识地接受失去直接控制权。

三、系统性盲点：被访谈双方同时忽略的"元悖论"

这段对话最深刻的矛盾是双方都没点破的：

Ari说"我希望agent能适应你，而不是你适应agent"。James说"我们希望做出personalized software"。但他们同时在推销的是一个让所有软件变得对agent标准化的世界（WebMCP、确定性沙箱、enterprise controls）。

这是一个隐藏的收敛悖论：你越想让AI适应个体，就越需要让世界的接口标准化。因为agent要"读懂"每个人的意图，它必须先把世界翻译成它能处理的格式。所以表面上我们走向"一百人用的软件、一个人用的软件"，但底层正在发生的是一种比SaaS更彻底的接口统一——所有软件都在被重新训练成"对agent友好的"统一形态。

个性化的表层下，是前所未有的同质化底层。这就像语言：当所有人都说Esperanto来保留自己的方言，方言就死了。

还有一个被遮蔽的真相：James无意中说出了computer use最诚实的商业模型——"restaurant groups不懂tech"。整个computer use的大市场不是取代SF工程师，而是把90%不懂AI的中小企业强行拖入AI时代，而他们甚至不知道自己已经被拖入了。这是一场无需用户同意的智能部署，一个"沉默的大规模自动化"。

最后一个让你发凉的观察：当agent使用速度"超越人类专家"时（Ari明确说很接近了），人类将永远失去审计agent的能力。你不可能用慢速观察的方式监督一个比你快10倍的agent做10万次操作。所谓"human in the loop"将在超人类速度到来的那一刻，从实质控制退化为仪式性确认——就像今天的cookie同意弹窗。

这才是computer use真正的奇点时刻：不是AI能做人类的事，而是人类同意了一个自己再也看不清的新世界。

嘉宾介绍

Welcome to the A16Z podcast. I'm Sema Amble. I'm joined by my colleague Fabrizio Saraphiniti. In August, we wrote about computer using agents and how they're starting to do the real work inside companies.

Today I'm joined by Ari Weinstein and James Sun from OpenAI, who are going to help unpack what is going on with computer using agents from their perspective and share some thoughts on the future.

Hosts: Ari, James, thanks for joining us.

Guests: Of course, happy to be here. Yeah, thanks for having us.

一、Astra 带来的提升：速度、创造力与可靠性

Hosts: Ari, kick it off and tell us a little bit about what in Astra has made computer using agents move forward and what's really unlocked.

Ari: Astra's an amazing model. It's good at so many things. Our computer use models were already so good before Astra — Soul itself is amazing at computer use. So Astra really helps with a few things around the edges, in my sort of anecdotal experience:

  • 更快：It uses fewer thinking tokens to do the same task.
  • 更擅长创造性工作：In our launch video, you were talking to it and it's drawing things on Microsoft Paint. It's way better at that sort of thing, which I think probably transfers to other kinds of creative tasks also.
  • 边缘更可靠：I feel like I trust it a little more. It's the kind of thing where there's a little difference that is hard to perceive but really important between something being 99% reliable and 97% reliable.

James: Astra is also our most aligned model. If you look at the system card for it, it is much better at being resistant to prompt injection. It's much better at not taking any kind of unintended actions.

So when you think about it for enterprise work, especially for companies using it for sensitive things — whether it's procurement or talking to vendors or talking to customers — you're going to feel a lot safer using it, and that's really exciting.

彩蛋：Astra 玩电子游戏

Internally we had Astra play video games against 5.6, and it wins every time. There are some cool tweets where Astra is able to beat Fallout in like 30 hours. It's also just really amazing at playing video games.

二、消费端 vs 企业端：两种不同的推进逻辑

Hosts: Consumer versus enterprise use cases — very different implications around all the scaffolding. How do you think about where things are more exciting?

James: Our goal at OpenAI is really about building products that's useful for everyone. Ari is more of a consumer guy; I spend more time on the enterprise side.

  • 消费端：The place where we try to push the frontier on what's possible. With Astra, it's much faster compared to previous models, so we think about what new consumer experiences can we enable.
  • 企业端：Safety becomes more interesting. Inside enterprises, the use cases for computer use are actually fairly obvious — there's lots of legacy software that doesn't have any MCP tools, software that's been used for 15–20 years. A lot of times it's actually kind of hard to use for a normal person. Lots of UI from the last decade. We've seen companies build skills that teach the model to use them better.

Enterprise is where capabilities have been there maybe for a little longer and the companies are catching up. Consumer is where we're trying to figure out the next types of use cases that's not possible today.

Ari: The consumer use cases are so fun for me because it's like: how can you put your agent to work doing the things in your daily life that are so annoying and save you tons of time?

It's been really fun to see Dot — each Dot gets its own computer and you can ask it to do things for you in the cloud. It gets a full web browser. It can buy things for you, book haircut appointments, anything else you wanted to do.

三、Dot 的实战：主动性 + 云端计算机 + 本地浏览器联动

Hosts: James, you probably use a Dot to walk through product feedback. How are you using Dots?

James: Dots is really cool for a few reasons.

主动性（proactive）

I've been very surprised a lot of times when, in both my personal life and work, Dots will just flag something that completely slipped through the cracks. Just the other day — on our internal email system, whenever we get an external email for an invite, it doesn't actually show up on our calendars, so I end up missing a bunch of external meetings. Dots now catches these: "There's an invite in your inbox. It's not on your calendar. Do you want me to accept it in your Gmail so it shows up?"

形状不固定的任务

We use Slack internally, and there's a ton of messages going on at all times. I used to have this Slack job using automations and Codex that every 30 minutes would pull things, and I ended up tuning out notifications.

With Dots, I can give a high-level goal: - If anybody in my reporting chain says anything, flag it to me. - If anybody is giving critical feedback — use your judgment — about certain products, go for it.

云端 + 本地双浏览器联动

When someone reports a bug, they usually have a Sentry log. I can have Dots use the cloud computer, drive my local browser, log into Sentry, pull the logs, analyze it, give me feedback. It saves the entire loop of figuring out which feedback is important, looking at it, going to Sentry, downloading the logs, feeding into Codex, asking for thoughts — all can now be automated.

四、速度、成本与可靠性的权衡

Hosts: How do you balance reliability, speed, token usage, and efficiency?

Ari: We're really excited about computer use at OpenAI. We've invested in it a lot and we've gotten to a place where I think we have the fastest, cheapest and most reliable computer use product.

为什么速度如此重要

On one hand, the power of computer use is it can do tasks in the background — in some cases it doesn't matter how long it takes. But also sometimes you want to watch it to make sure it does it correctly. Speed is so important because you don't want this feeling of "oh, I could have just done that myself and it would have been easier."

We've gotten computer use to a place where it's faster than the average human at using a computer. And we're getting really close to a place where it is superhuman — faster than an expert computer user like one of us at this table.

That's going to be a sea change — it's going to change the way we all interact with computers. Anything that you could do manually, it could do faster. In the default case, you probably just want the agent to do it for you.

多模型多价位策略

We offer multiple different models at multiple qualities and price points. Our less expensive models are getting much better at computer use over time, so there will actually be more variation over time in which models people want to use for which tasks.

James: The flip side: how do we give customers control over safety, reliability, autonomy versus speed?

When the model is slow, you can watch it, but you're limited to the tasks you can do because you can't sit watching it. Once you can no longer observe and audit everything, how do we give enterprises the ability to control the amount of human-in-the-loop and the auditability?

A few months ago, as part of Astra, we launched a set of enterprise controls: - Human-in-the-loop level: Do they want the agent to automatically approve everything? We have an awesome system called Guardian / auto-approve — a smart model looking at every action the agent takes to decide if it's safe and aligned. - Consumer vs enterprise defaults: A consumer might want it to do everything without being asked. An enterprise is able to decide which types of actions actually go through.

The control part becomes more and more important as our computing agents become superhuman.

五、应用软件的反应：开放网络的张力

Hosts: Have you seen the response from application software — now there's computer using agents accessing legacy workflow software?

James: This problem becomes really interesting on the open web.

Within software approved and used by the company, it's more straightforward — companies want their people to automate tedious work.

But on the internet, you have a few different camps:

阵营一：商业模式与 agent 冲突

Advertisers, publishers whose business model is entirely on advertisement. If the agents using the website for them, where's the ad revenue coming from? Most places, an agent's ad impression does not count towards real revenue.

阵营二：拥抱协同的标准

Companies who do want to embrace computer use agents are adopting standards that let humans and agents use products together. WebMCP is a standard we're really excited about — we added support for it in the in-app browser.

You can imagine scenarios where the agent is elevating the experience of using the site, but not entirely replacing it. Browsing the internet is still very fun — I like doing shopping, looking at hotels and flights. The agent does all the tedious work, but carves out a UX where you're doing the browsing. "Okay, now I want to finish the transaction, put in my credit card…" — then hand it back to the agent.

WebMCP is an interesting way where your interface with the website is still the site itself, but the person is kind of using it together.

六、什么任务可以放心交给 Agent？

Hosts: How do you define the right narrow repeatable task? What's ready to hand over versus still requires checking?

James: Generally the model is pretty capable to do anything you can do on a computer now. One exercise I force myself to do: whenever I have a task, the first thing I think is "can I just have the agent do it?"

  • There are some sensitivities — e.g., if I'm sending a message to someone, I want it to feel like it's coming from me.
  • But in general, computer using agents now, since Astra, is capable of doing anything a person can do.
  • With Astra's flexible input, when there's vagueness, it'll ask you about details — and if you don't answer in time, it'll just keep going and pull the context that's necessary.
  • For repeatable workflows, it's nice to define requirements early, similar to writing a product spec.

Unless there's something incredibly sensitive, I just reach for the computer model for everything I do now.

Ari: I'm trying to build that impulse to reach for it, because sometimes it's so easy to get locked into the old way of doing things.

The really cool thing about computer use as a technology is the universality of it. It works with every application. Unlike anything else we've built where the developer has to do work to adopt it — someone has to build a connector, MCP server. Computer use works with everything. And it works by using the application the same way a human uses it. It makes the agent have all the capabilities you do.

James: Over time I've stopped thinking about "am I using them on a computer use task or a non-computer use task." They're frequently connected. Computer use is really the universal API that the model has to do whatever it takes. The more ambitious the task, the more likely it will touch computer use at some point.

The only time I don't reach for computer use is if the task is so simple it's easier to just click two buttons.

七、让企业信任 Agent：两层防护

Hosts: What do you have to share with an enterprise user to get them comfortable? There's hesitance — "the human would click through it and probably do it worse, but there's accountability, that person's trained…"

James: Two layers.

第一层：确定性控制（deterministic controls）

Even though our model is the most aligned ever and better than most people at protecting against prompt injections, there's a feeling of safety when enterprise admins can say: for certain tasks or data sources, it's just too sensitive to be used.

We launched two things: 1. Deterministic sandbox: ability to say the agent can use certain apps / websites and not others. 2. Human-in-the-loop configuration: what type of actions require human intervention? E.g., anytime there's a download/upload, a person has to approve. Anytime it goes to a new website, a person has to approve.

These are all dials an enterprise can go through.

第二层：对齐评估

Showing enterprise admins all the evals we've run internally around how aligned these models are — both internal and third-party evals.

Ari: We also do baseline work to help people build trust. We put a lot of work into product design: - You can always see the cursor if you want to watch it perform a task, and it animates in a fun way so it's not boring to watch. - We ask for permission before using a new application or website.

You want this trust-building moment where you figure out what it feels like and what you want it to do, and over time feel more comfortable.

Hosts: The Codex cursor is so cute. Watching it use the computer gives you confidence and makes the experience nice.

八、企业最值得自动化的领域

Hosts: Models are capable, getting cheap to run at scale. What should companies automate? Where are you most excited?

James: Two big categories.

类别一：乏味的工作流（the boring one = opportunity）

  • ERPs / CRMs / systems of record：Every single system of record.
  • Procurement：Companies have a giant spreadsheet with a thousand rows, filled out by teams. An ops team puts it into procurement software; a procurement team reaches out to vendors. Computer use can automate all of that.
  • Finance / reconciliation：Lots of ledgers within a company — expenses, etc. End of month there's a lot of reconciliation; many recon financial software don't have APIs. Computer use can look through ledgers, reconcile, flag anything interesting.
  • Sales：Different software for transcripts, data, prospecting, CRM — computer use goes and does prospecting, puts data into CRM or outreach software.
  • Market research：Also a common one.

类别二：更有创造力的工作

Astra is really good with visual design: - Circuit design - Architecture work - Hardware engineering - Game design

Less common for enterprises to think about these right now because they're focused on the boring opportunities. But as folks understand the model's capabilities more, that's where we'll see more usage next.

James 的个人例子

In my free time I've been building a video annotation software for Pokémon. I like to film myself playing the game and have the agent go look at stuff. I had computer use log in, create accounts on pickleball/squash/tennis annotation software, try them, take screenshots, give me feedback, then build it back into the app.

消费者端的乏味工作

Ari: - Filling out DMV forms. - Unsubscribing from a bunch of emails. - Doing things people wouldn't have had time or thought to do: maintaining spreadsheets about finance, meal planning. A personal trainer friend is making customized plans for his clients.

I use Apple Numbers, which is like an obscure spreadsheet program, but the model still knocks it out.

— "I don't think I've ever heard someone use Apple Numbers."

It's a surprisingly great spreadsheet software.

九、第三类：软件形态本身的改变

Ari: The third category I'm most excited about: a different way to use your entire computer or interface with software. In our Astra ad, really cool examples of people just talking to their computer with their voice. Over time we're going to see the form factor of software itself change due to this technology.

Hosts: Imagine an enterprise user used to a clunky ERP from 30 years ago. One world: unleash a set of agents operating that software. Another world: AI-native players using computer use agents. Which direction does the world go?

Ari: Such an interesting moment where simultaneously the cost and complexity of creating new software is so much lower, but also there exists so much legacy software that computer use is well suited to interact with.

So much software in production today was written 10, 20, 30, 40 years ago — it's not going away overnight. But computer use may put more pressure on companies to make software work better with agents, because all software is going to work with agents by default.

WebMCP is a great example. Both will be super important, but will shift over time.

James: There's a lot of art and craft in building great products.

If the internet becomes just this faceless thing where agents are talking to each other and people aren't using anything anymore, I would be very sad.

Something about craftsmanship and artisan software feels nice to use because the designer really understands the experience the customer wants.

个性化软件的例子：妻子的五子棋训练器

My wife recently got into playing a board game — connect five pebbles to win (I think it's called Gomoku). She's playing online with friends and getting her ass kicked. I was like, "I'm going to build you a tactical trainer for going through different gambits."

I created a first version. I know she likes to learn in a certain way. I was able to craft software that feels really good for her.

If anybody can build these craft software in a short amount of time for niche use cases that are so well tailored for people — I think that's a beautiful world.

I don't think UI is going away. The pressure of cheap software will make software has to be better. I don't think everything will have an MCP/API and computer use will never be useful.

Ari: Humans are so hardwired for direct manipulation. You want to move and do things with your own hands.

Software in the past was so one-size-fits-all — designed for millions, tens of millions, billions. We will enter an era where any piece of software could be designed for a hundred people or one person.

十、B2C 的"乐趣"与 B2B 的"审计日志"

Hosts: My mental model: two buckets.

  • Consumer side：Something you get joy out of, enjoy using, or learn from. Not the utility — the joy of interacting or learning. You want to spend time on it.
  • B2B side：You may want the agent to complete tedious work, but there's the concept of the audit log. The product is me as the human user setting the goal and being able to understand the logic — but not necessarily running through the entire chain. "Why did that payment get made? Pay this person at this time, 30 days, this discount applied." They want the agent to execute, but some level of control still needs a UI.

Why should we settle for shitty software?

Ari: I'm optimistic we will see new kinds of software where it has traditional user interfaces but is also using agents under the hood. And sometimes those agents are themselves using computer use to automate legacy software — giving you a nicer, more purpose-built experience.

James: This is what we call internally the shared intelligence layer. If every website has its own agent that doesn't talk to your agent, it's a very fragmented world. Figuring out how your agent can plug in and use your other software — that's going to be really interesting over the next few months.

十一、给创业者的建议

Hosts: If you were starting a company tomorrow using computer use to solve an enterprise workflow — what advice would you give founders?

Ari: It depends on the modality: - Small team wanting to use existing software more efficiently: our products (ChatGPT etc.) serve this use case. - Building something that itself interacts with existing software: maybe you have a machine in the cloud doing computer use in the background, via the API. Then it's interesting to figure out when the human is in the loop — is the agent telling you when something's wrong / right? Summarizing so you don't get bombarded with notifications?

James: Both Ari and I were startup founders before OpenAI. I'm still very bullish on startups.

创业机会一：垂直深度

Even though we're thousands of people, teams are not very big for all the problems. If you have a problem you deeply understand — industry expertise, regulatory, go-to-market, how to service customers — it's still green field. Our APIs let you accelerate. Speed and pain are the mode that exists today.

创业机会二：AI 扩散较慢的垂直行业

A company I was talking to the other day uses computer use to help restaurant groups: 1. Take pictures of their back storage. 2. Vision looks at what's going to be missing based on tomorrow's projected traffic. 3. Computer use goes to a procurement site to order groceries for the next day. 4. Goes into ERP to adjust the timetable for employees — maybe more people needed because last year, same time, there was more traffic from a holiday.

Restaurant groups are not tech companies super familiar with available tools. For the average American, average SMB owner, average enterprise: - Understanding what tools are capable of = step one. - Connecting tools in a way that makes sense = step two. - Deploying = step three. - Servicing = step four.

If there are complex workflows requiring disparate software, computer use is a great way to join them and complete the entire intent flow. Building it in a UI that feels good to hold still feels like a really big opportunity.

十二、未来：实时协作、主动性、一致性

Hosts: What's next on the frontier?

Ari: - Speed：Making computer use superhuman. - Blended interfaces：Multimodal inputs and outputs for more fluid experiences. - Real-time collaboration：Today much of our computer use product is background-focused — give the agent a task, do something else. In the future, more real-time collaboration between you and the agent. - Better, cheaper, more available, easier to use.

James: With Dots we're giving folks computers in the cloud. Codex also has a browser in the cloud.

一致性（coherence）问题

Today you can install the Chrome extension, which uses your password manager and everything in Chrome. We have an in-app browser in the desktop app with a different set of cookies and passwords. Your computer in the cloud has different things. For the average consumer it's confusing — "why do I have four different browsers that don't talk to each other? If I open a tab in one, does it show up in the other?"

How do we make computer use go from this product used by enterprises and tip-of-the-spear users to something that's actually understandable for people?

It's kind of an oxymoron — computer use is actually the most easy to understand AI product: it's an AI using your computer. But because of the complexities of managing different states, implementation details sometimes seep through.

主动性（proactivity）

Ari: Another challenge today: you have to put thought into how you're going to use it, remember to use it, convince yourself to do things differently from how you're used to.

Dots have this really powerful proactivity where they can come to you, identify situations, and help you solve problems. I'm really excited about a world where the agent can adapt to you instead of you adapting to it.

十三、Computer Use 的发展曲线

Hosts: Talk about the momentum behind computer use.

Ari: James and I have been working on computer use for some time at OpenAI. It's been an incredibly exciting past six to nine months.

  • We started working on these products and very few people were using them.
  • Earlier this year, the models suddenly became great at these tasks because of amazing work by the research team.
  • In the past couple months, the product's growing like crazy — people are really seeing the value.
  • Still so early — only some portion of our user base is using computer use. It's going to grow quite a bit.

James: I joined OpenAI in January, worked on the Atlas product.

Love love Atlas, RIP Atlas.

In Atlas, the agentic experience wasn't a big selling point — most people treated it like a normal browser. Over the last few months, as model capabilities got better, we've incorporated browser use into all our existing products where agentic usage already existed — and we've seen YC-level growth week over week.

下一个拐点：云端

Desktop is still very much a power user thing. Most consumers are on their phones. How do you give every ChatGPT user — everybody who's just using their phone for day-to-day life — a powerful computer that they don't even need to understand how to use?

Hosts: Computer using agents have had a ton of momentum. Now it's the moment of: how do we get it into more people's hands? They trust it, they feel like they can really use it. Coherent experiences — as that gets better, consumers will feel more comfortable using it.

Ari: I think we're at the scaling moment of computer use — both for consumer and enterprise at the same time. Really excited to see where it goes and what people build with it.

结束语

Hosts: Thank you so much for joining us. This was awesome. We love talking about this topic and it was really fun to hear it from you guys directly.

Guests: Thank you. A lot of fun as well. Thanks.

# 隐藏的系统性真相：当"看"变成"做"的时刻
## 一、意外观察：这不是关于AI的，而是关于"软件已死"的讣告
表面上这是一场关于计算机使用代理的对话，但如果你把访谈倒过来读，会发现一个被埋藏的秘密：**OpenAI实际上在宣告"软件作为交付物"时代的终结**。
注意Ari那句看似随意的话："任何软件默认都会与agent协同工作。"——这不是功能描述，这是一个**存在论宣言**。过去40年，软件的本体是"人类通过UI操作的程序"；而computer use把软件的本体悄悄替换成了"可被任何智能体像素级操控的接口"。你的ERP、CRM、财务系统，它们的用户群在一夜之间从"员工"变成了"员工+无数个agent实例"。这意味着**所有软件的产品经理，正在失去对自己用户是谁的定义权**。
更惊人的是：当James说"广告商的商业模式与agent访问其产品不一致"时，他实际上在描述**互联网原始契约的崩塌**。整个Web的经济基础（广告、点击、曝光）建立在"人类注意力的稀缺"假设之上。Computer use不是绕过广告——它是在**彻底否认广告存在的前提**。

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、信用利差与 VIX 的"认知分裂"：一场只有机构在参加的危机

小涛敏锐地抓住了垃圾债利差 3.37 已经逼近 2022 年 3 月水位这个事实，但他没有点破的是一个更诡异的现象——信用市场在喊着"战争级压力"，而 VIX 却在往下走。这种分裂几乎从不出现在健康的市场里。它意味着什么？

机构正在偷偷从后门撤出，而散户还在前门排队买入波动率的平静。信用利差是债券基金经理用真金白银投票的结果，VIX 是期权交易员对未来 30 天的押注。当这两者方向相反，历史上几乎总是信用市场赢——因为债券持有人掌握着企业的现金流信息，而股票期权交易员只是在交易情绪。

这里的意外洞察是：AI 融资热潮本身正在成为一个"信用负债化事件"。星云（CoreWeave 类）、OpenAI 的 1.4 万亿基建承诺、Oracle 发债买 GPU——这些故事表面上是"科技牛市"，但在债券市场的记账本里，它们是非投资级信用供给的爆炸。换句话说，AI 牛市正在制造自己的负债阴影，而这个阴影首先会在信用利差里显形，然后才会在股价里显形。

二、鲍威尔 2021 年那句"危险的话"：联储作为阶级机器的意外自白

小涛复述了鲍威尔 2021 年 11 月那段话——"是不是因为资产价格太高、家庭太富有，所以人们不愿意回去工作"——然后说"这是多么危险的一种思考方式"。他说得对，但他只说了一半。

这段话的真正危险不在于它是"鹰派暗示"，而在于它无意间揭穿了现代中央银行的真实功能：联储不是通胀管理者，而是劳动力纪律执行者。当 Powell 承认"降低资产价格以迫使人们返岗"是一个政策考量时，他实际上在用央行语言复述一个历史上非常古老的机制——在中世纪，领主通过货币贬值把农民从土地上赶回磨坊；在 21 世纪，联储通过资产贬值把人们从家里赶回办公室。

跨领域连接：这与行为经济学里的"参照点效应"合拍得惊人。联储要操纵的不是价格，而是人对自己财富状态的感知。而这就是为什么下周三凯文·沃什的措辞比数据本身更重要——因为预期管理 = 感知操纵 = 劳动力定价。这三者在当代货币政策里是同一件事。

三、"参与度"框架的意外用途：它其实是一个流行病学 R₀

小涛反复提到纳指参与度 30%、通胀参与度从 54% 降到 43%、标普等权 70%……他把"参与度"当作一个独立的技术指标。但如果你把它翻译一下，你会发现：

参与度就是流行病学里的基本再生数 R₀——一个"价格上涨"或"下跌"在多少标的里"传染"开来。

  • 通胀参与度从 54% 跌到 43%：疫情（通胀）在萎缩，但还没消失。
  • 纳指参与度 30%：悲观情绪传染率低，意味着恐慌是局部的、是"科技股的流感"而不是"全市场的瘟疫"。
  • 标普等权参与度 70%：价值股的反弹是广泛的，是集体行为而非个股独走。

这个洞察的实操意义是：真正该担心的不是指数跌多少，而是参与度何时从一个状态跳到另一个状态。2021 年 11 月 ECI 之所以成为转折点，不是因为它涨到了 1.2%，而是因为那个数字把"工资通胀"从一个局部现象翻译成了一个系统性参与度跳升。本周四 PCE 和周五 ECI 的真正看点，不是数字本身，而是看它们会不会把目前已经降到 43% 的参与度重新顶回 50% 以上——那才是鹰派转向的扳机。

四、一个让人意外的双向观察：可口可乐和微软正在交换"身份"

必需品消费板块 10 月涨了近 10%，可口可乐估值破了 5 年新高 26.6 倍。微软经历了下跌，估值 25 倍左右，低于其历史均值。

换句话说：防守股正在变得像成长股一样昂贵，而真正的成长股变得像价值股一样便宜。

这是 2025 年最被忽视的宏观叙事反转：当市场认定"AI 泡沫要崩"时，资金躲进了可口可乐；但资金躲避 AI 的行为本身，正在让可口可乐变成一个比微软更脆弱的"类成长股"——因为它所有涨幅都来自 PE 扩张，一个 1% 的利率上行就能把这个 PE 打回原形，而微软还有基本面兜底。

这是本周财报季真正的赔率机会所在：赌微软/谷歌给惊喜，同时隐性做空"类比可口可乐"的伪防御板块，可能是全年里 risk/reward 最不对称的一次布置。

📝 转录文本

开场与本期提要

十月份的股市走到现在，还有一周就要结束了。从体感上不是非常的好，但实际上整个十月份标普500只下跌了0.4%。而从板块这一个角度去看，十月份和九月份正好是相反。某种程度也可以理解为10月份大科技和半导体相对的弱势，是对于整个全年以来的一个走势进行一部分的修复。

那随着本周会有更多大科技发布财报，我认为整个市场的一个 setup 是不错的。那借由今天的这期视频，我们首先当然回顾一下上周市场的走势、10月份的走势、当下市场的一个 select 参与度、估值、等权指数的估值等等；然后我们就对于本周将要发布财报的一些公司去做一个展望，包括本周还会有美联储会议，我们一起去做一个展望，好吗？

欢迎大家来到一个不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。那么废话不多说，马上开始今天内容。在开始之前，大家记得留言、点赞、加转发，让更多人可以看到我们这期内容。

一、上周资产价格与板块走势回顾

先回顾一下过去一周资产价格的走势。美债收入出现了下跌，三大指数这边都出现了小幅的波动——标普和纳指出现了下跌，道指出现了反弹。黄金下跌的幅度比较大，收 3996，下跌了4.1%。原油出现了小幅的上涨，VIX 下跌，IGV 上涨幅度非常的好，6%。罗素两千也反弹了2%。那罗素两千的一个反弹和美债收入的一个下跌有关。

从板块这一个角度去看，防守属性的板块表现出相当的强势。可以看到过去一周，大多数的板块其实都出现了上涨，只有国防板块出现3.3的下跌，七大科技股出现2%的下跌，芯片板块出现3.1%的下跌。

所以上周结束完之后，标普的等权指数是上涨了1.1%。那我们看倒数第二列 QDD，到现在为止等权指数上涨，也就 QDD 就是整个10月份，等权上涨4.1%，前七大科技股下跌2.5%，罗素1000的成长 ETF 下跌4.5，价值上涨3.8。价值和成长股之间的这个回报差出现了非常大的差距在那边。芯片下跌了16%。那么所以从体感上来说非常的差。

二、当下市场 Setup：信用利差与融资压力

那经过9月份和10月份的走势之后，我们来看一下当下市场的一个 setup。

首先第一个是，其实是过去这一两周市场在 AI 这一块聊得比较多的就是融资这一块、信用程度这一块。那信用程度也好、融资也好，可以反映在一组数据里边，就是债券市场这边的一个利差。

债券市场的利差呢又分为两部分：一部分是投资级别，类似于这些大科技都是投资级别；另外一部分叫做非投资级别，那类似于像这些星云，它们叫做非投资级别。

图里白色这条线是投资级别债券的这个利差，截止到上周五是0.89，就是89个基点，那接近于今年3月份的水平。那今年3月份差不多是在0.92、0.93左右。其实现在离今年的3月份是非常的接近。

图里蓝色这条线是垃圾级别债券的这个利差。我们看到截止到周五的收盘是左边的这个 Y 轴 3.37。3.37已经超过了今年3月份的水平，当然，离上一年3月份的水平还有一定的一个距离。但其实整个当下债券市场这块的一个融资成本也好、还是一个压力也好，现在已经有一部分的压力积压在那边，而这个压力的一个水平或者程度是和今年的3月份类似。

那看到这边不少观众可能会问，那么有没有可能去到上年3月份的水平，利差继续扩大，指数继续下跌？当然有这个可能，那这边我并没有这个答案。我认为我们可以做的是，我们知道现在利差在什么的一个位置——这是我们唯一可以做的。

就好比 VIX，如果去到了30，如果去到了35，你说 VIX 在去到了35之后，有没有可能去到50？有没有可能像疫情的时候去到比50还要高？当然有这个概率在那边。但是能不能去到那边我真的不知道。而在现在这个位置，我认为我们可以做的是加一些风险回这个市场。

三、三大指数参与度与估值

参与度这边和上周的收盘其实变化并不大。

  • 纳指：几乎所有的均线都是在30%左右，参与度都在30%左右，就是处在一个悲观的一个阶段。
  • 罗素2000：比上一周稍稍微好了一些，20均线50%处在中性的位置，100日均线和50日均线38%处在一个中性偏悲观的位置。
  • 标普500：是三大指数里边相对最乐观的一个指数，参与度20均线70%，是在一个乐观的一个情况下。为什么？是因为整个10月份，大多数的标的、价值股标的其实都出现了反弹，那主要是因为利率的回调。

估值这边，标普500向前看的市盈率、前瞻市盈率截止到上周五的收盘18.5倍。前瞻市盈率18.5倍其实已经低于今年3月份的水平，离上年3月份的18倍其实已经非常的接近。

当然了，我们知道标普500里边，如果看前瞻市盈率，比如说整个第三季度盈利增速来自于哪，主要1/3或者不到，差不多1/3吧，主要是来自于美光这一个标的本身。所以另外一个标的我们可以去参考的是，我们可以看一下标普等权指数现在的前瞻市盈率在什么的一个位置。

那截止到上周五的收盘在16.36倍。我们可以看到和九月底低于16倍的这种情况已经出现了反弹。为什么反弹？是因为10月份到现在，价值股的标的出现了反弹，所以这些价值股，因为这些标的价格出现了反弹，所以它们的估值也出现了反弹。而因为是等权指数，因为整个10月份，大多数的个股其实是出现了反弹，所以标普等权指数前瞻市盈率在整个10月份其实是出现了反弹。

而反观我们看前面，标普的前瞻市盈率是反而出现了下跌。为什么？因为标普的前瞻市盈率受到了一些科技股、受到了芯片板块的一个影响，而芯片板块科技股10月份是下跌的，所以标普的前瞻市盈率是下跌，标普等权指数的前瞻市盈率反而出现了反弹。

那反弹完之后，我认为标普500的等权指数的前瞻市盈率仍然处在一个中性偏低的一个位置。中性位置是我这边画的一条横线，红色的这条线，17倍左右。

当然，其实从前面市场的参与度，我们也可以得出这样的一个结论：标普的参与度在70%，代表什么？代表大多数的个股的一个价格都在20均线以上，那就说明从等权指数、前瞻性这个角度去看一定是出现了反弹。

然后我们看纳指。那纳指我这边用的是一个 NDX。其实 NDX 也有一个等权指数，我不知道大家知不知道。我这边用的就是 NDX 一个等权指数。NDX 如果去看，NDX 的估值和标普外的估值是一样的，都是处在一个历史上相对比较低的这个位置。

但是我们为了把个别的一些权重股对于前瞻市盈率所造成的这个影响给剔除在外，所以我们看，我在看纳指的时候，我现在现在也把纳指的一个等权指数给放进来。那那纳指的等权指数其实从年初到现在是出现了下跌反弹，然后之后从6月份一路开始出现下跌，到现在截止到上周五的收盘，20.72倍。那今年的3月份其实在一个相对比较低的位置，目测的话差不多在18.5倍，上年的3月份差不多是在19.5倍左右。

所以纳指的等权指数现在是不是在一个相对比较低的位置？我认为是的。那么有没有到今年的3月份和上年3月份那么悲观的这个位置？还没有到。那反映在哪？其实也反映在前面纳指市场的一个参与度里面。可以看到纳指市场的一个参与度现在就是在一个悲观的位置。那当参与度在一个悲观的位置，那我们知道大多数的个股是都出现了下跌。

四、本周财报前瞻

然后我们一起对于本周发布财报的公司做一个展望。

周二盘前：可口可乐（KO）

周一有些公司，但是我认为不是那么的重要。周二盘前就开始有比较重要的公司发布财报，比如说可口可乐。那可口可乐其实 YTD 到现在为止走得相当的强。

我们一起来看一下可口可乐的估值。前瞻市盈率我这边看的是过去5年那个前瞻市盈率，从2021年一直到现在，最低点是在什么时候？是在2023年的时候，曾经跌到了20倍以下。而整个今年我们可以看到我鼠标所在这个位置，今年年初可口可乐的一个估值差不多是在21倍左右，截止到上周五的收盘26.6倍，前瞻市盈率。

所以整个全年影响，从21倍到26倍、26.6倍，差不多正好是30%左右 PE 的这个扩张。整个全年可口可乐价格的上涨几乎全部是来自于 PE 的这个扩张，从21倍涨到了26.6倍。但是26.6倍从历史的一个横向去做对比的话，明显是处在一个相当高的位置，甚至于是破了过去5年的一个新高。

那除非我们认为可口可乐的基本面出现了质的这个改变，不然的话，以可口可乐现在的一个每年 EP 的这个增速和以前历史上的这个估值范围，26.6倍绝对处在一个相对比较高的这个位置。所以现在这个位置，你说你再去追可口可乐，我认为是绝对会追高的。

必需品消费板块：与年初 1-2 月的相似性

然后我们来看一下可口可乐所在的这个板块——必需品消费。我们知道过去10月份到现在三周左右的时间，必需品消费整个板块上涨了将近10%。而短时间之内，基本面没有出现非常大改变的情况下，价格的这个上涨几乎全部是来自于 PE 的这个扩张。前瞻市盈率从9月底的20.5倍来到了周五收盘的22.8倍。其实周五还是出现了一些下跌，周四的这个估值的话更高。

但是整个板块和可口可乐有一些不一样的是：可口可乐是破了历史上的一个新高（估值），板块这个角度去看其实还没有破今年2月份的一个新高。

今年年初刚开盘的时候，还记不记得一二月份价值股板块走得相当的强、科技股是走得相当的弱？我觉得刚开盘一二月份的时候，我整个投资组合是下跌了7%还8%，远远跑输了标普，当时标普是上涨了1%、2%。

而整个10月份的一个走势，我的感受是完全和今年的一二月份非常的类似，就是价值股板块表现得相当的强势，然后科技股就走得相对比较的弱势。可以看到这一个上涨的一个幅度和速率，这条直线上涨的速度非常的快，和今年一二月份非常的类似。

但是毫无疑问，从估值这个角度去看，现在整个必需品消费板块的这个估值仍然是在一个高位。从这张图里我们可以看到，如果看过去两年必需品消费板块估值的一个波动区间的话，那就是21倍至22倍左右，那么高于22倍就是比较高的，像今年一二月份的时候去到了将近24倍，这处在一个非常高的这个位置。如果把22年、23年放进来的话，合理的估值区间波动区间就是在20倍至21倍左右。

好吧，那我们还是回到这边。所以现在必需品消费板块估值绝对是处在一个相对比较高的这个位置。那对于其他那些价值股板块，我认为大家也可以去参考一下。

那如果我们认为未来利率可以长期保持在高位的话，我认为对于这些必需品消费板块、对于这些价值股板块，都会从估值上进行一个 rerating，是 rerating down，估值应该会出现下跌，而市场会更加偏向于 ROIC 比较高的这些公司，从投资回报这个角度去看。

周二其他财报：SPGI / Robinhood / SK Hynix

那我们继续回到周二发布财报的公司。早上还会有 SPGI，那这家公司也是从两三个月之前因为一些软件板块被杀跌的时候和其他随之一起下跌。但是我认为他们的数据这一块还是有一个护城河在那边。Consulting 可能会受一些影响，所以这个季度财报可以再次去观察一下他们到底核心业务是不是会受到影响。我认为数据端这一块反而会变得更加的重要。

周二的盘后会有 Robinhood 和 SK Hynix。那 SK Hynix 可能是市场里面的一个焦点了。但是在美光已经发布完财报之后，我认为 SK Hynix 的这个财报受关注的这个影响度可能就没有那么的高了。

Robinhood 在前段时间也有人让我聊一下，Robinhood 发完财报之后能不能聊一下它基本面。那也是我持股之一，持仓的比例相当的小，但是这家公司发布完财报之后，我会进行更新的。

周三：Vertiv / GEV / 微软 / Alphabet（本周核心）

然后是周三。周三的盘前市场的焦点应该会放在 Vertiv 和 GE Vernova 这两家公司身上，整个和 AI 基建是相关的两家公司。

周三的盘后就是整个市场这一周的一个重点。因为周三的一个下午，首先周三的下午有美联储会议，那稍后我会聊一下美联储会议。那其次就是周三的盘后会有两家大科技发布完财报，分别是微软和谷歌。那这两家公司我都持有，而且占比都不小。那么我占比第一大的公司是英特尔，英特尔是在周四发布财报。所以基本上我占比里边、我投资组合里面占比比较大的几家公司，前三家公司全在本周发布财报。

所以我还是非常的期待微软、Alphabet，然后还有 ServiceNow。ServiceNow 是和软件板块相关。那软件板块，包括微软也是，微软和 ServiceNow 其实在过去这段时间表现是相对比较强势的。为什么？因为市场一部分的一些仓位在开始追回软件板块公司。为什么呢？因为市场意识到，哦，似乎 Claude Code 的一个面试，或者似乎 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 这两家公司没有实实在在地对于软件板块整个板块造成非常大的一些影响。

那并且在上一个季度发布财报的时候，我有聊过，我强调过很多次了，我再强调一遍：我认为从上个季度刚刚开始，我们才看到软件板块在 AI 这一块的一个落地，并且接下去每一个季度我认为都会加速。

那我个人对于微软和谷歌财报的一个展望是：谷歌的财报是最有可能会给一些 surprise，因为谷歌有一个 risk reward 在那边，有一个风险和回报的一个匹配在那边。因为市场现在对于谷歌其实并没有那么的待见，对于他们的模型的公布也好其实没有那么的待见，包括在 AI agent 这一块的落地，似乎市场认为谷歌也落后于 Meta，那么落后于 Meta 的这个缪斯。所以 Alphabet 谷歌是有一个 risk reward 在那边。

而我认为微软的确定性是相对比较高的。而我个人对于微软财报的一个期待其实相当的高。并且其实我在准备这些内容的时候，其实前面我不是和大家聊了很多指数的一些估值、个股的一些估值嘛，我特地去看了一下微软现在的估值，前瞻市盈率差不多在25倍左右吧。你知道微软在这一波2025年下跌之前，微软的估值在哪里？微软的估值是在30倍左右。所以即使从估值这个角度去看，从最低点的20倍出现了25%左右的这个反弹，但现在微软的估值和历史上的一个平均估值去做对比的话，仍然处在一个相对比较低的这个位置。所以我认为从估值这个角度仍然会有扩张的空间，只要财报继续越来越好。

所以下周三应该会成为整个市场里面关注焦点的核心中的一个焦点。

周四：Caterpillar / Eli Lilly / 英特尔 / 亚马逊 / Reddit

然后周四一个盘前会有 Caterpillar，然后 Eli Lilly。Eli Lilly 这家公司财报我会去看一下，这家公司可能相对来说是最稳的一家受益于 AI 的一家医疗板块的一个公司。然后，Caterpillar 基本可以把 Caterpillar 理解为和周三盘前发布财报的 Vertiv 和 GEV 放在一个标题里面——AI 硬件这一块。

周四的一个盘后，英特尔、亚马逊、Sandisk。那我个人肯定是比较关注英特尔和亚马逊。基本上我前四大持仓在本周全部发布财报，分别是微软、Alphabet、英特尔和亚马逊。那么所以注定了本周我自己的一个投资组合的一个波动将会非常的大。

最后周四的盘后会有，还会有 Reddit 的一个财报。那 Reddit 我上一个季度财报我是有跟过，我是有看过这家公司的一个。问题是在市场担心他们流量的一个最高点可能会受到谷歌 Overview 的这个影响。那这个点如果被证伪的话，它的估值是有可能会出现反弹。从它那个盈利增速去看，Reddit 这家公司估值是在一个比较低的位置。

五、宏观事件展望：美联储会议、PCE、ECI

最后我们一起来聊一下本周的一些宏观事件和数据。

周三美联储会议

首先当然是周三的美联储会议。那这一次是不会加息的，市场定价也不会加息。市场定价不会加息，凯文沃什就一定不会加息，因为他不是来惊吓这个市场。

那怎么去理解他在之后的一个讲话里边、之后的 QNA 里边到底是鹰还是鸽呢？我们看他到底从哪一个角度去解释通胀。

如果他单纯地从字面或者从数据这个角度去出发，比如说本周四将会公布的核心 PC 数据，市场预期是0.3，你把它展开之后，华尔街和彭博都预期差不多是在0.34，这个数据可能会有一些危险。危险的点在哪？市场预期都是在0.34，你稍微比市场预期高一点，四舍五入之后就是0.4，所以有一个 headline news 的一个风险在那边。

但如果反观它从一个通胀参与度这个角度去（稍后有张图和大家分享），那就是一个鸽派的一个解读。所以完全看他从哪个角度切入去解释现在的通胀到底在什么那个位置：单纯只是从字面和数据就是鹰派的，如果从参与度这个角度就是鸽派的。

周五 ECI：2021 年加息周期的那把"钥匙"

另外，本周五10月30将会公布一组非常非常重要的一组数据——ECI Employment Cost Index 工资的一个增速上涨。市场预期是0.8，彭博他们的预期是在0.9%。

这组数据为什么那么重要？因为2021年打开加息周期的一个关键数据就是 ECI Employment Cost Index。

这张图里我们看到两条线：图里蓝色这条线是实际 ECI 所出来这个结果，紫色这条线是市场这个预期。我左边的这个箭头指向的就是2021年的第三季度。第三季度的数据公布是什么时候？公布是十月底。所以当时2021年的一个背景就是十月底公布了九月份或者第三季度的一个 ECI 工资增速的一个上涨之后，11月2日那一天的美联储会议，美联储就变得鲍威尔当时就变得相当的鹰派。

因为我到现在都记得那一次美联储会议里边鲍威尔所聊的所有的一些内容，里边让我印象最深刻的一句话就是："有没有可能很多人没有回到这个劳动力市场，使得劳动力市场现在非常的紧缺，是因为家庭收入非常高，是因为家庭资产的扩张非常的好，有没有可能是和资产价格相关？"

他当时已经暗示得非常的明确了，因为资产价格非常的好，因为股市非常的好，所以人们不愿意回到工作岗位。那背后的一个含义，我说含义是什么？含义就是有没有可能一种情况：你把资产价格带下来，使得人们回到劳动力市场，从而去解决通胀这个问题。我说这是多么危险的一个思考方式。

那当时这一组数据就是我箭头所指的这个方向，蓝色这条线直接上涨，环比增速上涨到了1.2%，当时市场的一个预期就是0.9，所以最后的数据出来是远远超出了市场这个预期，才使得11月2日那一次直接出现了一个 pivot。那当时没有进行加息，为什么？因为我说美联储它加息是一个缓慢渐进的一个过程，但是态度明显是在看到那组数据之后出现了改变。这也是在之后鲍威尔其他的会议里边，他所聊到当时一个非常关键的一个转折点。

所以这组数据，这一次我们非常有关，这基本上这组数据每一次公布，我们都应该去关注，好吗？前两个季度，第一季度和第二季度，市场预期都是在0.8%，最后的结果都是在0.9。如果能够继续维持在0.9的话，OK，不用太过担心。如果但凡它上涨到1%的话，我认为这组数据是需要一些担心的。

通胀参与度

最后这张图就是通胀的一个参与度。那通胀的参与度如果越低，就代表可能短期之内的一个通胀越不需要去担心。

那图里白色这条，你们可以看到，从三四个月之前吧，通胀的参与度最高点可能是在百分之五十三、五十四左右，然后一路出现下跌，现在差不多是在43、44左右。那白色这条线代表的是：首先它是一个6个月的年化；其次它代表的是 PCE 所有的项目里边，有超过年化有超过3%的通胀比例。或者通胀的这个项目，超过3%的通胀这个比例和项目越高，就代表我们越需要去担心，就代表通胀在扩张开来；但是如果这组数据在下降的话，就代表通胀其实在收缩，就通胀的一个参与度其实在收缩，是一个好消息。

所以像我前面说的，如果在凯文沃什之后的一个讲话里面，他只关注一个 headline，他只关注通胀数据本身，那就是鹰派的讲话；如果他关注到参与度这一块，那就是一个鸽派的讲话。

六、合作推广：Seeking Alpha Alpha Picks

最后，今天的活动来自于 Seeking alpha alpha picks，一个量化选股策略。我把他们 YTD 和 since inception 从有这个策略到现在为止的走势汇报全部拿出来。

YTD 他们终于低于标普500的这个回报了。YTD 他们的回报8.3%，标普500是11.4%。那很多人可能会有一个疑问：那么他们 YTD 都没有跑赢标普，还有什么参考的一个意义在那边？

那有一点我想讲的是：无论什么样的一个策略，在一个时间段里边它一定会跑输市场的，这是没有办法所避免的一个结果。所以我在上周四直播的时候我也说过，在这个市场里边，我们时间久了之后，每一次下跌都是去检验自己方法的一个过程。我们找到一个能够经得起时间考验、然后经得起时间考验、能够验证是一个可行的策略，然后就针对着这个策略继续执行下去，stick to it。

不要在不同的时间段里面试图去用不同的策略，没有用的。这个市场里面没有人可以在市场下跌的时候去做空这一个市场，然后当市场开始出现长期上涨的时候就长持中间没有卖飞的一个过程，一定不可能。你只要在下跌的时候，你选择去探这个市场、选择卖出、选择去做空，我敢保证，比如说你在今年四五月份出现反弹的时候，中间一定有卖飞，不可能不卖飞。这就是盈亏同源。方法论也是一样，你用同样的一个方法，在下跌的时候你承担什么那个下跌幅度，你在上涨的时候就能够接受什么样的一个上涨幅度。

所以他们这个策略，我之所以 YTD 我不会隐隐蔽，就他们虽然 YTD 走得不好，但是我同样把他们 YTD 的一个走势拿出来和大家分享。但是你看他们 since inception，标普500上涨了101%、翻了一倍，他们这个策略本身上涨了296%。

另外在最近4个月之前，他们推出了一个同样另外一个量化选股策略，只是它针对的一个标的都是一些价值股板块。所以你看价值股板块，那过去就整个这一段时间以来上涨了12.8%，同期的指数只上涨了1.54%，那就是价值股板块明显在过去这一段时间表现出了一个相对强势。那当一个板块、当一个策略本身表现出了一个相对强势，那它这个量化选股策略自然的表现就会非常的好。而前面那一个量化选股策略，因为它所针对的一些标的可能是 Momentum 相关的，可能是和芯片相关的，所以走的就会相对弱一些。

所以第一个量化选股策略现在有免费的一个试用期，并且首年的订阅可以立即节省50美金。那如果大家对于这两个量化策略都感兴趣的话，现在有一个 combo 的价格，原价是998美金，现在是719美金。大家如果感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里边找到订阅的链接。

那今天这期内容就到这边，下期见。

## 一、信用利差与 VIX 的"认知分裂"：一场只有机构在参加的危机
小涛敏锐地抓住了垃圾债利差 3.37 已经逼近 2022 年 3 月水位这个事实，但他没有点破的是一个更诡异的现象——**信用市场在喊着"战争级压力"，而 VIX 却在往下走**。这种分裂几乎从不出现在健康的市场里。它意味着什么？
机构正在偷偷从后门撤出，而散户还在前门排队买入波动率的平静。信用利差是债券基金经理用真金白银投票的结果，VIX 是期权交易员对未来 30 天的押注。当这两者方向相反，历史上几乎总是**信用市场赢**——因为债券持有人掌握着企业的现金流信息，而股票期权交易员只是在交易情绪。
这里的意外洞察是：**AI 融资热潮本身正在成为一个"信用负债化事件"**。星云（CoreWeave 类）、OpenAI 的 1.4 万亿基建承诺、Oracle 发债买 GPU——这些故事表面上是"科技牛市"，但在债券市场的记账本里，它们是**非投资级信用供给的爆炸**。换句话说，AI 牛市正在制造自己的负债阴影，而这个阴影首先会在信用利差里显形，然后才会在股价里显形。
